en: **Imperial Preface to the Continued Record of the Lamp of Jianzhong Jinggu** [Song Dynasty Edition] In the past, when Śākyamuni Tathāgata appeared in the world, he received the prediction of Dīpaṃkara.

Born into the household of King Śuddhodana, he pointed his fingers toward heaven and earth, and the true mechanism [of enlightenment] was already revealed. He wandered through the gates of life and death, and his youthful conditions were suddenly [fulfilled].

Śākyamuni personally propagated the Way at the Kukkutārāma, spreading its fragrance upon Vulture Peak. Thus, the boundless realms of all lands appeared within the tip of a single hair, and the entire scripture of the great trichiliocosm was revealed from within a minute speck of dust.
To the west, it reached the land of India; to the east, it flowed into China (Zhendan).
When written by inscribing upon leaves, the holy teachings were transmitted to Ānanda in a single moment; when held as a flower with a smile, the True Dharma... [was entrusted].
The Eye-Treasury was already entrusted to Kāśyapa. Since the arrival of the Dharma from the West, he has truly been the First Patriarch.

Through the transmission of the second, third, fourth, and fifth [patriarchs], it reached Caoxi; thus, the Way of the Double-Tree Forest shone ever more brightly, and the flow of that single drop gradually spread wide.
From Nanyue and Qingyuan downward, it divided into five schools, each excelling in its own family style and responding to circumstances with appropriate answers.
Although their established methods differ, they ultimately converge upon a single truth; there are none whose sharp points do not meet like arrowheads, nor whose whips do not strike in unison.

In benefiting sentient beings and bringing them to awakening, they have been manifold. As the source and tributaries flow on and the branches and leaves spread wide, the two schools of Yunmen and Linji have come to flourish preeminently throughout the world. I, the Emperor, having received...
Heaven has bestowed its mandate, and he succeeds to the great sovereignty of the state.
We reverently reflect that the Founder, Emperor Yizu, opened the gateway of the Way throughout the vast realm,
and the Second Emperor, Taizong, elucidated the profound meaning across all under heaven.
Emperor Zhangsheng transmitted the lamp of the Dharma at Jingde, and Emperor Yongzao widely illuminated it at Tiansheng;
both extensively propagated the true wind and assisted in divine transformation to achieve a governance of non-action. How majestic!

The Divine Emperor was particularly devoted to the Empty School (the Mahāyāna). In the third year of the Yuánfēng era, he issued an imperial decree to establish two Chan monasteries at Dàxiàngguó Temple:
Huìlín was opened in the eastern wing, and Zhìhǎi was built along the right corridor.
Reaching the year of Rénxū, [he honored] the present Imperial Grand Princess and Zhāng [Shèng], the Commandery-Inspector and Retainer of the Jíqìng Military Command and Cavalry Commander-in-Chief.
At the request of Dunli, the Fayun Chan Temple was rebuilt in the south of the kingdom. Thereupon, the patriarchal seat shone with brilliance and the monastic groves flourished in prosperity;
those throughout the realm who donned the square robes and yearned for the joy of Chan gathered like clouds at the capital.

Now, Dunli has presented for imperial inspection the thirty fascicles of the *Jianzhong Jingguo Xudeng Lu* (Continued Lamp Record of the Jianzhong Jingguo Era), compiled by the presiding monk of his temple, Chan Master Weibai of Foguo.
He also requests a preface for this work. Weibai has explored the Supreme Vehicle and realized the First Principle;
he has frequently entered the inner palace and thrice ascended the high seat to proclaim the wondrous teachings, which is truly most satisfying.

I recall that in the past, when the Tathāgata Śākyamuni preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he emitted a ray of light from the white tuft between his eyebrows, illuminating eighteen thousand worlds in the eastern direction.
Thereupon, Maitreya posed questions and Mañjuśrī resolved the doubts; it was said that such was the original auspicious radiance of the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa.
The Dharma Master Varaprabha was one who upheld this sutra, and the Tathāgata Samantaprabha was one who attained its realization.
The title "Continuation of the Lamp" (Xu deng) signifies that lamps are transmitted from one to another and lights interpenetrate one another; the meaning lies precisely in this. Alas!
The perfectly clear ocean of awakening originally encompasses all ten directions, yet the empty bubbles of birth and death have consequently sunk into the three realms of existence.

Because of clarity, the objective world is established; because of sensory objects, cognition arises. Delusive falsehoods are woven together to form a continuous whole, leading beings to revolve through the various destinies—this is truly to be lamented.

If one turns the light inward to illuminate, giving rise to the true and returning to the source, then this is indeed the record. It points directly to the essence of the nature (xìngzōng) and transmits the seal of mind (xīnyìn) alone;
it may be attained within the space between the eyebrows and the eyelashes, and may be realized before a single word is spoken. Raising a hand, one upholds the world of Wondrous Joy;
snapping the fingers, one manifests the pavilions of adornment. Such applications of supernatural powers (shéntōng) are truly inconceivable.

How worthy of deliberation! I joyfully join with the multitude to establish this superior affinity, so that we may all leave the ford of delusion behind and proceed together upon the path to enlightenment.
This is my resolve. Written on the fifteenth day of the eighth month in the first year of the Jianguo era of Jianzhong Jingguo. Bestowed as a preface.
*Jianzhong Jingguo Xudeng Lu*, Scroll One.
Compiled by the Dharma-transmitting Chan Master Foguo, Abbot of Fayun Chan Temple in Dongjing, (Subject) Weibai,
for the Orthodox Lineage.

At that time, the World-Honored One had perfected the knowledge of all modes; having cultivated his traces through practice, his compassion was profound and his vows vast. He manifested birth in response to the world;

his nature was as pure as frost-flowers and his mind yearned for the Snowy Peaks. At midnight he leaped over the city wall and practiced meditative contemplation for six years, finally bathing in the Nairañjanā River.

He proceeded to the Bodhi tree, ascended the Vajrāsana, and spread the auspicious *kuśa* grass. He cultivated all meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) until the morning star appeared and he attained awakening, suddenly achieving perfect enlightenment.
With equal compassion for all sentient beings, for forty-nine years he made the Three Vehicles manifest. He universally demonstrated the teaching by holding up a flower.

When the initial smile was first transmitted, before the great assembly, he sealed the True Dharma Eye and charged it to be practiced outside the teachings, entrusting it separately to those of superior faculties.
With lotus eyes gazing universally, he personally spoke the Flower Verses.
The Dharma is fundamentally without Dharma; that which is without Dharma is also the Dharma.
Now, at this moment when the non-Dharma is transmitted, how has any dharma ever been a dharma?
At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa shared his seat and received the robe; he attained enlightenment through the flower and dwelt in a stone chamber within a mountain crag.

He expounded the Dharma to deliver sentient beings. When the World-Honored One manifested his parinirvāṇa, the holy teachings were compiled, and Ānanda was excluded because he had not yet exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*).
Before the Bimbā Rock, upon a flat stone slab, he sat until midnight and immediately realized the fruit of the Path. He then manifested supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*).
It penetrated through the stone. Thereupon Kāśyapa entrusted him with the Eye of the True Dharma and spoke this verse:
"Phenomenon after phenomenon is the fundamental Dharma; There is no phenomenon, nor is there any non-phenomenon.
Why, within a single phenomenon, Could there be both phenomenon and non-phenomenon?"
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda sat upon a rock and realized the Way. As he compiled the sacred words, the moment he uttered "Thus have I heard" once, his three doubts were instantly extinguished.
Having accomplished this great task, he sought a successor to the lineage. He went to the River Nairañjanā, which was transformed into a field of gold, and gathered the assembly of noble ones.
Looking toward his disciple who had attained the Way, Śāṇakavāsin, he entrusted him with the Eye of the True Dharma and spoke these verses:
The Dharma originally entrusted has been entrusted; having completed the entrustment, one speaks of the non-existence of the Dharma.
Each must awaken for themselves; once awakened, there is neither existence nor non-existence.
At that time, the Venerable Śāṇakavāsin, wearing natural robes, manifested birth and acted as a great caravan leader.
Suddenly realizing impermanence upon hearing that the Buddha had entered *parinirvāṇa*, he went forth under Ānanda and realized the fruit of the Path.
One day, seeing the elder’s son Upagupta, he asked him, "How old are you? Upagupta replied, "I am seventeen years old.
The Master said, "Is it your body that is seventeen, or is it your nature that is seventeen? Upagupta looked at the Master and asked, "But your hair is white."
"Is it that my hair has turned white? "No," said Upagupta, "my hair alone has turned white; my mind has not.

Kātyāyanīputra replied, "My body is seventeen years old, but my nature is not seventeen. Upagupta then conferred the precepts upon him and transmitted the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, speaking this verse:
Neither is it non-dharma, nor is it mind; there is no mind, nor is there any dharma.
When this teaching on the dharma of mind was spoken, this dharma was not a mental phenomenon.
At that time, the Venerable Upagupta had been ordained for seventeen years and had realized the fruit [of Arhatship] at twenty; he extensively delivered sentient beings.
The tally-sticks filled the stone chamber. There was a son of a householder named Gandhahastin who entered the order under a teacher.
The teacher then asked him, "Have you left home with your body, or have you left home with your mind? He replied, "My leaving home was not for the sake of body or mind. The teacher said:

"It is not for the sake of body or mind; who, then, would leave the household life? He replied, "As for one who has left the household life, because there is no self or 'mine,' the mind neither arises nor perishes.
That the mind neither arises nor perishes is itself the eternal Way. Since it is eternal, the Buddhas are also eternal. The fundamental nature of the mind is likewise so.
The Master said, "You have now attained great enlightenment. Your mind is naturally clear; you have realized it suddenly and completely."
He changed his name to Tiṭṭibha (or Dīdaka) and entrusted him with the Treasury of the Eye of the True Dharma, speaking these verses:
"The mind is itself the original mind; The original mind is not a dharma that exists.
Where dharmas exist, there is originally mind; It is neither mind nor original dharma."
At that time, the Venerable Tīṣya was born in response to auspicious omens: as the golden sun rose and shone, sweet springs gushed forth. This was indeed rare.

Having left the household life and attained the Way, he transmitted the Dharma and saved sentient beings. There was the Venerable Mucilinda, who, upon seeing his teacher’s compassionate countenance, immediately realized his past causes.
Abandoning his original arts of immortality, he sought the fruit of holiness and earnestly asked: "I, regarding the arts of immortality..."
The Way has no further progress; one merely maintains emptiness and stillness. [Māṭhara] did not yet penetrate the ultimate principle. The Master said, "The Buddha taught:

'Those who seek to become immortals and revere minor paths are like being pulled by a rope. You should know this for yourself. If you cast aside the small stream and immediately return to the great ocean of the Buddha-dharma, you will realize non-arising.
Upon hearing these words, Māṭhika suddenly realized the wondrous Way, and [the Master] immediately transmitted to him the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye.
And he spoke in verse:
"Penetrating the mind of the fundamental dharma, There is neither dharma nor non-dharma.
Realizing that awakening is the same as non-awakening, There is no mind and likewise no dharma."

At that time, the Venerable Mijia (Mecaka) abandoned his life as a rishi to join the Buddha, leaving the household life to realize the Way. While traveling to convert beings in Northern India, auspicious clouds appeared as omens.
There was one named Vasumitra, whose body was majestic and pure; holding a vessel of wine in his hand, he asked the Master:
"From where have you come? Where do you wish to go? The Master replied: "I have come from my own mind; I wish to go nowhere. He said:
"Do you recognize the object in my hand? The Master said, "This is a vessel for contact that has been rendered pure.
[The monk] said, "Do you recognize me? The Master said, "I do not recognize 'me. If it were recognized, it would not be 'me. You should state your name, and I shall know you. [The monk] said:
His surname was Bharadvāja and his name was Vasumitra. His teacher said, "The Buddha has prophesied that you shall succeed to the lineage of the Dhyāna patriarchs.
Thereupon, he abandoned his wine vessels and suddenly awakened to his past causes. He left the household life, received full ordination, and entered deeply into the Way of Awakening.
Mīzhéjiā (Mecaka) transmitted to him the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye and spoke this verse:
There is no mind that can be attained; what is spoken of cannot be called a dharma.
If one realizes that the mind is not the mind, only then does one understand the mind and mental phenomena.
At that time, the Venerable Vasumitra, reflecting upon his past karmic conditions, set aside his vessel and left the household life to travel through various kingdoms.
He extensively performed Buddha-works. There was one named Buddhānandi who said, "I now wish to debate the principles with the Venerable One.
The Master said, "Principles are not to be debated; debate is not the Way of Principles. If one intends to debate principles, it will ultimately not be a discussion of principles.

At these words, Buddhānandi attained self-awakening of the mind and immediately submitted with reverence, seeking to leave the household life under the Master, wishing to be saved and delivered. The Master knew that the time had come to transmit the Dharma.
He entrusted the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye and spoke this verse:
The mind is identical to the realm of empty space; It reveals dharmas equal to empty space.
When the realization of empty space is attained, There is neither "is" nor "is not."
At that time, the Venerable Buddhatrāta had a fleshy protuberance upon his crown, which was brilliantly translucent;
his wisdom was profound and deep, and his eloquence was swift and unimpeded. A certain Puṇyamitra asked him: "If parents are not my kin, who is the most intimate kin?
If the Buddhas are not my Way, who is the ultimate Way? The Master replied: "That which you speak of is more intimate than the heart; it is the Father."
The Mother is beyond comparison. Your practice is in harmony with the Way; the mind of all Buddhas is precisely this. To seek outwardly for a Buddha with form is not in accord with you.
If you wish to recognize your original mind, it is neither joined nor separate. Upon hearing these sublime verses, Vajra [said]:

He entered the Buddha-way instantaneously. Prostrating himself with his five limbs touching the ground, he rejoiced deeply within himself. [The Master] immediately granted him the tonsure and ordination, entrusted him with the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, and spoke this verse:
Space has neither interior nor exterior; the same is true for that which is outside the mind.
If one realizes the nature of space, then one penetrates the principle of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
At that time, the Venerable Puṇyamitra had been living for fifty years, sitting upon a single mat, never having spoken a word.

His feet did not touch the ground. Upon hearing a verse, he attained the Way. He transmitted the Dharma to benefit others; whenever there were those who encountered hardships and sought a teacher to leave the household life, he would immediately grant them the tonsure and ordination.
At the moment of the *karmavācanā*, auspicious light shone upward, and he further manifested *śarīra* relics as a sign of auspicious response.
He sat upright without reclining and practiced constant diligence. Having realized the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), he attained the fruit of the Way.
Entrusting him with the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, he spoke these verses:
Ultimate truth is originally nameless; it is through names that ultimate truth is revealed.
One receives the true Dharma, which is neither true nor false.
At that time, the Venerable Pārśva remained in the womb for sixty years. Through the divine response of a dream of a pearl, he was finally born, filling the room with light.
This radiance was not an ordinary omen. Having attained the fruit of the Way, he prioritized benefiting sentient beings. Upon arriving at a grove, the ground transformed into the color of gold.
Pūrṇaśāya approached the Master and stood with palms joined. The Master asked, "Where have you come from?
He replied, "My mind does not go. The Master asked, "Where do you dwell? He replied, "My mind does not stay. The Master questioned him further.
[The Master] said, "Are you not fixed? He replied, "All Buddhas are likewise. [The Master] asked, "Are you not all Buddhas? He replied, "All Buddhas are likewise not.
The Master, knowing him to be a vessel for the Dharma, transmitted the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye and spoke this verse:
The true essence is spontaneously real; because of this reality, there is a principle to be explained.
When one realizes the dharma of true reality, there is neither practice nor cessation.
At that time, the Venerable Pūrṇayaśas was clear-minded and broadly erudite; by nature he sought nothing, yet he encountered the Venerable Pārśva.
Having attained the Dharma, he traveled about converting and guiding others. The Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa asked him, "I wish to recognize the Buddha; what is it that is the Buddha?
The Master said, "If you wish to recognize the Buddha, that which you do not recognize is it. Aśvaghoṣa said, "If one does not recognize the Buddha, how can one know that it is so?"

The Master said, "Since you do not recognize it, how can you know that it is not so? Asangha said, "This is the meaning of the saw. The Master said, "That is the meaning of the wood. Asangha asked, "What is the meaning of the saw? The Master said, "It levels you out. Asangha asked, "What is the meaning of the wood? The Master said, "You have been cut by me. At these words, Asanga attained sudden and complete enlightenment. Consequently, the Master entrusted him with the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye and spoke this verse: The mind is originally pure; It is not produced by conditions. If one seeks it through conditions, One will never find it. When the mind is suddenly awakened, All dharmas are seen as they truly are. The Tathagata’s treasury of the eye of the true dharma Is now transmitted to you, Asanga. Do not let it be lost. Go forth and save sentient beings. Do not let the lineage be broken. Do not let the lamp go out. Do not let the teaching decline. Do not let the Buddha-dharma perish. Do not let the world be in darkness. Do not let the great ocean of suffering remain. Do not let the wheel of birth and death continue. Do not let the three realms be filled with sorrow. Do not let the four demons prevail. Do not let the five turbidities increase. Do not let the six paths be in distress. Do not let the seven treasures be lost. Do not let the eight winds blow. Do not let the nine orifices leak. Do not let the ten directions be obscured. Do not let the eleven organs be deluded. Do not let the twelve links of dependent origination arise. Do not let the thirteen abodes of ignorance persist. Due to delusion, it is like concealment and manifestation; light and darkness are not separate from one another.
Now I entrust this dharma of concealment and manifestation, which is neither one nor two.
At that time, the Venerable Aśvaghoṣa, by virtue of his superior merits of both conditioned and unconditioned deeds, heard the meaning of the wood and attained the Dharma.
He turned the sublime Wheel of Dharma. A great Māra King contended with the Master for power; he immediately manifested his true form, prostrated, and repented.
The Master asked, "What is your name? He replied, "My name is Kambala. The Master said, "Exert all your supernatural powers."
"What kind of transformation is this? he asked. [The monk] replied, "To transform the great ocean would not be difficult for me. The Master said, "Can you transform the ocean of nature (xinghai)?
He answered, "What is meant by the 'ocean of nature'? I have never known it. The Master said, "The ocean of nature is the mountains, rivers, and the great earth."
All are established upon this; through it, the three samādhis and six supernormal powers are manifested. Upon hearing these words, Kambala suddenly awakened and entered the ocean of nature.
He was then entrusted with the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, and he spoke this verse:
Manifestation and concealment are the fundamental Dharma; Brightness and darkness are originally non-dual.
Now I entrust this Dharma of realization, Which is neither grasped nor abandoned.
At that time, the Venerable Kambala had originally practiced as a non-Buddhist (tīrthika). Having turned his heart toward the Buddha Vehicle, he traveled through Western India.
Upon arriving at a deep mountain, the Venerable Nāgārjuna came out to welcome him and asked, "This deep mountain is solitary and secluded, a dwelling place for dragons and pythons.
Why has the Great Virtuous One, a most holy being, deigned to trouble his divine feet by coming here? The Master replied, "I am not a most holy being; I have come to visit a worthy man.
Nāgārjuna thought to himself, "Has this master attained the nature of certainty and clarified the eye of the Way? Is he a great sage who continues the True Vehicle?"
"No," the Master said. "Although you spoke with your mind, I have already known it by my own intent. Simply prepare for ordination; why worry about not becoming a sage?
Having heard this, Nāgārjuna repented and apologized. The Master immediately granted him ordination and transmitted the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, speaking these verses:
Neither hidden nor manifest phenomena—this is called the true limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
To awaken to these hidden and manifest phenomena is neither folly nor wisdom.
At that time, the Venerable Nāgārjuna possessed great wisdom and insight, there was nothing he did not penetrate, and he widely expounded the religious teachings throughout antiquity and the present.
"How rare! One day, Deva came to visit. The Master had his attendant bring a bowl filled to the brim with water and showed it to him.

Deva dropped a needle into it; he was delighted by this, as it perfectly accorded with the Master's intention. He immediately invited him to speak of the Way. Furthermore, [the Master] manifested the form of a full moon and showed it to him.
Furthermore, having realized the subtle intent and entrusted the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, he spoke this verse:
"To clarify the principle of concealment and manifestation, I shall now explain the logic of liberation:
When one does not realize [the truth] within the mind regarding phenomena, There is neither anger nor joy."
At that time, the Venerable Kanadeva was widely learned from his youth; his eloquence was versatile and profound, and his fame spread far and wide, such that he was highly esteemed by all nations.
Reflecting upon his own mind, he felt no shame whatsoever. He pierced the Way with the point of a needle and extensively benefited all living beings.
There was one named Rāhulabhadra who questioned his teacher regarding the causal conditions of a fungus growing on wood. The teacher showed him the way through a verse;

he was moved to realization by his past causes, left home under the teacher, and immediately realized the fruit of the Way. The teacher entrusted him with the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye and spoke this verse:
"To those who transmit the Dharma, I have explained the principle of liberation;
yet in the reality of the Dharma, there is nothing realized—neither end nor beginning.
At that time, the Venerable Rāhulata left the household life to transmit the Dharma, benefiting sentient beings wherever he went, until he arrived at Śrāvastī.
On a river of golden water within the city, Saṃghanandin was peacefully absorbed in meditative concentration (*samādhi*). He remained thus for seven days before finally arising from his trance.
The Master asked him, "Is your body in concentration, or is your mind in concentration? He replied, "Both my body and my mind are in concentration.

The Master said, "If both body and mind are in concentration, how can there be entering and emerging [from it]? He replied, "Although there is entering and emerging, I do not lose the characteristics of concentration (*samādhi-lakṣaṇa*). The Master said, "Since..."

He lost the characteristics of meditative concentration. [The Master asked: "What is it that moves or is still? He replied, "Movement and stillness are not things; things are not movement or stillness. The Master said, "This meaning is not so.

After several rounds of questioning and cross-examination, his words were exhausted and his arguments defeated. His mind became suddenly clear; he bowed his head in refuge and immediately grasped the profound essence.
Consequently, the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye was entrusted to him, and he spoke this verse:
In the reality of dharmas, there is nothing to be realized; one neither grasps nor abandons them.
Since dharmas possess neither the mark of existence nor non-existence, how could they arise internally or externally?
At that time, the Venerable Saṃghanandin, who was the Prince Ratnavyūha, was able to speak from birth and constantly offered praise.

The Buddha’s work was such that he caused his mother not to have faith [in other teachings]. Later, he practiced *dhyāna* and *samādhi*. When the time came for him to succeed to the Patriarchate, he was finally transmitted the Mind-Seal (*citta-mudrā*) and extensively transformed sentient beings.
There was a young boy who held a precious mirror and approached the Master to leave the household life, serving as his attendant.

Once, when the wind blew and the bronze bells atop the hall rang out, the Master asked, "Is it the wind that sounds, or are the bells that sound? The boy replied, "It is neither the wind nor the bells that sound."
"I hear my own heart," [the student] said. The Master asked, "And who is it that hears the heart? He replied, "Because both are utterly tranquil. The Master said, "Excellent! Excellent!
You have truly attained the principle of the Buddha. Thereupon, he transmitted the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye and spoke this verse:
The mind-ground is fundamentally without birth; the ground of practice arises from conditions.
The seeds of conditions do not obstruct one another, and the flowers and fruits are likewise so.
At that time, the Venerable Gayāsīta took up a mirror and left the household life; upon hearing the sound of a bell, he realized the Way. Thereupon, he traveled through various kingdoms.
While he was seeking an heir by contemplating his vital breath (*prāṇa*), Kumāralāta saw him and asked, "Who are you, Master?
The Master replied, "I am a disciple of the Buddha. Upon hearing these words, Kumāralāta’s spirit was struck with awe; he returned home, shut the doors, and remained within.
The Master then slowly approached and knocked on the door. Kumāralāta answered, "There is no one in this house. The Master said, "If there is no one, who is it that speaks? Kumāralāta...
Dahuhu suddenly attained awakening; he must have been a man of wisdom. He opened the door to pay his respects, distinguished the dog from the gold, and thereby attained the fruit of the Way.
The Treasury of the True Dharma Eye was entrusted to him, and he spoke this verse:
There exists a seed within the ground of the mind; through causes and conditions, it is able to sprout.
When conditions do not obstruct one another, that which was to arise does not arise.
At that time, the Venerable Kumāralāta, having been born as a sovereign deity (Īśvara), possessed sharp faculties for hearing the Dharma; the time had come for him to succeed to the Patriarchate.
He descended into the human realm, verified his attainment of the fruit through the test of gold, and brought salvation to all classes of beings.
Once, Śāṇakavāsin asked him: "In my family we have faith in the Buddha, yet we are constantly beset by illness and suffering. Our neighbors, the Caṇḍālas, achieve everything they desire.

Why are they so fortunate, while what fault do I possess? The Master said: "Why is there need for such doubt? Furthermore, the retribution for good and evil spans three lifetimes. You see that the benevolent die young and the violent..."
Longevity [brings] misfortune when opposed to righteousness; thus one loses the cause and forfeits the fruit, vainly incurring guilt and blame.
Little do they realize that cause and effect correspond like shadows and echoes, without the slightest deviation, remaining undestroyed even throughout hundreds of thousands of kalpas.

Upon hearing these words, Śāṇakavāsin was suddenly released from his doubts and deeply awakened to the principles of karma. Resolving to seek renunciation, he shaved his head and received the precepts before the Jewel Stūpa, whereupon the Buddha emitted—
Kāśyapa, I now entrust to you the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, and speak this verse:
In the ultimate nature, there is originally no arising; The Dharma was taught only to meet the needs of seekers.
Since nothing can be attained, Why harbor doubts regarding what is or is not resolved?
At that time, the Venerable Śāṇakavāsin possessed a profound and deep wisdom and guided immeasurable beings. He extensively promoted Buddhist activities throughout the city of Rājagṛha.
There was a man named Bāṣpa who constantly ate but once a day and never lay down to sleep; he performed prostrations and recitations during the six periods of the day.

When the Master saw him, he asked, "Though your diligence is such as this, you are far from the Way. Even if you pass through kalpas as numerous as dust motes, it will all remain rooted in falsehood. Bāṣpa replied:
"What virtues do you, Master, possess that you should criticize me? The Master replied, "I do not seek the Way, yet I am not deluded.
I do not prostrate to the Buddha, yet I do not treat him with contempt. I do not sit in perpetual meditation, yet I am not indolent.
I do not eat only once a day, yet I do not eat at irregular times. I am not content with little, yet I have no craving. My mind has no expectations; therefore, it is called the Way. Vāśpa.

Having heard the Master’s instruction, he gave rise to untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*). He recounted his past causes and conditions and transmitted the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, speaking these verses:
"Under these words, one accords with the non-arising [of phenomena], Identical to the nature of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*)."
If one can understand in this way, having thoroughly mastered both phenomena and principle,
at that time the Venerable Pauṣkarasādi— who had received a prediction while in the womb that he would surely become a lamp for the world— grew up practicing asceticism.
Having attained the fruit of the Way, he traveled to the kingdom of Nādi. There, the prince Maṇḍara joined the Master as a renunciant;

he acquired great supernormal powers and suddenly awakened to the essence of the Mind. He was destined to succeed to the Patriarchal seat and transmit the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, whereupon he spoke this verse:
Bubbles and illusions are equally unimpeded;
how could one fail to awaken to the fact that all dharmas are contained therein?

Neither now nor in the past—then the Venerable Mañjula, renouncing the pleasures of the royal palace, left the home life to realize the Way. With the fragrance of faith as an auspicious omen, he departed.
In the country of Yuezhi, there was a man named Helena who asked, "Why is the dragon’s son so intelligent, and why do the flock of cranes feel such devotion?
The Master explained their past causes; immediately, their minds were awakened. He asked again, "What karma should I now cultivate so that this flock of cranes may eventually attain human bodies?
The Master said, "The Buddha possesses the unsurpassed Dharma-treasure, which has been transmitted from one to another. I now entrust it to you; you should [preserve it]."
Believe and accept this; let it not be severed, but widely deliver all sentient beings. Thereupon, the flock of cranes attained liberation.
He entrusted them with the Treasury of the Eye of the True Dharma and spoke these verses:
The mind turns following the myriad objects; where it turns is truly profound and mysterious.
If one recognizes one's nature while following the flow, there will be neither joy nor sorrow.
At that time, when the Venerable Harelana was born, celestial flowers scattered like colorful silks and gold coins were spread upon the ground. He was raised by the King.
At the palace, he extensively manifested divine transformations. Later, he left the household life to transmit the Dharma, guiding sentient beings toward enlightenment wherever he went.
A bhikṣu named Siṃha asked him, "I wish to seek the Way; how should I apply my mind? The Master said, "If you seek the Way, do not apply your mind to anything.
Siṃha asked, "If there is no application of the mind, who performs the Buddha-work? The Master said, "If there is an application of the mind, it is not a meritorious deed."
"If there is no application of mind, that itself is the work of the Buddha. Upon hearing this, Śiṃha attained immediate enlightenment.
The treasury of the true Dharma-eye was then entrusted to him, and he spoke these verses:
When one recognizes the nature of mind, it can be described as inconceivable;
it is clearly manifest and nothing can be grasped. At that moment of realization, there is no "knowing" to speak of.
At that time, the Venerable Siṃha taught the Dharma to the five assemblies, guiding and transforming them; his fame spread far and wide among humans and devas.
They were filled with reverence. An elder was leading his son by the hand when the boy prostrated with one fist clenched. The Master asked, "Give me back my pearl.

The boy immediately opened his hand and presented the pearl. The assembly was all struck with wonder. The Master explained the prior causes and conditions in detail, and immediately ordained him as a monk, naming him Vāśeṣṭha.
Intending to repay his former debt, the Master entrusted him with the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye and spoke this verse:
It is said:
When speaking of the knowledge and vision, both knowledge and vision are the mind;
when the mind is present, there is knowledge and vision; knowledge and vision are right here and now.
At that time, the Venerable Vasiṣṭha’s mother dreamed of a divine sword and immediately became pregnant.

Once he was born, he met the Venerable Siṃha, who revealed his past causes and secretly transmitted the mind-seal to him. He then traveled to the kingdom of South India, where he subdued and defeated the non-Buddhists.
The King’s Crown Prince, Amṛtodana, went forth into homelessness under a teacher. The teacher asked him, "You wish to go forth;
for what purpose do you do so? The prince replied, "I now go forth not for the sake of that. The teacher said, "If it is not for the sake of that..."

"For what reason have you left the household life? The Prince replied, "My leaving the household life is itself the work of a Buddha. The Master asked, "If it is the work of a Buddha, what should one do?
The Prince replied, "To do nothing at all is the true work of a Buddha. The Master sighed in admiration, saying, "The Prince’s wisdom is as sublime as the heavens;
he must surely be an incarnation of a holy sage. He then conferred upon him full ordination (*upasampadā*). At that moment, the great earth shook, and miraculous wonders appeared.
"Very much so. I entrust to you the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye," he said, and spoke these verses:
"The Sages speak of knowledge and vision; Within the objective realm, there is neither right nor wrong.
I have now awakened to true nature: There is no path, and there is no principle."
At that time, the Venerable Rāhula relinquished his status as a crown prince and entered the monastic life under the Venerable [Śākyamuni].
Transmitting the Dharma to benefit sentient beings, he traveled to Eastern India. There was a son of a Brahmin who wandered through the streets and alleys without a fixed destination.
The Master asked him, "Why do you walk so hurriedly? He replied, "Why does the Master walk so slowly? The Master asked, "What is your surname now? He replied, "It is the same as the Master's."
Regarding his surname, the Master asked, "Do you remember past events? He replied, "I recall that in a distant kalpa, I lived together with you.
The Master asked, "What did we do together? He replied, "You expounded the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, and I recited the profound *Sūtras*.
The Master said, "What you have discussed today deeply accords with our former causes. He was immediately ordained and given the name Prajñātara, and the Dharma was entrusted to him.
The Treasury of the Dharma-Eye spoke in verse:
"The treasury of the true nature of the mind-ground has neither beginning nor end;
responding to conditions to transform sentient beings, it is expediently called wisdom."
At that time, after the Venerable Prajñātāra had received the Dharma, he traveled to South India to propagate the teaching.
He was held in high esteem by Prince Yu of the kingdom, who offered him a precious jewel as a gift. The Master then questioned them, each to state their understanding;
only Bodhidhara said: "This is but a worldly treasure; it is not sufficient to be considered supreme. Among all treasures, the Treasure of the Dharma is supreme."
This is the light of the world; it is not yet supreme. Among all lights, the light of wisdom is supreme.
This is the clarity of the world; it is not yet supreme. Among all clarities, the clarity of the mind is supreme. This is the jewel of the world; it is not yet definitive as supreme.
Among all jewels, the wish-fulfilling jewel (cintāmaṇi) is supreme. If the master possesses the Way, that treasure will immediately appear. The master asked again:
"Among all things, what thing is the characteristic? He replied: "Among all things, non-arising is the characteristic of the signless. The master said:
"Among all things, which is the highest? He replied, "Among all things, the self (ātman) is the highest. The Master asked, "Among all things, which is the greatest?
He replied, "Among all things, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is the greatest. Having seen that his answers were so refined and profound, the Master immediately granted him the tonsure.
Thereupon, the sun and moon appeared in white radiance, and the earth shook in three ways; he then realized the state of sainthood (arhatship).
The Fruit. Entrusting the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, he spoke this verse:
"The seeds of all things arise from the ground of the mind; Through causes and conditions, both phenomena and principle, The fruit ripens and Bodhi is perfected;
When the flower blooms, the world arises."
At that time, the Venerable Bodhidharma, the First Patriarch of the Tang land, was the third prince of the King of South India.
Having offered his pearls and clarified the meaning, he illuminated the nature of the mind and attained immediate penetration into the reality of all dharmas.

When the time arrived to transmit the Dharma, he traveled far to this land. The Emperor of Liang did not accord with him, so he sat facing a wall at Shaolin. There, the Dharma Master Shenguang stood [before him].
Huike severed his arm in snow. Resolutely seeking the essential path of all Buddhas, the Master changed his name to Huike.
One day, he asked: "May I hear the Dharma-seal of all Buddhas? The Master said: "The Dharma-seal of all Buddhas is not obtained from another.

Huike said: "I beg the Master to pacify my mind. The Master said: "Bring forth your mind, and I will pacify it for you. Huike said: "When I search for the mind, it cannot be found. The Master said: "..."

"It does not fall into emptiness. The Master asked, "By what means do you realize that it does not fall into emptiness? He replied, "It is vividly clear; there is neither sensation nor cognition.
The Master said, "So it is. So it is. As the Master was about to return to the Western Heaven (India), he instructed his disciples, saying, "Each of you state your realization;
I wish to entrust my robe and bowl as a token of proof. Dao Fu said, "As for me..."
[The Master asked: "What do you see? [She replied: "I do not cling to words and letters, nor am I separated from them, yet I take them as the functioning of the Way.
The Master said: "You have obtained my skin. Nini Zongchi said: "As I see it, it is like Ānanda seeing the land of Akṣobhya Buddha;
having seen it once, one does not see it again. The Master said: "You have obtained my flesh. Daoyu said: "As I see it, the four great elements are fundamentally empty, and the five [aggregates]..."
"The aggregates do not exist; not a single dharma can be apprehended. Master [Bodhidharma] said, "You have attained my bones.

Huike performed three final prostrations and stood in his place. The Master said, "You have attained my marrow," and subsequently entrusted him with the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, speaking these verses:
"I originally came to this land to transmit the Dharma and save those lost in delusion;
one flower blooms and five petals unfold, and the fruiting will naturally be accomplished.
At that time, the Second Patriarch Huìkē, the Chan Master Pǔjué of the True Lineage, stood in the snow and severed his arm, receiving the bowl and the robe.

Continuing the propagation of the profound Dharma, he widely sought a successor in the Dharma. There was a lay practitioner who came to pay his respects and asked, "I, your disciple, have long been entangled in chronic illness;
I beg the Master to repent for my transgressions on my behalf. The Master said, "Bring forth your transgressions, and I shall repent for them with you.

After a long silence, the layman said, "I search for the nature of transgression, but it cannot be found. The Master said, "I have finished repenting for your transgressions. You should now abide by the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha."
Jū said, "Today I have come to know what this Sangha is, but I do not yet understand what is meant by 'Buddha-dharma'. The Master said, "This very mind is the Buddha;
this very mind is the Dharma. The Dharma and the Buddha are non-dual; so too is the Jewel of the Sangha.

The Layman said, "For the first time, my disciple understands that the nature of sin is neither within, nor without, nor in between. As it is with the mind, so it is with the Buddha-dharma: they are non-dual."
The Master held him in high esteem and said, "You are my treasure; you should be named Sengcan.
He then shaved his head and transmitted to him the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, speaking these verses:
Originally, there is no ground because of conditions; Because of the ground, flowers grow from seeds.
Originally, there were no seeds; The flowers have likewise never grown.

At that time, the Third Patriarch, Meditation Master Sengcan of Jingzhi, attained the Way through the repentance of his transgressions. He shaved his head and received the robe, following conditions as they arose.
He benefited others, dwelling in no fixed place. A śrāmaṇera named Daoxin saw the Master and asked, "Please grant me the Dharma-gate of liberation.
The Master said, "Who has bound you? He replied, "No one has bound me. The Master said, "Since no one has bound you, what liberation do you seek?
At these words, Daoxin attained great enlightenment. He served the Master for nine years, after which he was entrusted with the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, and the Master spoke this verse:
Although the seeds of flowers depend upon the earth, and from the earth the flowers and seeds grow, if there is no one to sow the seeds, neither flowers nor earth will ever produce anything.
At that time, the Fourth Patriarch Daoxin, the Great Physician Chan Master, was born with extraordinary qualities; he suddenly realized the essence of the Way and attained profound understanding.
The gates of liberation were as if long-practiced; having continued the ancestral tradition, he was about to seek one to inherit the Dharma.

On the road to Huangmei, he saw a young boy whose skeletal features were remarkably refined and extraordinary compared to ordinary children. The Master saw him and asked, "What is your surname? He replied:
“Surname” indeed exists, yet it is not a permanent surname. The Master asked, “What is this surname? He replied, “It is Buddha-nature. The Master said, “You have no Buddha-nature.
He replied, “Because Buddha-nature is empty, I say that there is none. The Master recognized him as a vessel for the Dharma and appointed him as his attendant.
Later, he entrusted him with the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, speaking these verses:
The seeds of flowers possess the nature of arising; Depending on the ground, the flowers arise.
When the great conditions unite with the nature, Then arising becomes non-arising.
At that time, the Fifth Patriarch, Grand Master Hongren Daman, was a child who had attained the Way. He was later known as Daozhe, the Planter of Pines.
Dongshan resided at Mount Huangmei and greatly propagated the profound wind of the Dharma. A layman named Lu came from afar; the Master asked him, "Where have you come from?
He replied, "I have come from Lingnan. The Master asked, "For what purpose have you come? He replied, "I have come to seek to become a Buddha."
The Master said, "As a person from Lingnan, you have no Buddha-nature. He replied, "People may be from the north or the south, but how could Buddha-nature have a north or a south?
The Master rebuked him, saying, "Go to the fodder shed! He immediately entered the millhouse and performed labor at the pestle and mortar, with a stone hanging from his waist.

Day and night without ceasing, the time arrived for the transmission of the robe. He then summoned him into the room and said to him: "The appearance of all Buddhas in the world is for the sake of the one great matter.
The unsurpassed, wondrous Dharma is truly perfect and luminous. I now entrust it to you; you must protect and uphold it well, lest it be severed.
Then he spoke this verse:
Sentient beings originally plant seeds; because there is ground, fruit arises again.
Insentient things have no seeds; lacking intrinsic nature, they do not arise.
At that time, the Sixth Patriarch, Zen Master Huineng of Dajian, heard the sutra while selling firewood and attained sudden enlightenment regarding the Seal of the Mind. He traveled far...

Huangmei sought his secret realization and was consequently entrusted with the robe and bowl. He remained in seclusion at Huaiji, where, through the discourse on the wind and the banner, he brought forth the Great Matter.
Monastics and laypeople alike took refuge in him; dragons and devas gazed up in reverence. He expounded the Unsurpassed Vehicle and delivered immeasurable multitudes.

Those who encountered him were awakened, attaining a profound and hidden resonance with the truth, like seasonal rain universally moistening all things. As he was about to return to the ultimate reality, he then announced:
The assembly said, "Your faculties of faith are fully matured; you are resolute and free from doubt. The robe and bowl shall not be transmitted; each of you shall undertake the great task.
Those who follow my practice will certainly realize the fruit of sainthood. He then addressed the great assembly and spoke these verses:
The mind-ground contains all seeds; When rained upon universally, they all sprout.
Once the nature of the flower has been awakened to, The fruit of Bodhi is spontaneously realized.
Chan Master Huairang of Nanyue arrived at Caoxi. The Patriarch asked him, "Where have you come from? The Master replied:
[The Master] said, "I have come from the presence of National Teacher An of Mount Song. The Patriarch asked, "What thing comes in such a manner?
After eight years, one day the Master suddenly attained realization and told the Patriarch, "To describe it as a single thing is not to hit the mark.

The Patriarch asked, "Is there still any need for cultivation and realization? The Master replied, "Cultivation and realization are not non-existent; it is simply that there is no defilement. The Patriarch said, "Just this..."
"Unpolluted and protected by the mindfulness of all Buddhas, you are thus now;
I am thus; the twenty-eight patriarchs of the Western Heaven were thus; and the six patriarchs of the Tang land were thus.
Prajñātāra prophesied that from beneath your feet would emerge a colt that would trample the people of the world underfoot. You must guard and uphold this well. Later, he resided at Mount Nanyue.
He transmitted the Eye of the True Dharma.
Master Xingsi of Qingyuan Mountain in Luling went to Caoxi to pay his respects to the Patriarch.
He asked, "What should one apply oneself to in order to avoid falling into the gradual stages? The Patriarch replied, "What have you been doing? The Master said:

The Patriarch said, "Even the Noble Truths are not to be practiced. The Master said, "To what stage or rank would one then fall? The Patriarch said, "Since even the Noble Truths are not to be practiced, what stage or rank could there be?
The Patriarch said, "So it is! So it is! You must preserve and uphold this well. Although the disciples at Caoxi are many, you shall be foremost among them.
Later, he returned to Qingyuan Mountain to propagate this matter and transmit the True Dharma Eye.
While Master Dashi Ma of Jiangxi was sitting in his hut, Monk Rang asked him, "What are you doing here?

The Master replied, "I am practicing *zazen*. Rang asked, "What do you hope to achieve by practicing *zazen*? The Master said, "To become a Buddha. After a short while, Rang took a brick and began polishing it in front of the hut.

The Master asked, "What are you polishing the brick for? Rang replied, "I am polishing the brick to make a mirror. The Master said, "If you polish a brick to make a mirror, how can you sit in meditation to become a Buddha?"

[The Master] said, "How can you expect to produce a mirror by polishing a tile? Huairang replied, "If polishing a tile cannot produce a mirror, how can you expect to become a Buddha by sitting in meditation?
The Master rose in alarm and asked, "What then is the way? Huairang said, "If you practice meditation, meditation is neither sitting nor lying down.
If you practice as a Buddha, a Buddha is not a fixed form. It is like a person driving a cart: if the cart does not move,"

"Whether driving a cart is it, or driving an ox is it. The Master suddenly attained sudden enlightenment. He served [the teacher] for ten years, and his understanding became increasingly subtle and profound.
Later, while in Jiangxi, he propagated the True Dharma Eye everywhere.
Chan Master Xituan of Shitou on Mount Nanyue went to the Sixth Patriarch to shave his head.

Having received the patriarch’s instructions, he contemplated them for three years before finally awakening to their meaning. He went directly to Qingyuan, where Master Si asked him, "Where have you come from?
The Master replied, "From Caoxi. Si asked, "What did you gain upon reaching Caoxi? The Master said, "Even before reaching Caoxi, I had nothing."
Huangbo said, "I once lost it. Mazu said, "If that is so, why did you go to Caoxi? Huangbo said, "If I had not gone to Caoxi, how would I have known it was not lost?
Mazu said, "Though elephant horns may be many, a single unicorn's horn suffices. Later, he resided at Mount Nanyue and transmitted the True Dharma Eye.

One day, Chan Master Baizhang Huaihai of Hongzhou, the Great Wise One, was walking in a field with Master Mazu when they saw some wild ducks. The Master asked, "What is that? The Master replied, "Wild ducks. Shortly thereafter, the ducks flew away. The Master asked again, "Where have they gone? The Master replied, "They have flown away. The Master said, "You do not even know where they have gone; how can you claim to understand the Way? At these words, the Master was greatly enlightened. He immediately returned to the monastery and said to the assembly, "In the past, I thought I had attained something, but today I have finally realized it is not so. From that time on, he never again spoke of the Dharma. Later, he composed a verse which says: "In the vast expanse of the great void, There is no north or south. The Master said, "Where have you gone? The Master replied, "I flew away. The Master pinched the Master's nose, and the Master made a cry of pain.
The Master said, "And yet you say you flew away. Thereupon, the Master attained realization. Later, he resided at Baiyang.
Transmitting the True Dharma Eye:
Zen Master Daowu of Tianhuang in Lizhou first studied under Zen Master Guoyi of Mount Jing, and subsequently visited the seat of the Great Master Mazu;
in both cases, he attained realization of the essential core of the mind. Later, he went to Shitou and asked: "Setting aside concentration and wisdom, by what dharma..."
He showed this to the people. Shitou said, "I have no servants here; what is there to be separated from? The Master asked, "How can one understand this?
Shitou said, "Can you grasp empty space? The Master said, "If that is so, then I shall not go from here today.
Shitou said, "When did you ever come from 'that side'? The Master said, "Daowu is not a person from 'that side'."
Shitou said, "I already know where you have come from. The Master said, "Why do you frame me with false charges? Shitou said, "Your body is right here.
The Master said, "Even though this is so, how ultimately will you show it to future generations? Shitou said, "Who is the 'future generation'?
From this point on, the Master attained sudden enlightenment. Later, he resided at Tiantong and transmitted the True Dharma Eye.
When Chan Master Xiyun of Huangbo in Junzhou first visited Baizhang, he asked, "Master, you studied under Mazu; what was the karmic connection there?
Baizhang recounted the circumstances of his second visit to Mazu. Upon hearing this, the Master involuntarily stuck out his tongue. Baizhang said, "What are you doing?"
The Master said, "Today, because of you, I have seen the great function of Master Ma’s great capacity. Baizhang asked, "Will you, in the future, receive the Dharma-lineage of Master Ma?
The Master replied, "I do not know Master Ma. If I were to succeed him, I fear it would cause the loss of my own descendants.
Baizhang said, "So it is! So it is! Thereafter, the mutual resonance between master and disciple was manifold. He resided at Huangmei...
Yeshan. Regarding the transmission of the True Dharma Eye:
One day, Chan Master Longtan Chongxin of Lizhou asked National Teacher (Tianhuang) Huairang, "I, your disciple, have served you for a long time, yet I have not received your instruction.
The National Teacher said, "Every day there is no lack of instruction. The Master asked, "In what way?"
This was a pointing-out instruction. The Emperor said, "If you bring me tea, I shall receive it from you; if you perform a bow, I shall simply raise my hand.
Thereupon, the Master attained awakening. Later, he resided at Longtan and transmitted the True Dharma Eye.
When Chan Master Linji Yixuan first visited Huangbo at Zhentufu, he asked about the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma.
He posed this question three times, and each time Huangbo struck him with sixty blows of the staff. Later, when he went to Dayu, he recounted these circumstances.

Dayu said, "Huangbo possesses such a compassionate and skillful heart. At that moment, the Master suddenly attained sudden enlightenment; he then returned to serve Huangbo. Subsequently, he went to He...
In the north, he propagated the teachings and transmitted the Eye of the True Dharma.
Zen Master Xuanjian of Deshan in Dingzhou was attending upon Longtan when he stood in service. Deep into the night, as it grew dark, Longtan lit a paper candle and gave it to the Master.
As soon as the Master took it, Longtan blew it out. The Master suddenly attained great enlightenment and prostrated himself before Longtan. Longtan said:
[The Master] asked, "What principle have you seen? The Master replied, "From this day forward, I shall no longer doubt the tongues of all the old monks under heaven.

The next day, Longtan addressed the assembly, saying, "Among them there is a man whose teeth are like sharp swords, whose eyes are like shooting stars, whose mouth is like a blood basin, and whose face is like black lacquer. He cannot be turned back by a single blow of the staff; in the future..."
He built a thatched hermitage atop a solitary peak facing the sun; there he reviled the Buddhas and scolded the Patriarchs before departing. The Master immediately burned his texts and set out.
Later, he resided at Deshan and transmitted the True Dharma Eye.
Chan Master Xinghua Cunjian of Weifeng first studied under Linji and attained enlightenment. Later, he encountered Dajue, who struck him twenty blows;

through this, he realized the circumstances of Linji’s own studies under Huangbo. Subsequently, he emerged from seclusion to reside at Xinghua, where he became a successor to Linji and transmitted the True Dharma Eye.
Chan Master Yicun of Xuefeng in Fuzhou went up to Dongshan nine times and visited Touzi three times before finally arriving at Deshan.
There, the karmic affinity between master and disciple was established. One day, he asked, "By what Dharma do the sages of antiquity instruct people?

Deshan struck him with a staff and said, "Say something! At that moment, the Master attained sudden enlightenment, as if the bottom had fallen out of a bucket. He then proceeded to Aoshan, where Yantou served as his witness.
Flowing forth from his own breast, it was capable of covering both heaven and earth. Later, he returned to Xuefeng and transmitted the True Dharma Eye.
Chan Master Huiyong of Nanyuan at Baoying in Ruzhou visited Master Xinghua; he attained great enlightenment into the profound principle and entered into a secret resonance with the patriarchal style.

In responding to stimuli like the "cracking" and "pecking," and in the mutual exchange of host and guest, he confronted opponents with such brilliance that he stood alone as the preeminent figure among all quarters. He resided there...
At the Nanyuan Dharma Hall, the True Dharma Eye was transmitted.
Chan Master Yunmen Wenyan of Shaoyou first studied under the venerable elder Chen of Muzhou, where he realized the ground of his own mind.
He subsequently entered the Lingnan region to study under Xuefeng. One day, upon ascending the hall, a monk asked, "What is the Buddha? Xuefeng replied, "Heaven! (Cangtian).

"O Heavens! Upon hearing these words, the Master suddenly resolved his doubts and realized the essential point of the school. Later, the ruler of Guang, the Liu clan, invited him to reside at Yunmen, where he transmitted the True Dharma Eye.
When Chan Master Yanzhao of Fengxue in Ruizhou first visited Jingqing, he realized the meaning of the Patriarchs. Later, he visited Nanyuan.
As soon as the Master reached the gate, Nanyuan said, "Upon entering the gate, one must discern the host. The Master said, "I ask the Master to distinguish this for me definitively.
Nanyuan struck his knee with his left hand; the Master then shouted. Nanyuan struck his knee with his right hand; the Master shouted again. Nanyuan then raised his left hand.
[The Master] said, "In this place, I follow you. He raised his right hand and asked, "What about that place? The Master said, "Blind! The Abbot took up his staff.
The Master said, "Take away the staff and beat the Abbot; do not say I did not warn you.

The Abbot said, "I have been the abbot for thirty years, yet today I have been brought low by this yellow-faced man from Zhejiang. The Master said, "The Abbot is much like one who holds a bowl but does not know how to eat."

[The Master] attained [enlightenment]. He feigned hunger. The Abbot asked, "Have you ever been to this place? The Master said, "What kind of talk is that? The Abbot said, "I am asking you for certain.
The Master said, "I cannot let you off the hook either. The Abbot said, "Sit for a moment and drink some tea. The Master then performed a prostration.
Thereafter, he succeeded to the ancestral style, fulfilling the prediction of Miao-yang (Baizhang), greatly shaking up the patriarchal mechanism, and transmitting the True Dharma Eye.
Chan Master Shengnian of Shou Mountain in汝州 (Ruzhou) traveled extensively to study under various masters and constantly recited the *Lotus Sūtra*.
Upon arriving at the assembly of Fengxue, one day he encountered the master ascending the hall. Fengxue addressed the assembly, saying: "The World-Honored One did not speak what is spoken;

Kāśyapa did not hear what is heard. After a long silence, he descended from the seat. The Master [Shengnian] said, "This is the sudden realization of the essence of the mind," and thereupon entered the room to present his understanding in full detail.
[Zhaozhou] realized it. Fengxue asked again, "The World-Honored One did not speak what was spoken; Kāśyapa did not hear what was heard. How do you understand this?
The Master said, "Moving one's countenance to reveal the ancient path, without falling into the trap of silent stillness. Fengxue approved of him.
Later, he resided at Shoushan and transmitted the True Dharma Eye.

Chan Master Shanzhao of Taizi Yuan in Fenzhou was a native of Taiyuan. Having cultivated his studies through long-accumulated exposure to the teachings, he stood out with a singular character that transcended the mundane.

He discarded worldly adornments upon receiving full ordination and traveled on foot to visit various regions. He stayed briefly wherever he went, responding to questions as they arose according to the capacity of his interlocutors.

He studied under more than seventy spiritual mentors (*kalyāṇamitra*), and finally received the seal of approval from Chan Master Nian of Ruzhou. From this point on, his reputation became widely known.
Monastics and laypeople alike looked up to him with admiration, inviting him eight times in succession, yet he declined each time.

In the fourth year of the Chunhua era, a thousand monastics and laypeople welcomed him to Xihe, where he finally settled at this monastery. His conduct was strict and his teachings were profound; his subtle principles were difficult to grasp.

Those whom he certified as having attained realization all became vessels for the Way. His virtue and reputation spread far and wide, his fame reaching the capital. Lord Li, the Commandant, invited him to reside in Lu.
The Prefecture received the news from heaven. The officials and commoners of that region shed tears and blocked the way to detain him.

The Master said to the special envoy, "Go briefly to the refectory; after you have finished eating, take the letter. When the envoy arrived there, the Master had not yet risen from his seat, for he had already entered parinirvāṇa.

After the cremation, the śarīra relics were collected and a stūpa was erected. Throughout his life, the Master had read the Tripitaka six times and composed ten treatises summarizing the essential points of the school.
The remaining details regarding his responses to various sentient beings and circumstances are fully recorded in his own biography.
A monk asked, "When the mind-ground is not yet at peace, what should one do? The Master said, "Who is disturbing you? The monk said, "What can be done about this very thing?"

The Master said, "One who acts receives the consequences themselves. A monk asked, "How is it when a student has not yet attained awakening? The Master said, "Who says you have not yet awakened? The monk said, "And after awakening, how is it?

The Master said, "Do not deceive yourself regarding the 'bright head' (the state of realization). A monk asked, "Are the meaning of the Patriarchs and the meaning of the Teachings the same or different?

The Master said, "The crags are high and the pines are cold; the stream winds through the ravine and flows slowly. A monk asked, "What is the Patriarch’s West [India]? The Master said, "... (text fragment ends)
Regarding the meaning of his coming, the Master said: "A fan of green silk is sufficient for wind and coolness. Question: "What is the place where the student exerts effort?
The Master said: "Striking the Great Image at Jia Prefecture. Question: "What is the place where the student turns about? The Master said:

"Watering the Iron Ox at Shan Prefecture. Question: "What is the place where the student finds intimacy? The Master said: "Playing with lions in Hexi. Question: [How is it? The Master said: [As above].
"What is the first mystery? The Master said, "A personal instruction before Kāśyapa. The monk asked, "What is the second mystery?
The Master said, "Transcending forms and departing from verbal expression. The monk asked, "What is the third mystery? The Master said, "The clear mirror reflects without partiality.
The monk said, "If that is so, then the Three Mysteries have already transcended the bounds of past and present; the nine heavens all sing of the Great [Silence]."
A Song of Serenity. The Master said: "The bright sun spreads its light, leaving nothing unilluminated; the netherworld is fully radiant, opening wide heaven and earth.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Now, those who study must possess the eye of the fundamental division.

When facing circumstances, they must distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox, not being deceived by others, nor being obstructed by Buddhas or Patriarchs, nor turning according to words, nor being bound by any phenomena."
Deluded! They do not rely on any divine or wondrous understanding; rather, they seek to refute everyone who comes before them. Why?

Because they rely on intellectual interpretations and conceptualizations, playing with mental acuity and seeking after views and knowledge. Whether they ask about the Buddhas or the Patriarchs, whether they concern themselves with the "upward" or the "downward," whether it be their own intent or the intent of the Patriarchs—all of these may be struck down.
Even if they do not rely on anything at all, this is precisely the occasion for a reprimand. Ten thousand waters, a thousand mountains...
"Mountain! You deserve a blow of the staff. At such a time, one must be a true man of character before it is possible.

Whenever there are words of evasion or concealment—whether covering over or hiding beneath—bring them forth to test the master’s discerning eye. Whether they present their own views or carry themselves with pride like a beast with its horns upraised, if you recognize them for what they are, they all deserve to be struck.
Or, you may simply see through them face-to-face, or humiliate and disparage them; their appearance is like that of a boastful ox.
When a mirror is set upon its stand, what kind of spirit or demon could possibly manifest within it? Why is this? For foxes are capable of concealing their true forms.
Be careful.

Chan Master Xianglin Chengyuan of Chengdu Prefecture was surnamed Shangguan and was a native of Mianzhu in Hanzhou.
He left home to become a monk at Zhenxiang Monastery in Chengdu and received full ordination at the age of sixteen. Later, he departed from Shu and entered Qin, ascending Mount Qingfeng.
He visited Ziliang and traveled through Jingzhou and Xiangzhou. He attended the later master Longya, where he found the ground for awakening.

Subsequently, he crossed the mountain passes and approached Master Kuangzhen of Yunmen, where he adjusted his robes to seek instruction on the meaning of the Patriarchs' intent; his doubts were greatly dispelled.
He served him for eighteen years, daily investigating the profound essence of the teachings. He then returned to Chengdu and was invited to reside at the Jiangshui Qinggong Wujun Yuan.
In the year of Jiǎzǐ, the Prince of Jiā petitioned for the Master to reside at Xianglín Chányuàn.
In the second month of the fourth year of Yōngxī (Dīnghái), Prefectural Governor Mìxué Sòng Gōng Dāng invited him to settle at Pǔ'ān Yuàn.

On the twelfth day, he took leave of all the officials, saying, "I, this old monk, am going on pilgrimage. The Vice-Governor remarked, "This monk is mad; he is eighty years old and yet he intends to travel!"
At that time, Miyuan said, "O Great Good Knowledge (Mahāsatpuruṣa), you have attained mastery over going and staying.

On the thirteenth day, he addressed the assembly, saying, "For forty years, this old monk has been unable to forge [my practice] into a single piece. Having spoken these words, he sat and passed away.
The provincial governor served as the master of ceremonies for the funeral. On the sixteenth day, he was returned to his grave at the north of the abbot’s quarters of Xianglin Monastery.

The Master said: "All of you here have been carrying your alms-bags and traveling abroad.
Do you yet recognize your own nature? If you do recognize it, come forth and speak of it. If you do not recognize it, you are merely being deceived by others.
Now I ask you all: Is this your study of the Way? Day and night you apply your minds, sweeping the floors and brewing tea. [He continued: "To travel..."
Gazing at the mountains and playing by the waters, you should first pin yourself down: what do you call "self-nature"? You all, tell me:
that which from beginning to end is neither changing nor different, neither high nor low, neither beautiful nor ugly, neither arising nor ceasing—where does it ultimately return?
Do you all yet know where its descent lies? If you can know its location here, [you have found it].
This is the dharma-gate of liberation of all Buddhas. Having awakened to the Way and seen one's nature, from beginning to end there is neither doubt nor anxiety;
one may proceed freely in any direction. No person can do anything to you. Every word spoken and every breath exhaled truly has its source.
You have recovered the original contract; it is like a person buying a field who must necessarily obtain the original contract—if they do not have that original contract...
A deed of sale is ultimately unstable; even if you bring it before the authorities and file a formal petition, you will still not prevail.
Alas, because you failed to retain the original document, it was inevitably lost to you. It is the same with all of you who practice Chan and study the Way:
has anyone among you managed to secure the original deed? Try bringing it forth and show it to me. For now, call out what it is!
This is the original fundamental contract; let everyone try to speak upon it. If one is truly sharp-witted, as soon as they hear it spoken thus, they will know its destination.
If they do not know its destination, then even if they have learned a thousand kinds of cleverness from the outside, it is of no avail.
You merely memorize and interpret, and though your mouth may seem like a pouring river, you will never reach the ultimate point;
this is worlds apart from your own true self. For now, go beneath your robes and alms bowl and seek it out for yourself.
If you have a place of realization, come here and the old monk will bear witness for you. If you cannot find it, then simply follow the ranks of practitioners.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Venerable seniors, from antiquity until now, there has been but one person of no affairs. They do not engage in fabrication;

they do not cling to conditions; they have nothing to attain. When a single thought accords with reality, they do not undergo further existence and do not see themselves beset by the afflictions of illness."
The four great elements are fundamentally empty; the five aggregates are false and illusory. To give rise to thoughts or harbor even the slightest doubt belongs entirely to the realm of Māra;

it all falls within the sphere of deluded conceptualization. If one attains the ground of reality, both favorable and adverse conditions will be permeated by it. On the ground of ultimate truth, no phenomenon can withstand scrutiny.
Whatever arrangements or manifestations there may be, they do not abide within the sensory objects. In the very substance of each and every thing, there is ultimately nothing to be attained.
They are primordially liberated, requiring no effort to achieve completion. Therefore it is said that all phenomena are eternally abiding, and there is nowhere for you to add or subtract.
Throughout the entire ten-direction Dharma-realm, in every speck of dust and every land, each and every instance is the body of a true person; these are all gateways through which one enters.

If one sets aside these, what other views could there be? They are all like flowers appearing to those who rub their eyes, or like three heads and two faces—externalists, demonic spirits, and throngs of ghosts and gods.
Furthermore, they are not included within the fundamental nature; they have no connection whatsoever with your own self.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Do you all still see a realm of sentient beings?
Do you still see coming and going? Do you still see the realm of the Buddhas? Do you still see the mundane and the supramundane?

People delusively identify themselves as ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). Do you truly recognize the nature of an ordinary being?

This body of yours is a temporary borrowing of the parents' womb, sustained by earth, water, fire, wind, and the essence of the five grains. It grows in accordance with the Yin and Yang until it takes on a physical form;
after a hundred years or fifty years, it returns to the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). Where, then, is your "ordinary being"?
As for this "nature," how do you know it? The Sage himself distinguished it by taking a fragment of his own mind and body and attempting to enter the rank of sainthood.
How would you enter? Where is your destination? Is there truly any coming or going?
Is there truly any casting off of the rank of an ordinary person to enter the rank of a sage? If you say there truly is, you are placing a head upon a head. If you say...
There is truly nothing here. You are like those who cut off their own heads and yet seek to remain alive. Each of you come forth; speak clearly.

"Why are you afraid of him? The Master said, "I am abashed; I am abashed. The monk asked, "How was it before the Buddha appeared in the world?
