The Master said, "The single shoe has long since returned to the Pamir Mountains; now, cease further questioning about its origin. The monk said, "If one departs in such a manner, what then?
The Master said, "Clouds rise on the southern mountain; rain falls on the northern mountain. A monk asked, "I have already taken up my staff and resided here."
One day, a monk requested, "Please grant me a single phrase to benefit humans and devas. The Master said, "The nostrils point downward.

The monk asked, "Is there anything further above this? The Master said, "There is. The monk asked, "What is it like? The Master said, "If you wish to exhaust the view across a thousand li, you must ascend one more story."

Ascending the hall, he said: "The Dharma-body has no form; it manifests its shape in response to things. All you practitioners of Chan, how would you explain the principle of manifesting form in response to things?
Taking up his staff, he showed it to the assembly and said: "The World-Honored One was six feet tall, and this staff is also six feet long.
Maitreya was a thousand feet tall, and this staff is also [a thousand feet long]."
A thousand feet tall; square or round according to the vessel; hidden or manifest depending on others. Vastly encompassing heaven and earth, it enters subtly into a speck of dust or a stalk of reed.
Like a donkey looking into a well, like a well looking at a donkey. Those who attain it direct strategy from within the tent and hold fast at the vital ford; those who lose it...
"Profoundly distant and suddenly fleeting; born in vain and dying in waves. Let go at once of both paths—gain and loss. I dare ask you all:
tell me, how long is this mountain monk’s staff, after all? (Pauses for a long while. He says with a smile:
'Pointing, from where does the guest come? He strikes the incense stand once."
Ascending the hall, he looked over the assembly and said: "If you are not yet able to act in this way, you must at least employ worldly expedients.
Therefore, when the midwinter cold is severe, everyone offers congratulations; and when the sun reaches its southern solstice, you Zen practitioners have come here.
You must immediately raise your eyebrows; do not be like Old Wang of the Eastern Village, who lost his nose last night. Examine!"
Chan Master Yunju Xiaoshun of Yuncheng was a dharma successor of Chan Master Dongshan Xiaocong of Junzhou.
A native of Yinyang, he was coarse and fierce in his youth; suddenly awakening to the nature of floating illusions, he entered the monastic life under a teacher and cultivated minute conduct.
He then went to visit Chan Master Xiaocong. One day, upon entering the inner quarters, Xiaocong asked him: "The ancient mirror..."

"How is it when being polished? he asked. [Dongshan] said, "Black as lacquer. Cuiyan asked, "How is it after being polished? He said, "It illuminates heaven and earth. Cuiyan said, "I do not think so.

[He] was summoned to the capital. From this, his reputation for the Way spread far and wide, and Zen practitioners relied upon him. Later, he resided at Dayu in Junzhou, as well as at Lushan and Qixian.
During the Zhi-ping era, one day he called to the assembly, saying: "Originally there is nothing to do; what words are there when departing? Moment by moment, go, go!
Having finished speaking, he passed away. Question: Whose song does the Master sing? To whom does his lineage of the school’s wind (zongfeng) succeed?
[The monk] asked, "Who? The Master said, "The clouds have the momentum to leave the mountains; the water has no sound as it plunges into the ravine.
The monk said, "One arrow from Xinfeng shoots straight at Dayu. The Master said, "Today you have nearly been caught in the rain.

[The monk] asked, "What is the phrase for benefiting others? The Master said, "When the sky clears, the sun rises. The monk said, "If so, then from now on I shall have no doubts. The Master said, "Rain falls and the clouds darken."
Question: "I do not ask about coming all the way from a thousand *li*, but what is the matter with opening a new shop where the old one stood?
The Master said, "What do you wish to buy? The monk lifted up his sitting mat (*kaṣāya*) and said, "Is there such a thing as this?

The Master said, "Going east, one does not see the profit of going west. The monk said, "With money, one can be a fine gentleman. The Master said, "Hūṃ! You are mocking me. Question: "I have received [your teaching]..."
The Master said, "I do not speak of the profound; I do not discuss the subtle. Having set aside these two paths, how can one provide instruction?
The monk asked, "How then can you point the way? The Master said, "A shrimp chasing a hawk. The monk said, "It is entirely because of this question. The Master said, "A rat playing with a monkey."
Ascending the hall, he said: "The single, firm, and secret body manifests within every atom of dust. Frogs and earthworms each have their burrows;
crows, magpies, doves, and pigeons each have their nests. At this very moment, for whom does the Dharma being preached?"
After a long silence, he said: "Things are grouped according to their kind; beings are divided according to their species. He ascended the hall and said:

"In studying the Way, do not give rise to discrimination. Once there is discrimination, it becomes conceptual understanding. Simply believe that your own mind is the Buddha, and throughout kalpas you will never again fall into delusion. He stood for a long time.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The Way of the Three Gorges has no distinction; morning after morning, it is spoken of only thus. Sengyou knows how to paint portraits;
the provincial government produces tempered steel. Take care! Ascending the hall, he said: "Neither long nor short, neither small nor large.
To whom does this principle belong? *Du!* (A shout)" Ascending the hall, he said: "Exerting all one's strength, it cannot be lifted; let it go, and there is no trace. Ask me—"

Regarding those who practice the various dhyānas: how can this principle be made to accord with them? He ascended the hall and said: "Words do not require elaboration; the Way does not require cultivation.
If a person can understand this, they may follow the flow according to their nature. He stood for a long time.
Chan Master Huaiyou of Miyin Monastery on Mount Daibei in Tanzhou asked: "People test gold with fire;
I wonder, with what do you test a patch-robed monk? The Master replied, "The staff. The monk said, "Ultimately, how is it?"

The Master said, "Step back. The monk responded with an "Amen" (ye). The Master then struck him and said, "You were told to desist, yet you refuse to desist; you will surely wait until the rain drenches your head.
Chan Master Mingjiao of Mount Furi in Hangzhou, whose name was Qisong, was a native of Dongsan in Tengzhou. His secular surname was...

Li [Shi] entered the monastic order at the age of seven and received full ordination at thirteen. At nineteen, she began traveling to visit various spiritual teachers (jñāna-kalyāṇamitra), eventually receiving the Dharma from Chan Master Dongshan Cong.
She resided frequently at the Yong’an Hermitage, where she diligently studied both Buddhist and secular classics and took great pleasure in composition and writing.

She strove mightily to support the Buddhist teachings and the religious tradition. During the Jiayou era, she compiled the *Chanmen Chuandefa Zhengzongji* (Record of the Orthodox Lineage of the Transmission of the Dharma in the Chan School). It was determined [that this work was authentic].
Zutang’s *Compilation for Aiding the Teachings* was presented to Emperor Renzong. By imperial decree, it was promulgated throughout the realm and included in the Tripitaka;

he was posthumously granted the title Mingjiao (Illuminating Teaching). On the fourth day of the sixth month in the fourth year of the Xining era, he passed away at Lingyin Temple at the age of sixty-six.
On the eighth day of that same month, his body was cremated; his eyes, tongue, and male organ remained uncorrupted, and a light emerged from the top of his skull.
The śarīra were crimson-white and translucent. Throughout his life, the Master wore an image of Avalokiteśvara upon his head and recited its name;

even his wooden *nāgapuṣpa* (myrobalan) rosary was not consumed by the fire. Such was the purity of his understanding and practice, and the luminous clarity of his nature and wisdom. Among the eminent monks of the Song dynasty, few could equal the Master.
A detailed account is found in the *Record of the Conduct and Virtues of the Worthy Cien*.

Chan Master Xingsi of Mount Qingyuan in Luoling, the eleventh generation descendant of Chan Master Huai Cheng of Baofeng Monastery on Mount Letan in Hongzhou; successor to [Chan Master Xingsi].
The Chan Master Dajue of the Shifang Jingyin Chan Monastery in Tokyo was named Huailian. His secular surname was Chen, and he was a native of Longxi County in Zhangzhou.

On the evening of his birth, a dream occurred that the monk Śāriputra (Sengqie) descended into his chamber; consequently, he was given the childhood nickname "Sizhou. As there were such extraordinary omens, everyone recognized them as auspicious signs.
He left home to become a monk at the age of six and received full ordination at the age of twelve. He devoted himself to the study of the Way, sleeping [little]... [text continues].
He never neglected his meals. One day, while washing his face, he splashed water onto the ground; this triggered a slight awakening, and he immediately yearned to seek out a teacher.

He traveled far to the Dharma seat of Chan Master Lètán Táng, where he attained realization and received formal certification. Subsequently, he visited various monasteries, and the assembly was drawn to his reputation for the Way.
Having passed the age of forty, his fame moved the Emperor Renzong. By imperial decree, he resided at Jingyin Chan Monastery.

On three occasions he was summoned to the inner gardens to expound the Dharma before the Sovereign; his teachings delighted the Imperial heart, and the Emperor bestowed upon him the title "Dajue" (Great Enlightenment) and composed a eulogy for him.

He was granted leave to respond [to imperial inquiries]. His heavenly favor grew ever deeper, such that he was treated much like a teacher or a friend. His worn cassock, golden bowl, and precious beads were all bestowed by imperial decree.
In his later years, he requested to retire to the seclusion of the forest; the Emperor’s edict granted his request, allowing him to reside and preside over the monastery as he pleased.
Consequently, he settled at Mount Yuyang, where his disciples gathered once more. His Way accorded with the Imperial mind, and his reputation became weighty within the realm.
Worldly beings, the patriarchs of our dynasty have never enjoyed such honor and fortune as you.

On the nineteenth day of the twelfth month in the second year of the Renshou era, Emperor Renzong summoned the Master to the Huacheng Hall in the Rear Garden and commanded that he ascend the seat and preach the Dharma exactly according to the ceremonial protocols used for the opening of a hall.
He ordered Qingman, the Vice Registrar of the Left Street and Great Master Ciyun, to offer the formal announcement. Qingman then offered his thanks.
The grace is ended. It is then said: "In the springtime radiance of the Imperial Garden, the Royal House inaugurates this assembly.

As the Ten-Thousand Chariots have ascended the Hall of Shun, the two streets are privileged to serve before the brows of Yao. This being a time of harmonious nurturing, it is precisely the day for proclamation and exaltation.
It is fitting to discourse upon the Way of the Patriarchs, so as to fully accord with the Imperial heart. This is respectfully submitted."
The Master then ascended the seat. Having offered incense and made his vow for the Emperor, he spread his sitting mat. Chan Master Huayan struck the gavel and said:
"O assembly of dragons and elephants at this Dharma feast, you should contemplate the primary truth. The Master said: "That gavel just now was a most auspicious omen.
Is there anyone who can provide verification? Come forth before the Sage and try to express it. At that time, there was the Xuanjiao [official]...
The Master asked, "The entire field of vision is a world of silver; I wonder where Samantabhadra is? The Master said, "It is as if you were face-to-face yet do not recognize him.
The monk said, "A six-tusked white elephant stands in the air; a sovereign of ten thousand chariots sits upon a jeweled terrace.
The Master said, "The layered net of Indra opens right here. The Master spoke again, "Within the hall of the ancient Buddhas, there has never been..."

There are various explanations. Within the circulating verses, there is indeed much discourse. If one attains this, the wondrous function remains unimpaired; if one loses it, obstacles arise at every turn.
Thus, the streams, mountains, clouds, and moon share the same breeze everywhere, while the water-birds and forest trees manifest the Way at every point.
Were one to enter the gate of Kāśyapa, one would find the wind of Yao sweeping vast and clear, and the sun of Shun shining brightly.

The village elders sing their songs; the fishermen dance with joy. At such a time as this, there is pure bliss and non-action. Having long troubled Your Majesty’s sagely hearing, I humbly pray that you will take care of yourself.
Question: When the Buddhas appear in the world, they benefit and deliver all living beings. Now that the Master has ascended the lion throne, by what means will you rescue and deliver them?
The Master said: "The mountains are high and the seas are vast. The monk said: "Flowers bloom on a rootless tree; fish leap from ten-thousand-fathom peaks."
The Master said, "In the land of Silla. The monk said, "When the Compassionate Boat does not row upon the clear waves, it is a vain labor to release wooden swans at the Sword Gorge.
The Master said, "Casting off one's garments, one lies amidst thorns. The monk said, "People test one with their words.

The Master said, "He is well-accustomed to seizing such opportunities. The monk clapped his hands. The Master said, "Jump about even more! A monk asked, "What is it like when the oars do not cease? The Master said:

The clear waves rush like arrows. The monk said, "In that case, one moves the boat to understand the currents; one raises the oars to distinguish the billows. The Master said, "The water of Ji flows all the way to Silla.
The monk said, "One cannot remain within the station of the ancient Buddhas; last night, as usual, I stayed among the reeds.

Chan Master Jingzhao, whose name was Daozhen, of the Jingyin Chan Monastery in the Capital (Beijing), was a dharma successor of Chan Master Fuyuan Yuanjian of Shuzhou. He was a native of Gutian in Fuzhou and belonged to the secular surname Cai.
His father dreamed that a person wearing a ceremonial cap and robes arrived at their residence with a retinue; subsequently, his mother, Lady Huang, became pregnant.
Furthermore, he dreamed that banners and streamers, accompanied by the chanting of *brahmā*-songs, led a monk with bushy eyebrows and blue eyes to him; this was his birth.

At the age of fourteen, he entered the Shangsheng Monastery to renounce the householder’s life and maintained the *dhūta* ascetic practices. At nineteen, he shaved his head and began a preliminary study of the sutras and śāstras.

Thereafter, he traveled abroad to visit various spiritual teachers (*kalyāṇamitra*). His realization accorded with that of Chan Master Yuanjian, who subsequently emerged from seclusion to open the hall [for ordination] under Emperor Yingzong.

The Emperor dispatched an envoy to bestow incense. Subsequently, Lady Miao memorialized to grant him a purple robe. Lan Yuanzhen, the Director of the Imperial Household, further memorialized to grant the master the name Juezhao.
The Great Lord of the Zhou State submitted a petition requesting a Chan title.

Emperor Shenzong issued an edict to the presiding ministers, saying: "Daohen possesses renowned virtue; you should select an elegant title and present it for my consideration. Thereupon, he was granted the title Jing... (the text ends here).
Chan Master Zhao established various Chan monasteries in the capital and selected and invited masters of the lineage; all were recommended by his teacher Shouju and fully met with imperial favor.
On the seventeenth day of the eighth month in the eighth year of the Yuanyou era, he ascended the hall to bid farewell to the assembly, wrote a verse, and passed away while seated.

In the spring of the third year of the Yuanfeng era, Empress Cisheng Guangxian passed away. A hundred-day vegetarian retreat (*zhāi*) was established at the Qingshou Hall, where one thousand Dharma masters were assembled.
On that day, Emperor Shenzong granted them seats and issued an inquiry: "Venerable Elder, by what means shall you offer posthumous merit for the Retired Empress?
The Master replied: "Your servant-monk has had the honor of beholding Your Majesty’s countenance; it is therefore by imperial decree that [I speak thus]."
The Master ascended the seat. At that time, a monk asked, "The Empress Dowager has passed away; where is she now? The Master said, "When the moon sets, it does not leave the sky.

The monk asked, "Since her celestial carriage has already departed into the distance, how can benevolence and filial piety be pursued? The Patriarchal intent came from the West; I beg the Master for a skillful means.

The Master said, "Though the imperial radiance may be obscured in the north, the teachings of the wind and culture naturally endure in the south. The monk said, "The sacred ruler’s words and phrases shall be proclaimed far and wide."
[The Emperor] departed. The people throughout the realm received and recited [the decree]. The Master said, "A sharp-witted monk. [The Emperor] asked:

What need is there to engage in questions and answers regarding going and coming?

if you can express the various Buddhist services performed today, and furthermore, if anyone can utter that final word, please speak.
[He remained] silent for a long while, then said: "When one person rejoices, the myriad people depend upon it. I, your servant—a humble monk from the mountains—am devoid of any merit in my practice.

I have presumed to offend Your Majesty’s august majesty; yet, as I look up and am deeply indebted for Your Imperial Grace, I cannot help but be filled with alarm and trepidation.

Chan Master Remyue of Xinghua in Luzhou was a native of Southern Quan. He stood out preeminently among the Chan groves of the Jianghuai region and emerged as a distinguished talent at the seat of the Yuanjian lineage.
He first expounded the Dharma at Longshu and later transmitted the lamp of the teaching at Feishui.

In the autumn of the tenth year of the Xining era, one day he wrote a verse, saying: "The golden rooster embraces the jade hare; The jade rabbit raises a phoenix chick. Lifting its head toward the south..."

a stūpa was erected to the west of the commandery. A questioner asked: "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master said: "A wooden boat upon the river."

This is the great purport of the Buddha-dharma. The Master said: Linji asked Huangbo. A monk said, "I do not understand. The Master said:
"He has come three times to receive blows. Question: "One flower opens into five petals; the fruiting occurs naturally. What is that one flower? The Master said:
"Unfit to be an offering to the Buddha. The monk said: "Where would you pluck it and place it? The Master said: "In the ten directions."
At the dung heap. [A monk] asked: "The entire Great Canon consists of names and phrases. Apart from these names and phrases, how can you point it out?
The Master said: "A mangy horse rubs against a withered willow. The monk said: "I do not understand, Teacher. The Master said: "A dappled horse loves to eat salt.
The monk said: "Ultimately, how is it? The Master said: "Where the iron whip points, the horse neighs in vain. [Another monk] asked: "In the Buddha’s realm, it is profound..."
[The monk asked: "What is it like when he is in the palace? The Master said, "He wears precious imperial robes. [The monk] said, "What is it like when he leaves the city to become a renunciant?
The Master said, "He hangs on a tattered, filthy garment. [The monk] said, "What is it like when he neither goes out nor stays within? The Master said, "One cut, two pieces."
Ascending the hall, he said: "The single phrase of the present moment is already prior to words; it is heard before being uttered, its coarseness already manifest.

To wait further for the twisting of the waist and pressing of the knees, to take even half a step forward, or to intend to move the tip of the tongue—this is to fall into confusion and lose the thread.

If one relies on the standing ground of a monk, how could one fall into the present age? To establish the lineage of the Dharma, one responds to conditions as they arise. This is why he brandishes the hammer and raises [the whisk]."

A wave of the whisk; a blink of an eye, a raising of an eyebrow; discussing antiquity and presenting the present—these are all skillful means. Furthermore, one must observe the wind to discern the target; the radiance should be held within the heart.
When the staff and the shout are fully brought forth, how could they be considered trivial? It is simply that, having no other recourse, one has provisionally adapted to the times.
Reaching this point, if you have long been refined through training, you will turn your head toward the high current; having traversed the vast waves, you will know for yourself.
Cold and warm. If you encounter a beginner practitioner of Chan whose black and white are not yet distinguished, you must temporarily deploy your spiritual sharpness to clarify their great wisdom.

You must cause them to turn the light back upon themselves to shine inwardly, so that they may directly manifest their capacity beyond the pointing finger, returning to the root and source rather than seeking utility along the way.
For a transformative patch-robed monk, there is no need for hesitation: when the pivot moves, it reaches as far as Silla and Bohai. Long time standing.
Take heed.
Chan Master Jingyun of Guangjiao Monastery on Mount Baiyun in Qi Prefecture was a native of Xia County in Shan Prefecture.

His surname was Li. From birth, he abstained from meat and pungent roots; his kinsmen regarded this as extraordinary. He entered the monastic order under the Venerable Zhen of Lingshan Monastery in the Western Capital. II.
At fifteen, he shaved his hair and traveled to various places to seek instruction. He attained the Dharma under Chan Master Yuanjian.

Later, when the Governor of Qi, Lord Qiao, heard of the Master’s reputation for the Way, he ordered him to reside on this mountain. The Governor asked, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? The Master said:

A monk asked, "Whose song does the Master sing? Whose ancestral wind does your lineage follow? The Master said, "Striking a golden bell atop the summit of Mount Sumeru."
Question: "What is the seamless stupa? The Master said: "Even if one were as a skilled hand as Gu Kaizhi, there would be no way for you to paint it.
The monk asked: "Who is the person within the stupa? The Master said: "Raising an eyebrow and beckoning with a hand—few encounter such a person face-to-face.
Xu Neihan asked: "What is the realm of Guangjiao? The Master said: "A single sheet of white clouds stretches across."
At the summit of the mountain, Han asked, "What is it like to be a person within the realm? The Master said, "Today, a high official enters the monastery.
He ascended the hall and said: "Clouds enshroud the Jade Palace; the wind sweeps the golden sand. The spiritual sprout finds its ground;

flowers bloom everywhere across the wilds. Travelers admire and enjoy them; Zen students sigh in wonder. *Tut!* If you do not awaken to the true essence of Shaolin, you turn your back on Amitābha to seek elsewhere."
Śākyamuni ascended the hall and said: "Upon the flames of the red furnace, golden snowflakes bloom; within the Hall of White Clouds, the wooden man claps his hands.
It reaches the point where heaven sheds sweet dew and the earth wells up coral. The insentient speak the True Dharma day and night;
who knows who is in accord with Suchness? He struck the meditation seat once. He ascended the hall again and said: "Speak! Speak! Within this, there is no purple or black."
Zen. Zen. The gate connects with the white clouds. The path beyond—where the sages of a thousand ages have not transmitted it—is this: how does one sing the song of the Hu family? Do you understand?
Under the clear wind and bright moon at night, the waves strike the fishing boat. *Duḥ!* He ascended the hall and said: "Realized! Realized!"
Everyone says it is good. Wondrous! Wondrous! Who understands this fragrant incense? If one understands, one attains perfect penetration; if one appreciates it, one discusses the wondrous Way.
Boundless pure breezes arise beneath the seat; within the body, one realizes ageless non-birth. Ageless non-birth—let me inform you of this!
A single flawless piece, radiant for all eternity. *Duḥ*.
This is the record of Chan Master Ji of Wuweijun Temple on the West Bank of the Jiang River. He was asked: "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?"
The Master said, "Before the withered tree at the edge of the cliff. A monk asked, "What is the meaning? The Master said, "A stone shoot putting forth branches.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The green mountains are lush and verdant; the clear waters are tranquil and flowing. If even all things are thus, how do you Zen practitioners know it?
If you can know it, then everything you encounter is the truth; there is nothing else. In each and every dharma, there is a Tathāgata."
Within each and every atom there is a Maitreya. If you do not know this, for now, beneath the three rafters and before the six-foot mat, you must quickly investigate it.
After a long silence, he said: "It is simply because the source of one's own mind has not been tamed;
the Patriarch was originally a man of the world. He gave a shout.
Chan Master Huichen of Dinglin in Suzhou asked, "Regarding the hundreds of billions of transformation bodies, I wonder which one among them is the Tathāgata’s body?
The Master said, "He manifests forms in response to things. The monk said, "If that is so, then he is universally manifest before all living beings. The Master said, "..."
"Retreat three thousand paces. A monk asked, "What is the Way? The Master said, "It is right before your eyes.
The monk said, "Why do I not see it? The Master said, "Blind!"
Chan Master Ruozhu of Benjue Monastery in Xiuzhou was a native of Fuzhou. His surname was Zhuo. While his mother was pregnant with him, she frequently experienced extraordinary dreams.
Upon his birth, auspicious light illuminated the room. At the age of seven, he left home to become a monk; through the sponsorship of his late father, he received full ordination.

Later, aspiring to travel to study under various masters, he arrived at the Dharma seat of Chan Master Yuanjian of Tiantian Monastery in Suzhou. Yuanjian asked him, "Before your parents were born, who were you?"
"This is your original face. Upon these words, the Master suddenly attained realization. He then attended upon [the teacher], carrying his towel and water flask, until they reached Fushan in Shuzhou.
Every time he entered the room for instruction, Yunshu would roll a stone once.

Thereafter, [the Master] withdrew from public view, reciting the Lotus Sutra three volumes daily and remaining in a seated posture without lying down. Later, he resided at Jucheng, where the Way of the Dharma spread widely. The first year of the Yuanyou era, the tenth month...

On the tenth day of the month, he instructed Master Yuánzhào to complete the demarcation of the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*). On the following day, he bathed and purified his hair, then summoned the assembly, saying:

"My worldly ties are about to end; you must skillfully preserve and uphold [the Dharma]. Having finished speaking, he sat in the lotus posture and passed away. For seven days, his body did not lean or fall.
After cremation, five-colored *śarīra* relics were obtained, which were enshrined in a stupa at his home mountain. Question: "What is the Way? The Master said:

[The Master] raised his fist. The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "You do not even recognize the fist. A monk asked, "Whose song does the Master sing? Whose ancestral style does he succeed?
The Master said, "A single sound rends open the sands and seas of worlds; vast and penetrating, it accords with ten thousand functions.
The monk said, "If that is so, then you are the true grandson of Ye-xian and the legitimate son of Fu-shan. The Master said, "Why do you fail to grasp the meaning of my words?"
The monk asked, "What were you talking about? The Master said, "Eighty thousand miles. He ascended the hall and said: "To speak of Buddhas and Patriarchs is to bury the lineage;
to cite the ancients and discuss the present is to detain the monks. Clearing the path ahead, who dares face it head-on?
All must stand downwind without effort, for there is no need to bring it forth. How can one distinguish the weight with a scale that has no markings? If one can indeed distinguish it..."
It can be obtained. Sumeru weighs only half a *zhu*. If you cannot discern this, you shall break the scale and meet me with all of you inside the land of Japan.
A monk asked Chan Master Weifang of Jingde on Mount Yuquan in Jingmen Prefecture, "How do the sages of all generations instruct people?
The Master picked up his staff. The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "Handed over with both hands. As the monk hesitated, the Master struck him.
Another asked, "What is the master’s house style? The Master said, "Performing acrobatics on the tip of a needle."
[Dou] asked, "What is the essential meaning? The Master said, "A piece of lapis lazuli atop the flames of a red furnace. He asked, "What is the Dharma of the One Vehicle?
The Master said, "Dust and a single hair manifest directly. Ascending the hall, he said: "Before the celestial steed has yet been yoked, guest and host, illumination and function, proceed in unison.
Once the poisonous drum sounds, the blind patriarchs and ignorant worthies lose the true source. Sometimes he brandishes the high staff of awakening; sometimes..."
The secondary categories are as numerous as a thousand threads. The shadow-grass shines like a torch atop a staff; the precious sword blazes amidst the golden-maned lion’s roar.

From the perspective of the Host, South is Yang and North is Kan; from the perspective of the Guest, East is Mao and West is You. Wind and clouds converge, and their intersecting lights are fully gathered from all eight directions.
As function and application occur simultaneously, the array-diagrams are completely encompassed and cut away. Opening both and closing both, the command rests with the person present.
Pressing straight and lifting straight, the point is concealed within the sleeve; others perish and this is extinguished. Yet, one still carries embroidered sachets;
having obtained the seal, the spearhead is turned back, and only then are the ranks of civil and military seen. One must distinguish victory from defeat; how could one permit wandering east or west?

The seven-starred flames radiate their light—one must know that the hundred flowers compete to bloom. Before the golden needle is raised, the mountain and river points are exposed; before the jade seal is opened...
Light spreads across the vast fields; the colors of dawn do not intrude by even a hair’s breadth. In the midst of darkness, eyebrows and eyes must be clearly distinguished.

It is not hidden beneath White Ox Rock, nor is it locked away in the secluded courtyard of the Golden Phoenix. Ruler and subject meet in harmony; there is no gate through which to enter their dance. Vast intent melts into a unified heart.
When the honey moves even a single step, its horns have not yet appeared. As it spreads through various species in a continuous flow, the jade-threaded gate opens;

all belongs to the realm of benefiting sentient beings. Throughout the entire great earth there is no fixed stopping point; for ten thousand ages, the moon shines upon the clear pool. On the desolate fields of battle, the brows do not relax;
at midnight, when the array is complete, one should undergo the transformation of the leopard. In the orthodox way, the dragon swallows the extraordinary treasure; in the partial way, however—
The crane rests in its silver cage; the Great Intent of the Orthodox and the Deviant is as fragmented as branches.

When dawn is lost, the pearl in the hand falls to the ground—seeing the extraordinary within the extraordinary, it is like dividing a foot-long jade disc with a foreign measure. When speech emerges without understanding, it is like falling headlong from mid-air.
To strike is for the great night to dissolve and be forgotten; to chant is for the long sky to escape its course. Unrestrained and drenched, the rain does not cause harm—it is still the night.
He was a guest beyond the bright curtain. One day, after bathing and cleansing his hair, the Master wrote a verse: "Breaking through at the third watch, there is no handle to grasp;
Striking open the midnight, the pivot of the Great Way is revealed. The marrow of the stone man from two thousand years ago— I shall not report it to others with a public proclamation.
Having thus cast down his brush, he sat upright and passed away.
Chan Master Hongshi of Guizong Temple on Mount Lu was asked, "What is the realm of Guizong? The Master said, "The ink-well of Wang Xizhi.
The monk said, "If one does not set sail, how can one know the vastness of the sea? The Master said, "I suspect you do not know where it leads.
On the nineteenth day of the seventh month in the second year of the Xining era, the Master ascended the hall to take leave of the assembly, saying, "Mount Sumeru has fallen."
Zhuo. The seawater flows backward; the stone man cleaves the waves as he rows his solitary boat. Clapping his hands with a laugh, "Ha ha! Who is my companion?
He wanders at will through the great chiliocosm of worlds. *Du!* Having finished speaking, he sat cross-legged and passed away.
Chan Master Puzi of Huayan in Tokyo was the son of the Xie family of Jianyang in Jianzhou.
In his youth, he studied Confucianism and Daoism, and subsequently read Buddhist scriptures until he recognized the source of his own mind.

His innate faculties were awakened, whereupon he entered the monastic order under the monk Kechong at Xilu Monastery in Taiping Xingguo, receiving both tonsure and full ordination. He then traveled to various regions to seek the Way, eventually arriving at Fushan in Longshu.
At the Dharma assembly of Chan Master Yuanjian, he entered the inner quarters to seek instruction and attained sudden enlightenment into the meaning of the Patriarchs.

At the request of the people of Shu, he was invited to reside at the two monasteries of Ganlu and Taiping, where his reputation for the Way spread far and wide. Later, he retired to Jingyin Monastery.

In the fifth year of the Yuanfeng era, he was appointed as the Monk Registrar (Senglü) of the Left and Right Quarters and took up residence at Huayan Monastery. There, he re-established the Chan regulations, and both within and outside the capital, people turned toward him with great enthusiasm. In the eighth year...
On the tenth day of the fourth month, he was summoned by imperial decree to preach the Dharma within the inner palace;

the Emperor bestowed upon him most generous gifts. On the fourteenth day of that same month, he took leave of the assembly and passed away while seated. His body was cremated and his remains enshrined in a stupa at Linjia Village in Kaifeng.

By nature, the Master’s mind was as still as clear water, and his speech was like falling frost. He had a profound mastery of the *zongmen* (the vehicle of the lineage) and his realization transcended both emotion and consciousness. He continued the legacy of the Linji school.

He had profoundly mastered the Three Mysteries and Nine Bonds, as well as the Five Ranks and Ten Mysteries of Caodong; thus, those who sought to enter his presence could only gaze at the distant shore.
A monk asked, "What is the guest within the guest? The Master said, "The traveler's road is as far as heaven. The monk asked, "What is the host within the guest?
The Master said, "The nobleman’s gate is as deep as the sea. The monk asked, "What is the host within the host? The Master said—

The meaning lies within the phrase; understand it clearly here. A pair of solitary wild geese soar high, crashing toward the earth.

Chan Master Fayan of Gānlù in Shūzhou, whose name was Qingyu, was surnamed Huang and was a native of Jiān'ān in Jiànzhōu.

He left home at Dazhong Temple on the mainland. Having passed the scriptural examinations, he attained ordination. He traveled through the regions of Jianghuai to visit various monastic seats and studied under Chan Master Yuanjian, whereupon his realization was certified.

Venerable One, Chan Master Zhonghe of Ruizhu in Taiping Prefecture asked: "When one has attained the seat and donned the robes, all have been entrusted;
how is it with the supreme vehicle of the ancestral lineage? The Master said: "One simply knows that ice is water. The monk asked: "Is there anything further? The Master said: [Silence].
"Do not ask how water becomes ice. The monk said, "One who plays with the tide must be a master of the tide. The Master said, "This monk has come from Zhejiang.

Chan Master Huiguan of Yijing Mountain in Taiping Prefecture was asked:

The monk asked: "Who is the person within this realm? The Master said: "A yellow bird sings before the withered tree on the crag; among the monastic dwellings in the forest, half the monks have white hair. The monk asked: "The Patriarch..."
[The monk] asked, "If the Master has come from the West, what then? The Master said, "The Five Peaks do not descend; the myriad trees have passed through many autumns.
Chan Master Zicong of Nanchan Fusheng in Changzhou asked, "When the Buddhas appear in the world, the heavens rain down four flowers.

[The monk] received the grace. The Master said, "The bright sun is in the midst of the sky. The monk asked, "Is there anything further above this?
The Master said, "There is. The monk asked, "What is the matter further above? The Master said, "Water is known to be pure because of the moon;
the sky is seen to be high because it is free of clouds."
Chan Master Xianzhong Zuyin of Shifosi in Xinchang, Yuezhou, asked:
"What is the Immovable Honored One? The Master said: "A monkey on a hot griddle. The monk asked: "What are the thousands of millions of transformation bodies? The Master said:
"Adding incense, changing water, lighting lamps, and sweeping the floor. The monk asked: "What is the Teacher of Vairocana, the Lord of the Dharma-body? The Master said: "Tying..."
[The monk] asked about the "horse pillar. The Master said, "What connection is there? The monk said, "I would rather bind and kill this fellow.

“If all that has been taught is the teaching of Māra, what then is the teaching of the Buddha? The Master said, “The Buddha does not speak.
The monk asked, “What about the five thousand scrolls [of the scriptures]? The Master said, “That is not a matter for you. The monk asked, “I wonder whose matter it is then?
The Master said, “Cease, cease! There is no need to speak; my Dharma is subtle and inconceivable. Question: “What is appearance (lakṣaṇa)?”

[The monk asked about] "arising. The Master said, "Mountains, rivers, and the great earth. The monk asked, "How is this 'arising through conceptualization'? The Master said, "A rabbit gazing at the moon.
The monk asked, "What is 'arising as a continuous flow'? The Master said, "Without interruption. The monk asked, "What is 'form and emptiness'?"
The Master said, "A five-colored screen. He then ascended the hall and said: "Tsk! Tsk! Tsk! The fish and dragons at the bottom of the sea are all parched with thirst;
a three-legged toad flies up into the sky; a shell-shedding turtle lives amidst the flames. He then ascended the hall and said: "When it is pointed out, one does not arrive."
Right and wrong have not yet been distinguished; when the time comes, there will be no illumination. To mix mud with water—let the *luzhu* (the wooden pillar) leap into the lantern for now.
But why are your eyebrows trailing beneath the heels of your feet?
Even if you were to understand this clearly, it would still be like a monkey wearing a bamboo hat; if you do not understand it, how is it any different from a cricket wearing boots? Nevertheless...
Even so, those who laugh at me are many, while those who smile at me are few.
Chan Master Jingzhu of Hangzhou, who resided at the Jingzhu Monastery, once visited Daguan.

He then asked, "I have a superficial understanding of the sutras and treatises, yet I do not believe in Chan at all. I pray that you, Master, will resolve my doubts. Daguan said, "Since you do not believe in Chan, how can you..."
"Clarifying the sutras: Chan is the mainstay of the sutras, and the sutras are the net of Chan. To grasp the mainstay is to straighten the net; to understand Chan is to see the sutras.
The Master said, "I shall explain Chan for you. Guo'an said, "The subsequent text is long. The Master said, "If it is so, then the sutras and Chan are one and the same body.
Guo'an said, "The Buddha and the Patriarchs do not have two minds; they are like a hand forming a fist, or a fist opening to become a hand. The Master [approved].
Thereupon, he attained a realization and composed this verse: "For over twenty years I have used my mind in vain suspicion; How many times have I tried to extinguish this heart?
Now, in my decline, I have met a true friend; It turns out Jiang Bai was truly the most talented scholar."
Chan Master Jizhen Wenjian of Guangjiao Monastery in Xuanzhou went to visit Daguan. He then asked:
"Aside from my own lectures and expositions, I have investigated the vast teachings spoken by all the Buddhas; how can I come to see their ultimate limit? Daguan said:

"Upon what do you usually rely when lecturing and expounding? The Master replied: "I rely on the teachings to explain their meaning. Daguan said: "Relying on the teachings to explain their meaning..."
"An enemy of the Buddhas of the three periods of time. The Master said, "To depart from even a single word of the Teaching is to speak like a demon.
Guoan asked, "I do not ask about the meaning of your teaching; who is it that expounds it? The Master said, "I see only movement, stillness, and speech; its form and appearance cannot be beheld."
Guanyun said, "This very formlessness is itself vastness. If you awaken to this mind, you will see its limits. From this point on, the Master attained a realization.
He ascended the hall and said, "One who wishes to be a patriarch must thoroughly understand the phrase of light and darkness.

In the middle of the night, it is applied to the eyes, entirely becoming a path laid out in emptiness. The busy Śākyamuni, at his birth, forcibly looked around in all four directions; he patted his own chest alone."
He was acclaimed as supreme. Furthermore, he walked seven steps; who could have known this in the light? Who could have been enlightened by this in the darkness?

Since then, for hundreds and thousands of years, the number of kalpas has been counted like grains of sand in the Ganges. One blind man leads a multitude of blind men; the blind follow one another, supporting each other up.
On that day, when they meet the Old Man Yama, they will stare blankly with eyes bulging. At that time, do not cry out, "The cauldrons of boiling water have no place to grow cool! Do not go hungry.
With a haughty air, he merely twirled his chopsticks and sent word to future generations: "Do not be deceived by the words of Xu Liu.
Chan Master Gongchen of Xiyu Mountain in Huzhou asked: "On this day, when the fourfold assembly has gathered like clouds, I request that the Master employ skillful means to display the family style.
The Master said: "Speech is never uttered in vain. The monk said: "It is entirely due to this very day. The Master said: "Merit is not..."
Langshi asked, "What is the matter that transcends [the ordinary]? The Master said, "The blazing sun hangs high. The monk spread out both hands. The Master said, "How is it? The monk bowed.
The Master said, "He is still thirty blows short. Ascending the hall, he said: "Lingyun seeing the flowers—there was a film over his eyes.
Xuansha wrinkling his fingers—his very body met with misfortune. It would be better to just pass the time in this manner."
Naturally, body and mind are at peace and happy. He ascended the hall and said: "Principle arises because of phenomena; the mind is born following objects.

When both phenomena and objects are forgotten, how can one reach the state of 'just so' amidst a thousand mountains and ten thousand waters? After a long silence, he said: "Do not yet gouge out flesh to create a sore.
He ascended the hall again and said: "To climb ten thousand feet, one must first take that first step. To fathom the thousand-fathom sea, it is truly..."
A single drop is the root. If it is thus, then from the minute to the manifest, and from the shallow to the deep, one transcends the gate-style;
a definitive realization can then immediately arise.
Chan Master Chengtian Chensu of Changzhou asked: "Whose song does the Master sing? Whose ancestral wind does he succeed? The Master said: "In speech, even Śāriputra would be afraid;
in movement and stillness, even Aśvaghoṣa would be startled. The monk said: "The Way of Daguan will flourish from this point on.
The Master said: "What are you talking about? What about Asaṅga and Vasubandhu? The Master raised his whisk and said: "O worthy ones!"
"Tell me, does this man have a Dharma heir or not? The assembly remained silent. The Master said, "Donning his robes, he crossed the Mengjin River," struck the meditation seat, and descended from it.
Chan Master Yongzhang of Fazheng Monastery in Yuezhou asked: "Whose song does the Master sing? Whose ancestral wind does he succeed? The Master said:
"The golden sun emerges from the sea; all people look up to it. The monk said: "The true son of Daguan; the grandson of Cizhao. The Master said:
"Already having ascended to the heavens, its flowing light scatters across the hundred rivers. The monk said: "Your vast and profound Dharma-talent startles the fourfold assembly."
The assembly of worthies all envy the sound of the rolling thunder. The Master said: "I rejoice that you have ceased looking upward;
it shoots through your dry skull. Chan Master Shaoming of Faxon Temple in Yuezhou asked: "What is the realm of Dharma-nature? The Master said:
"The ocean tide rises outside the door; the jeweled pagoda towers amidst the clouds. The monk asked: "What is the person within the realm? The Master said: "Half worldly, half..."
The monk asked, "Regarding the matter of the supreme vehicle (zōngchéng) above, what is it like? The Master said, "Six times six is thirty-six.
Chan Master Shànduán of Bānrùo in Kūnshān, Sūzhōu, asked, "When there is birth and there is extinction, these are all ordinary phenomena.
But when there is neither birth nor extinction, how is it? The Master said, "Kunlun puts on his boots and stands in mid-air. The monk said, "Is this not it?"
The monk said, "There is no place for a person to dwell. The Master said, "A stone woman adorns herself with flowers and sleeps amidst the flames. The monk said, "May the assembly bear witness.
The Master said, "Furthermore, behold the earthen oxen fighting as they enter the sea."
Chan Master Liang of Jianfu in Suzhou, a successor of Chan Master Huiyue of Dongting in Suzhou, asked:
"Without relying on verbal explanations, I request the Master to grant me instruction. The Master said, "The assembly all sees you asking in this manner.
The monk asked, "Is it not simply this very thing? The Master said, "Rarely encountered is one who pierces through..."
The Guest of the Ear. Ascending the hall, he said: "Clouds gather at the edge of the sky; the sun reaches the steps before us. The scenery is such as this—Zen practitioners, open your eyes!
*Chan*! Chan Master Suizhou Ruiyuan Song asked: "When the bright moon is in the heavens, why does it not shine upon the dark room? The Master [said]: [He]... (text fragment)

[The Master] said, "What can be done? A monk asked, "Where is your compassion? The Master said, "It is of no use. He ascended the hall and said: "Three times he was struck with the staff, yet he remained utterly silent.

This has burdened his descendants, who have been unable to explain it away. Tell me directly: where did he go wrong? Try to discern this for me. Examine!"* *Note: This passage refers to the famous story of Mazu Daoyi striking his disciple Baizhang Huaihai three times with his staff before Baizhang could utter a word.
The Master here challenges the assembly to discern the underlying principle of that encounter.*
Chan Master Shizhen of Chengtian Temple in Changzhou asked: "Whose song does the Master sing? Whose ancestral style does he succeed? The Master said:
"A single wheel of brilliant purity illuminates the realms of sand; ten-thousand-fathom green mountains press down upon Lake Tai. The monk said: "If that is so, then you are the true son of Dongting.
The Master said: "I leave it entirely to your own divination with the ladle. [Another] asked: "What is the Buddha? The Master said: "The hand-seal is divided."
Ming said, "The words reveal the profound principle; I beg the Master for a skillful means. The Master said, "Everyone joins their palms.
Zhangxi Xiushu, the Dharma heir of Chan Master Mingzhou, asked Chan Master Baixuan of Huangyan, Taizhou, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? The Master said, "A thousand..."
"Chopping firewood by day and burning it all night. A monk asked, "I do not wish to remain silent; how is it when one relies briefly upon provisional teachings?
The Master said, "Knowing it yet deliberately transgressing it. The monk bowed, and the Master struck him.
Chan Master Yunyan Zhi of Mingzhou asked: "To have a question and an answer is merely the ordinary. But what about when there is neither question nor answer?
The Master said, "Gazing intently at the white waves, one loses the oar. The monk asked, "I do not understand the meaning of this.
The Master said, "The front part is still tolerable."
Chan Master Zhicai of Mount Ruiyan in Mingzhou, successor to Chan Master Jin of Mount Shimen in Mingzhou, asked: "What is the phrase that cuts off all streams? The Master said:

"Excellent. The monk asked, "What is the phrase of 'following the waves and riding the currents'? The Master said, "Following. The monk asked, "What is the phrase of 'the casket covering the universe'?
The Master said, "Closing. The monk asked, "The three phrases have been pointed out by the Master; how does one distinguish between the ancient and the modern?
The Master said, "Henceforth, you must not misquote them. The Master further said, "The causal conditions regarding the question just posed by that monk must also be [understood]."
Only one who can bear this heavy burden is truly qualified. One must not compete in flowery and ornate phrases, mistaking them for the True Dharma (Zongcheng).
If you act in such a manner, even if you were to study until the kalpa of stone-wiping is exhausted, there would still be no end in sight.
Why? Have you not seen the ancient masters say: "Two mouths with but one tongue—this is my school’s principle"? O practitioners of Zen!
Do you understand? Unless you are a poet, do not offer a poem. He ascended the hall and said: "Because heaven is impartial, it constantly covers all;

because earth is impartial, it constantly supports all; because the sun and moon are impartial, the four seasons are eternally bright; because nirvana is impartial, ordinary beings and sages are non-dual;
because the human mind is impartial, there is no contention between high and low. He took up his staff, struck it once, and said: "All..."
Zen practitioner: This staff speaks the Dharma-gate of equality to all people day and night. Do you hear it?
If you do hear it, I dare say your journey as a wandering monk is complete. If you say you do not hear it, I nevertheless grant that the eye atop your crown is perfectly clear.
Why? Because this Dharma is equal; it has no high or low. This is called Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
[He attained] Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. After a long silence, he smiled and said: "The subsequent discourse is lengthy.
Chan Master Jingduan of Wushan, Huzhou, a successor of Chan Master Longhua Qiyue of Hangzhou, was a native of that same province.
Having once visited a patriarchal master, he suddenly awakened to the full functioning of his original capacity.
His understanding did not dwell in the abstruse; his insight was sharp and liberated. He presided over three successive Dharma seats, where the assembly was small yet responsive to his timing.
Later, he withdrew to live in seclusion at his home mountain. Entering the hall, he said: "The lion of Mount Wu has come to roar amidst the clouds.
There is no other Buddha-dharma to deliberate upon; it is better to perform a somersault. Having said this, he leaped down from the Dharma seat.
