six did not meet a true知音 (zhīyīn—'one who knows the sound'). As for this one alone, he is not even worth keeping. She then threw him into the water.
In the midst, one's own child is cast away and no longer recognized as kin. Letting go of the hand, one returns home; there is no need to ask for the ford.
A traveler on the waves who displays his oar and raises his paddle—do not seek a ferryman at the riverhead.
Chan Master Zhenneng Wen of Dongshan in Yunzhou (one case):
He cites the "withdrawing the glance" of Master Yunmen.
As for Master Yunmen’s withdrawing the glance, it has its own origins: not pointed out, not reached; "Rest! Rest! Rest! Rest!"
Case 1: Chan Master Shouduan of Haihui in Shu State (Two Cases).
A monk asked Dongshan, "What is the Buddha? Dongshan said, "Three pounds of flax."
The weight and measure are clearly defined; I shall not betray you. Let no anger arise within the pupils of your eyes.
Of the three hundred and sixty thousand days of a hundred-year life, when joy is found, simply rejoice.
Case: A monk asked Yangqi, "What was the meaning of Bodhidharma facing the wall at Shaolin? Yangqi said, "The man from the West did not understand the language of Tang;

heaven is high and earth is distant, so people are beyond seeing; the waters are broad and the mountains are layered, making them difficult to discuss; ten thousand ages cannot be moved by the eight winds."
[The Master] entered. A person from the Western Heavens did not understand the Tang language.
Chan Master Changzong Zhaojue of Donglin on Mount Lu [related one case]:
After Boatman Shang ascended to receive Jia Shan, he stepped upon and capsized his boat.
Under Jia Shan’s oar, he awakened to the mind and ceased; what need to worry about body or name? He stepped upon the overturned boat.
Through ancient times to the present, the fisherman at Huating who casts his line across the misty waves makes those on the river sigh with sorrow.
Case 1: Chan Master Baoning Renyong of Jiangning Prefecture (Five Cases).
The Sixth Patriarch asked Master Ren: "Where have you come from? Ren replied: "From Master An at Mount Song."
The Sixth Patriarch asked, "What thing comes in such a manner? Huairang replied, "To describe it as a single thing is not correct.
The Sixth Patriarch asked, "Is there still need for cultivation and realization? Huairang replied, "Cultivation and realization are not non-existent, yet it cannot be defiled."
The Sixth Patriarch said: "This very non-defilement is the protective mindfulness of all Buddhas. I am thus;
you are also thus. The twenty-seventh patriarch of India, Prajñātāra, prophesied that the Buddha-dharma would depart from your side.
Hereafter, a 'horse colt' shall emerge, who will trample the people of the world to death."
Horns upon his head and fur upon his back, he comes in this manner; the Iron Ring Mountains and all peaks are utterly shattered. He tramples the Jambudvīpa continent, killing countless beings;
his nose is pierced deep through, and he cannot be pulled back.
Case: Layman Pang asked Mazu, "The original body is not obscure; I ask the Master to cast his eyes high. Mazu looked straight up.
The Layman said, "This is a single-stringed lute; only you, Master, can play it with such subtlety. Mazu looked straight down. The Layman bowed.
As Mazu returned to his quarters, the Layman followed behind him and said, "Playing with cleverness leads to disaster."
Clumsy!
Vastly he comes, bearing mountains and supporting peaks; his stance is towering, propping up heaven and buttressing earth. Let him indulge in cleverness until it turns to clumsiness;
casting off his hands, he strides forward and never looks back.
Case: Nanquan addressed the assembly, saying, "The Way is not outside of things; that which is outside of things is not the Way. Zhaozhou came forward and asked, "What is the Way outside of things?
Nanquan struck him immediately. Zhaozhou caught the staff and said, "Master, do not strike me;
you will strike the wrong person later on. Nanquan threw down his staff and said, "It is easy to distinguish dragons from snakes."
It is difficult for a patch-robed monk to deceive him.
Wrapping himself in softness, he conceals his edge as he enters the fray; captured at the moment of painting, his eyes stare wide open. A hero who decides life and death in a single stroke;
one with the talent of both civil and military, a general and a minister combined.
Case: Shitou asked Changzi, "Where have you come from? Changzi said, "From Lingnan.
Shitou said, "Has the one shop at the head of Dayu Ridge been completed yet? Changzi said, "It was completed long ago; it simply lacks the dotting of the eyes.
Shitou said, "Do you not wish for the eyes to be dotted? Changzi said, "I request them at once. Shitou leaned forward.
He set down one foot. Long-Beard then prostrated. Touzi asked, "What have you seen? Long-Beard replied, "Like a single speck of snow upon a red-hot furnace."
One set of the Thousand-Handed and Thousand-Eyed Avalokiteśvara is ten parts complete, yet its consecration has not yet been performed;
behold how spiritual powers manifest beneath the brush—there is further miraculous trace remaining above.
Case: Bāzhuo addressed the assembly, saying: "If you have a staff, I shall give you a staff;
if you have no staff, I shall take your staff away."
If you have it, pick it up right before your face; if you do not have it, snatch it from behind.
How pitiable is that which possesses a lustrous black lacquer finish—once struck, a thousand doors and ten thousand gates swing open.
**Chan Master Dinghui Chaoxin Haiyin of Suzhou (Seven Cases)** Case:
When Shishuang Puhui passed away, the assembly appointed the Head Seat as abbot.

Attendant Qian said, "If you, Head Seat, can understand the meaning of our late teacher, only then may you dwell here. Our late teacher said: "Rest! Cease! In a single thought, ten thousand [thoughts]..."
The years have passed; it went into the incense burner in the ancient temple like a single white silk ribbon. Tell me, what was the meaning of the Master?
The Head Seat said, "This is merely clarifying matters on the side of the 'one color' (monochromatic). The attendant said, "The Head Seat does not understand the Master's meaning.
The Head Seat said, "Bring some incense. When the incense smoke breaks, if I do not cast off [this body], then I am not [enlightened].
He had grasped the meaning of the former master. As soon as the incense smoke ceased, the Head Seat passed away.
The attendant struck him once on the back and said, "It is not that he did not depart, yet he certainly did not understand the meaning of the former master."
The Zhang family raised several sons. The eldest followed his father’s example in managing the household estate. Among them was one son whose artistic skill was most refined;
his bearing was like that of a king, and his presence was fiercely majestic. Farewell! Farewell! He would have trampled the ocean floor, disregarding the pearl of the black dragon;
he would have dispersed the white clouds, caring not for the moon of the vast heavens.
Case: The Venerable Fu of Taiyuan went to visit Xuefeng. Upon arriving before the abbot’s quarters, he looked at Xuefeng and then went down to attend to the administrative affairs.
The following day, he entered the abbot’s quarters and said, "Yesterday I offended you, Master.
Xuefeng said, "Knowing it was such a matter, let it rest."
General Li Guang was peerless throughout antiquity and the present. Penetrating deep into the enemy's encampment, he preserved his life and avoided harm;
without raising a blade, he achieved minor victories that have left a reputation for glory at the frontier passes to this day.
Case: When Linji took his leave of Huangbo, Huangbo asked, "Where are you going? Linji replied, "Not south of the River, then north of the River.
Huangbo struck him. Linji seized the staff and gave Huangbo a slap.
Huangbo laughed loudly and called to his attendant, "Bring the meditation board and whisk of the former master. Linji said, "Attendant, bring fire! Huangbo said, "Although..."
It is indeed so. You may simply take it with you; hereafter, you shall silence the tongues of all under heaven.
The parting between teacher and disciple is not for long. Bring forth the meditation board and command the fire to burn it; even the ancestral Buddhas and patriarchs do not value their own spirits.
When faith and practice remain, who else could possibly uphold them?
Case: Guangzhao of Langya asked Master Ju, "Where have you recently departed from? Ju replied, "The Two Zhe provinces. Guangzhao said, "Did you come by boat or by land?
Ju said, "By boat. Guangzhao said, "Where is the boat now? Ju said, "It has walked off on its own.
Guangzhao said, "Please sit for a moment and drink some tea. Ju said, "Nyo! Nyo! (A bow of acknowledgment.)

The old fisherman is carefree, drifting east or west as he pleases. He plays his reed flute crosswise, the notes sounding irregular. When the night is still and the moon is bright, the fish do not bite;
he lies down upon his small boat and drifts into the Wuling Stream.
Case: Guishan addressed the assembly, saying, "The phrase with meaning and the phrase without meaning are like a vine leaning against a tree.
Later, Shushan asked, "What is it when the tree falls and the vine withers? Guishan laughed heartily and returned to his quarters.
The tree falls and the vines wither; he poses a single question. He laughs aloud with a reason: the antelope hangs from its horns, leaving no trace to be found.
Even until now, his laughter has not ceased.
Case: A monk asked Master Linji, “What is the Buddha? Linji said, “The reed sprouts pierce the knees.
To grasp with the hand as it comes is like a flash of lightning; the total function of the great capacity is swift as the wind. To let go and utter a single phrase that conveys the message:
in the deep night, the monkey cries amidst the jagged peaks.
Danyuan addressed National Teacher Huaihai, saying, "I am going south. If someone suddenly asks me about the ultimate matter, how should I respond?
The Master said, "Fortunately, you are already a pitiable being; why must you insist on having a talisman for protecting your body?"

If you do not value your own numinous spirit, it is still not enough; as for talismans to protect the body, how much less can they be relied upon? For your sake, I have communicated a message beyond the literal meaning:
the autumn moon, cloudless, falls into the azure pool.
Case 2: Master Fodeng Dexun of Huelin in Tokyo (Two Instances).
It is cited that Zhaozhou asked a monk, "Have you finished eating your congee? The monk replied, "I have finished. Zhaozhou said, "Go wash your bowl."
When the gruel is finished, he orders them to wash their bowls; often those with a beginner's mind become even more coarse.
Even if one reaches this point with clarity, they have already been no true man throughout their life.
Case: A monk asked Yunmen, "If one does not give rise to a single thought, is there still any fault? Yunmen said, "Mount Sumeru.
Their questions and answers were adapted to the capacity of the interlocutor, sometimes shallow and sometimes profound; Yunmen was truly one who had thoroughly mastered the monastic community.
Nowadays, people compete with one another, running after Mount Sumeru; countless ordinary people are thus submerged and lost.
Chan Master Yiqing of Mount Touzi in Shuzhou (Four Cases).
A monk asked Dongshan, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? Dongshan said, "Wait until the waters of Dong Creek flow upstream."
I shall tell you at once:

In the ancient source where there is no water, what sound can there be? A fresh current flows along the western bank in the full autumn wind. At the Onion Range, the inquiry into the Bear-Ear dream has ceased;
in the snowy courtyard, do not speak of the spring at Shaolin.
Case: A monk asked Shishuang, "What is the place of profound depth at Shishuang? Shishuang said: "A lockless door, both ends swinging;
the moon falls at the third watch, the two mountains shine bright. The ancient road is long and moss grows upon it; when the golden lock swings, there is no hand."
"Seize it! The moon-hare in the heart of the blue waves is constantly moving.
[The Master] raised his whisk. A monk asked Jia Shan, "What is the realm of Jia Shan? Shan said, "A monkey cradles its young and returns behind the green peaks;
a bird carries a flower and drops it before the azure cliffs."
The moon is bright; beneath the green pines, the crane’s dream is long. Azure clouds and vermilion pillars hang with wild goats. High cliffs and precipitous peaks are covered in a thousand-fold snow;
Stone shoots sprout branches amidst the midnight frost.
Case: A monk asked Caoshan, "How was it before the Buddha appeared in the world? Caoshan said, "Caoshan is not as good.
The monk asked, "How was it after he appeared in the world? Caoshan said, "Not as good as Caoshan."

The moon hides behind the green mountains as auspicious vapors rise high; the phoenix dwells in the *wú* tree, its gaze reaching far beyond. Suddenly, a stone horse passes through the depths of the pool;
the startled and enraged earth-dragon overturns the ocean tide.
Master Zhengjue Zhihai Benyi of Dongting (Six Cases) cited:
One day, Yunmen saw the *zhisui* (the temple steward) eating steamed buns in front of the Sangha Hall.
He asked, "How many buns have you eaten? The steward replied, "Five. Yunmen said, "How many can the pillar eat? The steward replied, "Please [ask it]."
The Abbot was drinking tea in the tea hall when the Gatekeeper returned directly to the Abbot’s quarters.
Under the guidance of Shao Yang, many were brilliant; the talent of the Steward was likewise sagacious.
Before the Yunhua Hall, the uneven ground was leveled all at once, without the need for laborious effort.

Case: A non-Buddhist asked the Buddha, “What Dharma did you teach today? The Buddha replied, “I taught the Dharma of certainty. When he asked again the following day, “What Dharma did you teach today?
the Buddha replied, “I taught the Dharma of uncertainty. The non-Buddhist said, “Yesterday it was certain; why is it uncertain today?
The Buddha said, “Yesterday it was certain; today it is uncertain.”
The Tathāgata’s Chan at the assembly on Vulture Peak—how could its questions and answers ever have been anything other than profound? Today is not fixed;
yesterday was fixed. Borrowing a neighbor’s skirt to bow in greeting for the New Year.
Case: Once there was an elder who, throughout the summer retreat, did not speak with his monks.
A certain monk sighed and said, "I have let this entire summer pass in vain. I do not dare hope for the Master to preach the Buddha-dharma;

even if I could but hear two characters of the True Cause (zhengyin), that would suffice. When the elder heard this, he told him, "Ācārya, do not speak so hastily. If we are to discuss the True Cause—"
"Not a single word. Having spoken thus, he tapped his teeth and said, "Just now, for no reason, I spoke in such a manner.
An old practitioner in the neighboring wall heard this and remarked, "What a fine pot of soup that has been defiled by two mouse droppings!"
Throughout the summer, he harmonized a single pot of soup; even Fu Yan would not have granted him equal standing.
Do not say that it was defiled and unseen—next door, the Chan elder’s single eye is bright.
The Case: The Second Patriarch stood in the snow at Shaolin and severed his arm to inquire: "May I hear the Dharma-seal of all Buddhas? Bodhidharma said:
"The Dharma-seal of all Buddhas is not obtained from another. The Patriarch said: "My mind is not yet at peace; I beg the Master to bring it to rest for me. Bodhidharma said:
"Bring forth your mind, and I will bring it to rest for you. The Patriarch said: "I have searched for my mind, but it is utterly unobtainable. Bodhidharma—
It is said: "I have finished settling your mind for you.
Severing one’s arm is more difficult than standing in the snow; when the mind is found nowhere, only then does the mind find peace.
Who knows that within this realm of ten-thousand-acre reeds, every single fisherman holds his fishing pole?"
Case: A monk asked Xianglin, “What is the matter beneath the patched robe? Xianglin said, “In the twelfth month, fire burns the mountains.
The monk asked about the matter beneath the robe; the Master said, “Fire burns the mountains; even a Buddha’s hand cannot block it. Human minds are as if indifferent.”
Case: A monk asked Foyan, "What is the matter above the Buddha? Foyan said, "The conch shell is the topknot.
[The monk asked,] "What is the matter below the Buddha? Foyan said, "The lotus seat."
A conch-spiral topknot upon a lotus seat; a fragrant elephant trumpeting and a lion’s roar.
Having fallen into the human world for three hundred years, it has silenced the mouths of all monks under heaven.
Case: Chan Master Shouyan of Mount Yinjing in Taiping Prefecture (Two Records).

It is related that when Master Yaoshan first visited Stonehead, he secretly grasped the profound essence of the teaching. One day, while they were seated together, Stonehead saw him and asked, "What are you doing here?
Yaoshan replied, "I am not doing anything at all. Stonehead said, "If that is so..."
Xianzuo said, "I am doing it. Touzi said, "You say you are not doing it; what is it that you are not doing?
Xianzuo said, "Even the thousand sages do not know it."

Striking grass with a stone to startle the snake; guarding the profound mechanism in secret, cutting off all emotional entanglements. To pursue the swift phrase that follows the wind, one must discern its true mark.
The report says: "The thousand sages do not know its name."
Case: One day, while sitting in his quarters, Mount Huangbo was attended by Yangshan and Xiangyan.
Mount Huangbo said, "Nowadays, those who act in this way are few, while those who do not act in this way are many. Xiangyan walked from east to west, and Yangshan walked from west to east.
Mount Huangbo said, "This causal connection will, thirty years hence, be like gold cast upon the ground."
Yanxiu said, "One must still have the Master provide a proclamation before it can be attained. Xiangyan said, "Even now, there is nothing lacking.
Guishan said, "Shut your mouth!"
Guishan’s hanging words distinguish the dragons from the snakes; a pair of *li* pearls, utterly free of flaw. Within the lion’s den there are no other beasts;
its glorious fame shakes the earth and reaches the ends of the world.
Case 1: Chan Master Liyuan Foyin of Yunju Mountain (Four Cases).
A monk asked the Sixth Patriarch, "Who can attain the essential meaning of Huangmei? The Patriarch replied, "One who understands the Dharma can attain it.
The monk asked, "Does the Master yourself attain it? The Patriarch said, "I do not attain it. The monk asked, "Why does the Master..."
"No. The Patriarch said, "I do not understand the Buddha-dharma.
On that day at Huangmei, those who transmitted the intent were as numerous as bamboo and reeds; those with the horns and heads of a qilin and a dragon have all become empty.
Old Lu has nothing by which to compare himself."
Case: Master Si asked the Sixth Patriarch, "What should one attend to so as not to fall into the ranks [of gradual cultivation]?
The Patriarch said, "What have you ever done? Si said, "I do not even practice the Noble Truths. The Patriarch said, "Into what rank would you then fall?
Si said, "If I do not even practice the Noble Truths, where could there be any ranks? The Patriarch said, "So it is, so it is. You must protect this well."
Maintain it!
Even the Noble Truths have not been practiced since of old; there is no further stage to be cultivated or maintained.
To this day, Lu Da is still pounding rice—mixed with grain and husks, to whom shall they be given?
Case: A monk asked Master Nanquan, “After a hundred years, when you pass away, where will you go?
Nanquan said, “I shall become a water buffalo at the house of a lay donor in front of the mountain. The monk said, “May I follow you there?
Nanquan said, “If you come, bring a blade of grass in your mouth.”
His conduct has always been among those of different species; one knows not with whom his horns may match.
If he comes to meet you carrying water and grass in his mouth, he will shake his tail and head, letting the wind blow through the four wilds.

Case: A monk asked National Teacher Longya, "How should one apply effort throughout the twelve periods of the day? Longya said, "It is only when one is like a handless person performing a fist that it is truly so."
The handless man possesses the greatest power of the fist. Longya once struck Duchanhe;
even if you exhaust all your efforts, it will not equal the shuttle on the wall of a potter’s kiln.

Case 1: Chan Master Ciyun Yuanzhao of Qianzhou (Two Rules). It is said that when Master Baima was alive, he would often cry out, "What joy! But at the time of his death, he cried out, "Alas! Alas! The temple steward asked him: [The Master] said: "I have been calling 'joy' all along; why do you ask? The steward replied, "When you were alive, you called it 'joy,' but now you are crying 'alas. Why is this? The Master said, "When I was alive, I was free from illness; now I am suffering from illness. The steward said, "If you are free from illness, why did you call it 'joy'? The Master said, "Because I was free from illness, I called it 'joy. Now that I am suffering from illness, I call it 'alas. The steward said, "If you are free from illness, why do you still call it 'alas'? The Master said, "Though I am free from illness, I cannot avoid the pain of illness. The steward said, "If you cannot avoid the pain of illness, why did you call it 'joy'? The Master said, "Though I cannot avoid the pain of illness, I can avoid the pain of death. The steward said, "If you can avoid the pain of death, why did you call it 'alas'? The Master said, "Though I can avoid the pain of death, I cannot avoid the pain of the Dharma-nature. The steward said, "If you cannot avoid the pain of the Dharma-nature, why did you call it 'joy'? The Master said, "Though I cannot avoid the pain of the Dharma-nature, I can avoid the pain of birth and death. The steward said, "If you can avoid the pain of birth and death, why did you call it 'alas'? The Master said, "Though I can avoid the pain of birth and death, I cannot avoid the pain of the three realms. The steward said, "If you cannot avoid the pain of the three realms, why did you call it 'joy'? The Master said, "Though I cannot avoid the pain of the three realms, I can avoid the pain of the four modes of birth. The steward said, "If you can avoid the pain of the four modes of birth, why did you call it 'alas'? The Master said, "Though I can avoid the pain of the four modes of birth, I cannot avoid the pain of the five aggregates. The steward said, "If you cannot avoid the pain of the five aggregates, why did you call it 'joy'? The Master said, "Though I cannot avoid the pain of the five aggregates, I can avoid the pain of the six sense bases. The steward said, "If you can avoid the pain of the six sense bases, why did you call it 'alas'? The Master said, "Though I can avoid the pain of the six sense bases, I cannot avoid the pain of the seven consciousnesses. The steward said, "If you cannot avoid the pain of the seven consciousnesses, why did you call it 'joy'? The Master said, "Though I cannot avoid the pain of the seven consciousnesses, I can avoid the pain of the eight consciousnesses. The steward said, "If you can avoid the pain of the eight consciousnesses, why did you call it 'alas'? The Master said, "Though I can avoid the pain of the eight consciousnesses, I cannot avoid the pain of the nine orifices. The steward said, "If you cannot avoid the pain of the nine orifices, why did you call it 'joy'? The Master said, "Though I cannot avoid the pain of the nine orifices, I can avoid the pain of the ten directions. The steward said, "If you can avoid the pain of the ten directions, why did you call it 'alas'? The Master said, "Though I can avoid the pain of the ten directions, I cannot avoid the pain of the twelve links of dependent origination. The steward said, "If you cannot avoid the pain of the twelve links of dependent origination, why did you call it 'joy'? The Master said, "Though I cannot avoid the pain of the twelve links of dependent origination, I can avoid the pain of the eighteen realms. The steward said, "If you can avoid the pain of the eighteen realms, why did you call it 'alas'? The Master said, "Though I can avoid the pain of the eighteen realms, I cannot avoid the pain of the twenty-two faculties. The steward said, "If you cannot avoid the pain of the twenty-two faculties, why did you call it 'joy'? The Master said, "Though I cannot avoid the pain of the twenty-two faculties, I can avoid the pain of the twenty-four seasons. The steward said, "If you can avoid the pain of the twenty-four seasons, why did you call it 'alas'? The Master said, "Though I can avoid the pain of the twenty-four seasons, I cannot avoid the pain of the twenty-five existences. The steward said, "If you cannot avoid the pain of the twenty-five existences, why did you call it 'joy'? The Master said, "Though I cannot avoid the pain of the twenty-five existences, I can avoid the pain of the twenty-six realms. The steward said, "If you can avoid the pain of the twenty-six realms, why did you call it 'alas'? The Master said, "Though I can avoid the pain of the twenty-six realms, I cannot avoid the pain of the twenty-seven afflictions. The steward said, "If you cannot avoid the pain of the twenty-seven afflictions, why did you call it 'joy'? The Master said, "Though I cannot avoid the pain of the twenty-seven afflictions, I can avoid the pain of the twenty-eight hells. The steward said, "If you can avoid the pain of the twenty-eight hells, why did you call it 'alas'? The Master said, "Though I can avoid the pain of the twenty-eight hells, I cannot avoid the pain of the twenty-nine paths. The steward said, "If you cannot avoid the pain of the twenty-nine paths, why did you call it 'joy'? The Master said, "Though I cannot avoid the pain of the twenty-nine paths, I can avoid the pain of the thirty realms. The steward said, "If you can avoid the pain of the thirty realms, why did you call it 'alas'? The Master said, "Though I can avoid the pain of the thirty realms, I cannot avoid the pain of the thirty-one states of existence. The steward said, "If you cannot avoid the pain of the thirty-one states of existence, why did you call it 'joy'? The Master said, "Though I cannot avoid the pain of the thirty-one states of existence, I can avoid the pain of the thirty-two marks. The steward said, "If you can avoid the pain of the thirty-two marks, why did you call it 'alas'? The Master said, "Though I can avoid the pain of the thirty-two marks, I cannot avoid the pain of the thirty-three heavens. The steward said, "If you cannot avoid the pain of the thirty-three heavens, why did you call it 'joy'? The Master said, "Though I cannot avoid the pain of the thirty-three heavens, I can avoid the pain of the thirty-four abodes. The steward said, "If you can avoid the pain of the thirty-four abodes, why did you call it 'alas'? The Master said, "Though I can avoid the pain of the thirty-four abodes, I cannot avoid the pain of the thirty-five dharmas. The steward said, "If you cannot avoid the pain of the thirty-five dharmas, why did you call it 'joy'? The Master said, "Though I cannot avoid the pain of the thirty-five dharmas, I can avoid the pain of the thirty-six elements. The steward said, "If you can avoid the pain of the thirty-six elements, why did you call it 'alas'? The Master said, "Though I can avoid the pain of the thirty-six elements, I cannot avoid the pain of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. The steward said, "If you cannot avoid the pain of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, why did you call it 'joy'? The Master said, "Though I cannot avoid the pain of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, I can avoid the pain of the thirty-eight views. The steward said, "If you can avoid the pain of the thirty-eight views, why did you call it 'alas'? The Master said, "Though I can avoid the pain of the thirty-eight views, I cannot avoid the pain of the thirty-nine fetters. The steward said, "If you cannot avoid the pain of the thirty-nine fetters, why did you call it 'joy'? The Master said, "Though I cannot avoid the pain of the thirty-nine fetters, I can avoid the pain of the forty afflictions. The steward said, "If you can avoid the pain of the forty afflictions, why did you call it 'alas'? The Master said, "Though I can avoid the pain of the forty afflictions, I cannot avoid the pain of the forty-one delusions. The steward said, "If you cannot avoid the pain of the forty-one delusions, why did you call it 'joy'? The Master said, "Though I cannot avoid the pain of the forty-one delusions, I can avoid the pain of the forty-two stages. The steward said, "If you can avoid the
"The Master usually calls me 'Happy' (Kuaihuo). Why is it now that he speaks thus?
The Master picked up his pillow and said, "Tell me, was it so at that time, or is it so now? The head monk was speechless.
Sweetness through and through is sweet; bitterness through and through is bitter. When you pick up your pillow, Silla beats the drum at night.
Case: A monk asked Zhaozhou, “What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? Zhaozhou said, “The ox is lost in the pen.”
"The ox is lost within the railing; if there is a question, there is an answer. If you seek further for the profound and mysterious, it is like a monkey kicking a breath-ball.
The Zen Master Weiyue Furi of Jingyin in Dongjing raised two cases.
A monk asked Touzi, "What is the first moon? Touzi said, "It is still cold in the first month of spring. How so?
This is the second month. My son says: "In the middle spring (*zhōngchūn*), the weather gradually warms;
in the first month of spring, it is still cold. (The first month is the middle spring; the second month is when it gradually warms.
If there are no idle matters hanging upon the mind, this is truly a fine season in the world. A fine season indeed! In Jiangnan and the two Zhe regions, the spring is cold and the autumn is likewise.
**Hot.** Case:
A monk asked Yunmen, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? Yunmen said, "Looking at the mountains in the daylight.
"Looking at the mountains in the daylight is fine; A clear breeze sweeps away the white clouds. Where was the fire last night? It burned out the ancient graves."
Chan Master Zhide of Dazhong in Fuzhou (Four Cases).
A monk asked Yantou, "What is it like when the solitary sail is not raised? Yantou said, "The donkey in the back garden is eating grass."
With a solitary sail unhoisted, what can be done? In the back garden, the donkey eats too much grass. Until this very day, it remains idly lowered;
who would have known there was such treachery on level ground?
Case: A monk asked Yunmen, "What is a person of great cultivation? Yunmen said, "A single cup in hand.
In hand, a single cup—utterly free of flaw or blemish. Hearing it from the road or passing it on hearsay only makes it more distant. Even now, those who claim to be masters cannot lift it up;
As before, they must carry it back home alone.
Case: A monk asked Baoci, "When emotion arises, wisdom is obstructed; when conceptualization changes, the essence becomes distinct.
Before emotion has arisen, what is it like? Baoci said, "Obstructed. The monk said, "If emotion has not yet arisen, what exactly is being obstructed?
Baoci said, "The boatman; you have not yet met the right person."
A Barrier. In the blue sky, cloudless, a thunderclap crashes. Among the monks of the monasteries, as numerous as rice and hemp, how many are true *siddha* travelers? Case:
A monk asked Xuansha, "What is the student's own self? Xuansha said, "It is your own self."
"This is your own self. Do not be negligent with one another. Two or three monks merely said, "Go to bed early and rise late.
Chan Master Huijue of Qianming Monastery in Yueyang raised two cases.
A monk asked: "A wild goose flies across the vast sky, its shadow sinking into the cold water. The water has no mind to sink the shadow; the goose has no [mind to cast it]."
"What is the meaning of 'traces left behind'? The Master said: "The matter is attained where there is no mind.
When a wild goose flies across the vast sky, how could it leave a shadow? The shadow sinks into the cold water, yet the water has no mind.
If you can realize this state of no-mind, there is no need for deliberate effort to be 'no-minded'; its depth speaks for itself."
Case: A monk asked Touzi, “What is the white ox on the open ground? Touzi said, “Heh! Heh!
The monk asked, “What does it eat and drink? Touzi said, “Eat! Eat!”
In the open field, the white ox raises the question; responding to the occasion with a "chi-chi," his tusks are chilling. One knows not what he consumes;
with every "chi-chi" bite, he dries up the vast blue sea.
Case: Master Tianzhang Yuanshan of Yuezhou (One Case).
When Yunju Woshou heard a monk reciting the Vimalakīrti Sūtra, he asked, "What sūtra are you reciting? The monk replied:
Regarding the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, the Master said: "I am not asking you about the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*; what is it that you are mindful of? That monk attained realization. [The Master] asked:
"I did not ask about the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, but about what you are mindful of. Do you see it clearly? If you wish to enter the dharma-gates as numerous as the sands of the Ganges..."
The Sea. One word is enough to express it; there is no need for much.
Chan Master Rizi of Shangfang in Huzhou (three cases) cited this:
When Yangqi was invited to take his seat at Jiufeng, after he had finished ascending the dais, the Venerable Jiufeng Qin grabbed him and said:
"Today I have fortunately found a fellow practitioner. Yangqi asked, "What is this matter of being a fellow practitioner?
Feng said, "Jiufeng plows the furrow; Yangqi pulls the handle. Yangqi said, "At such a moment as this, who is in front—Yangqi or Jiufeng?
As Feng hesitated, Yangqi pushed him aside and said, "I thought you were a fellow practitioner; it turns out you are not."
One holds the plowshare, one pulls the plow; on level fields and shallow ground, we follow one another for now.
Just when hunger strikes and there is no fodder, they let loose their horns and wander east and west. Old Yangqi, old Yangqi—everyone says he has always been skilled at prancing his hooves.
Case: Before Dasui’s Hermitage there was a tortoise. A monk pointed to it and asked, "All sentient beings have skin wrapping their bones;
why does this sentient being have bones wrapping its skin? Dasui took off a shoe and placed it upon the tortoise's back.
The bones are on the outside; the skin is on the inside. Though possessing spirit, one does not know how to apply it to oneself.
Even if the hexagram on one's back were clearly defined, nine times nine would still turn out to be eighty-two.
Case: A monk asked National Teacher Zhong, "What is the Dharmakāya Vairocana? The National Teacher said, "Bring me the pure water pitcher.
When the monk brought the pitcher, the National Teacher said, "Place it back where it was. The monk asked again.
"What is the Vairocana of one's own body? The National Teacher said: "The ancient Buddhas have long since passed away;
with both hands clearly passing the pure vase, they do not realize their bodies are already within the moat and city walls.
Even if one were to possess the adamantine eye, it would still be half a month’s journey behind Miaoshan."
*Continued Lamp Record of the Jianzhong Jingguo Era*,
Fascicle Twenty-Eight and Fascicle Twenty-Nine. Compiled by the Dharma-transmitting Chan Master Foguo,
Abbot of Fayun Chan Temple in Dongjing during the Song Dynasty (Subject) Wei Bai.
Verses by Chan Master Fajian Fuhui of Mount Jiangshan (Thirty-four Poems) Śākyamuni Buddha

Looking in the four directions, no one was there; the Dharma was not transmitted. Both the Deer Park and the Crane Tree are utterly desolate. Morning after morning, Great Beings are born into this floating world;
everywhere, the bright stars appear in the azure sky. Kāśyapa held the robe, his brows already furrowed; as the golden coffin was about to be set ablaze, his feet still hung suspended.
Who knows of the events of that year in Magadha? As the sun sets over the twin śāla trees, the evening cicadas cry out.
The First Patriarch, Venerable Mahākāśyapa, once bound the causes of purity with pearls and gold. For ninety-one kalpas he maintained an extraordinary body;

at the assembly of Nirvāṇa, he was a guest from the immortal realms, a man of no affairs amidst robes of discarded rags. Upon whom can this meaning of the wondrous dance be relied for understanding? Sitting alone on the green crags, he is of himself—*zizai*.
Shifting Spring. Where the World-Honored One spoke not for the śrāvakas, the golden garden leaped with auspicious qilin for a thousand ages.

Under the śāla trees at the gate of nirvāṇa, the Second Patriarch, Venerable Ānanda, alone received the golden robe as the honored one among the assembly. When the precious canopy collapsed, there was already [the sign].

A covenant: Where the banner-pole of the *kṣetra* fell, there was originally no root; the assembly of immortals requested testimony as they departed from the mountain foot. Two lords wailed in grief, leaving traces of blood upon the dew.
Who would say that the true body has already entered parinirvāṇa? The wind is fierce by the eternal river, and the flower-foam rushes on.
The Third Patriarch, Venerable Śaṇakavāsin, attained realization through neither dharma nor mind.
Six years after his passing, he emerged from the Sahā world. The Master received his prediction at the Green Forest;

his disciples, seizing the opportunity, were many with white hair. Having long been in the womb, he received the fragrant herb and donned the auspicious robe; he occupies a lofty station in the Brahma palace amidst the flames.
Longke: At present, you merely return with pride and arrogance; you would do better to go once more to the South Mountain.
The Fourth Patriarch, Venerable Upagupta, acted without interval between transformation and practice, and was without partiality;
he gathered others solely by means of the perfuming power of meditative concentration. Late in his life, he cast aside his counting-chip chamber and encountered the mark.

My son, offer this flower garland once more to the army of Mara. Do not rely on the Buddha-dharma as a path of permanence; if you remain attached to body and mind, you have not yet emerged from the crowd.
Hand back that bottomless object of original nature, and return to your old mountain to lie amidst the idle clouds.
On the evening of the Fifth Patriarch, Venerable Diṭṭhika’s birth, a miraculous dream once corresponded with an ancient prophecy: "The radiant sun shall rise to dispel the darkness;
the royal spring shall gush forth to save the parched and withered. Eight thousand cultivate causes that are not the true path; for six kalpas, the matter of parting shall unfold."
How could it be in vain? Today, atop the peak of Mount Bancha, ox-carts and crane-chariots travel the same path together.

The Sixth Patriarch, Venerable Mijia, diligently sought the descendants of the patriarchs and cherished the fleeting light of his years. Golden clouds shimmer and soar over the city walls; even when touching the pure time of fulfillment, one remains like a traveler.

He abandoned his home; consciousness was not his dwelling place, yet he remained close to his native land. The *Lamp of Transmission* foretold that after a hundred years, his ancient surname would be invoked and his far-reaching deeds made manifest.
From then on, he did not return to the Five Indias; he sported amidst the flames like a vajra.
The Seventh Patriarch, Venerable Vasumitra, wandered freely in coarse clothing and simple food;
he constantly held aloft a single drop of nectar. To insist that there is a "transmission of mind" is surely impossible;

if one seeks to debate its meaning, the meaning cannot be established. Through the manifestation of compassionate conditions, he was like clouds without attachment; in the narrow alleys, he sang wildly like the moon.
Self-evident. Turning my thoughts back, I recall that few guests come to the mountains; for whom shall I pour this jar of spring wine?
The Venerable Eighth Patriarch Buddhanandi’s crown-jewel towers high, and he is naturally joyful.
A pure breeze fills the monastery, strengthening the patriarch’s enclosure. His spring-like vigor tirelessly receives and guides weary wanderers.

Reverent. In response to his eloquent discourse, the ocean waves surge; the metaphors leave no room for further speech, yet he knows the true vessel. Seeking the mind within oneself, one relies on these ultimate words.
An old disciple whom others do not recognize—when the white light reaches its end, laughter rises from the carriage.
The Ninth Patriarch, Vimalamitra:
Pitying the passing of fifty years of springtime, he was loath to dwell in wealth yet loath to dwell in poverty. If the Buddhas and Patriarchs do not represent the Way, what other Way could one seek?
If parents are not kin, who else could be more kin? Did he need the lotus to support his feet for seven steps? One must trust that the mirror reflects without words.
How joyful it is! Since ancient times, the Zen gate has been a fastened barrier; it was this man who leaked out the family style.

The Tenth Patriarch, Venerable Xie, possessed a body that was no ordinary vessel and had already heard the voice of the Immortal. That he alone was called "Difficult to Give Birth To" (Nansheng) could not have been by chance. The waves of the bitter sea have ceased, and the whole elephant is revealed.

In the darkness of the mundane world, light radiates from a single perfect pearl; though words cannot fully proclaim it, the profound person attains awakening. When the earth transforms into gold, the Great Dharma is transmitted;
the legacy of the tradition left by Śāriputra endures for a thousand ages. Yet today, most people merely sleep soundly as the sun rises high.
The Eleventh Patriarch, Venerable Punanayasa, do not be surprised that he previously attained the Dharma through longing.
The profound path is vast and silent, severed from the subtle and the minute; awakening and delusion do not exist, and obscurity and clarity are exhausted.

Manifestation and concealment are fundamentally non-existent; one and two are not distinct. To ask the Buddha and not know him is not another way; returning home is to have no dwelling place. This is it.
True refuge. In vain do disciples boast of their纵横 (zōnghéng) eloquence; once the fundamental meaning is briefly indicated, all mental activity ceases.

The Twelfth Patriarch, the Venerable Aśvaghoṣa, achieved the heights of realization and transcended the flow of birth and death. Whether through action or non-action, we have already practiced together. Reaching the ultimate nature of things, he distinguished the multitude of beings.
Longing. On the path of returning clouds, the small insects are filled with anxiety. As the golden dragon passes through the rain, the perilous mountains tremble.
In the ocean of nature, where there is no wind, the terrifying waves cease. Only the sun’s disc, bearing the appearance of setting, still hangs today above the jagged peaks.
The Thirteenth Patriarch, Venerable Kāpimāra, sent Wen, not permitting him to reside in the royal palace.
Hanging his staff, he returned to the deep Xinku Grotto: cold peaks where he traveled alone as clouds swirled about;

a venomous dragon drawing near as trees stood in dense ranks. Who would have known that the place where he set foot in meeting [the Patriarch] was precisely where the Flower was plucked and entrusted?
Entrust this to your mind. Who would have expected that after a thousand years, the old python would cast off its worldly bonds and let out a thunderous roar?

The Fourteenth Patriarch, Venerable Nāgārjuna, out of profound compassion once untied the pearl from his topknot. When the pride of self is first crushed, meritorious karma becomes redundant; one need only ensure that birth and death are constantly understood.
All is understood; sounds and forms are entirely suchness (*tathatā*). The illusionist has vanished like spring ice dissolving; Buddha-nature remains solitary like the moon over the sea.
If you wish to recognize the non-abiding mark of *nirvāṇa*, the entire trichiliocosm is but one Vairocana.
The Fifteenth Patriarch, Venerable Kanadeva, ceased speaking: "There is no path to escape the cage;
when deluded, mountains and rivers appear; when awakened, they are empty space. When the garden was gifted as retribution, wood-ear mushrooms grew;
when the opportunity arose, heaven and earth shared a needle-point. Where the eight lights are exhausted, bubbles return to the sea; when heterodox arguments arise, the snow falls."
Sprinkling pine needles. After the people of the city of Bāveru have departed, the crimson banner still raises a pure breeze.
The Sixteenth Patriarch, Venerable Rāhulata, whose destiny was to respond for a thousand years—how could this be delusory?
His light connects with the five Buddhas to assist in forging the quest; when the gold of the well is smelted away, even the finest trace is severed.
The river water carrying ore flows back upstream; taking "no-self" as one's teacher clarifies the definitive meaning. Holding an alms bowl, he shares his seat to show his fellow practitioners;
though his disciples did not believe him, he had already attained the third fruit. Carrying fragrant food in vain, he passed through several provinces.

The Seventeenth Patriarch, Venerable Saṃghanandin, was able to speak immediately upon birth and attained realization at a young age. He was unwilling to be bound by the constraints of the precious throne;

unaware that the ancestral domain required the transmission of the Way, he needlessly cast aside his meditative practice and left the palace. Alas for the world, as he grieved over the setting sun of the Dharma, he opened his heart in hope for the rising moon.
The clouds gather thickly. Since time immemorial, those who have succeeded to the Dharma have been rare to find. Why begrudge the effort of carrying your staff across a single peak?
The Eighteenth Patriarch, Venerable Gayāsata, was born seven days after passing through the womb;
his skin and flesh were pure and radiant like the springtime of the Snowy Mountains. The people of Yuezhi had already attained awakening a thousand years ago.
Matter. Why should a youth be startled by a hundred-year-old body? Listen: the wind-bell has never been anything other than itself; the precious mirror brought along is naturally free of dust.
Having entered this humble, spacious dwelling, he calls forth the ancient host of the Three Heavens.
The path of the nineteenth patriarch, Venerable Kumāralata, is such that among all the heavens, who could possibly reach it?
It is solely because his compassion was profound that he entered the dusty realm of the world. His solitary spirit dwells in stillness beyond birth and death;
the three realms are but a vast, drifting dream and illusion. How could one easily forget these wondrous verses? Out of earnest concern, he has once again turned them upside down for you.
Mount Doubt: Since the days of old when the heavy gates were knocked, they have remained thus until now, never fastened with a bolt.
When the twenty patriarch, Venerable Jayata, lowered his hand, he lost the Way through his injury;
as the elephant king strides forth, who can pity him? He simply takes that which is birthless beneath words.
This meaning awakens those who sit long in the forest; the ultimate Way is not sought through distraction. To let this urgent moment slip away would be a source of sorrow.
Had I not encountered the assembly at Lacong at that time, my diligent toil would have been in vain for the dust of many kalpas.
The Twenty-first Patriarch, Vairocana (Baxiupantou), recalled how in the past he had earnestly sought the sound of virtue;
the principle that illusions and bubbles are unimpeded is profoundly deep. When the twin pearls depart in a dream, one forgets both light and darkness;

when the single Dharma is transmitted, it transcends antiquity and the present. How could one who has lost the fruit know the prediction of Yuejing? It was because [the Bodhisattva] attained the multitude while in the womb.
Xianqin: As he departs, he treads upon the place where the void is pierced; were it not for a man of true resolve, how could this be easily found?
The twenty-second patriarch, Venerable Maṇḍara, once distinguished between the wise and the ignorant through the division of a stupa.
Having emerged onto the diverging paths of the mundane world, he moved the hearts of the sovereigns of his time. His use of the analogy of almsgiving benefited many people.
Eons pass; listen as a flock of cranes soars and cries. By nature, the mountains and rivers are but vast and profound; the thoughts arising from a single hair-tip are all in turmoil.
Who would have known that on a day when incense is burned in a foreign land, the rising blue smoke once pierced through the white clouds?
The twenty-third patriarch, Venerable Harelana, was called "Holy Son" and "Worthy One" by all in his native village.
Though his physical form had crumbled before his youth, he encountered sorrow as a rainbow pierced the heavens beyond the world;

yet those who sought the Dharma from him returned to the very edge of the sun and moon. To be without self and without action is not the Way; to have merit and to have effort—[is likewise not the Way].
Forgetting the basket [of words]. After the physical relics were divided and he returned once more, his marvels were like a lotus blooming in fire.
The twenty-fourth Patriarch, Master Simha, knew directly from within the mind, transcending all detailed analysis;
among the five assemblies, who would dare to compare him? The youth, having the karmic affinity, was struck with awe as he unfolded [the scroll].
The hand offers a flawless pearl, its luster hidden; having realized emptiness, one has attained a body like an illusion. To boast of arms severed like frost-sharp swords is in vain.
Why need you, O Guangshou, worry that the Dharma will fall? Upon the stupa, the setting sun slants down.
The twenty-fifth patriarch, Varsaganya, encountered many hardships on the road as he intended to secretly propagate the Dharma.
Before I could advance, the Emperor first sent a challenge; yet through a divine sword that manifested in a dream, the net was severed.

When the patriarch’s robe was burned as a test, the banner of the Dharma remained firm. Poisoned food was offered but left him unharmed, and when he was urged to depart, it was due to the influence of others.
How pitiable! Where could there be fire within samādhi? A single bright moon shines in the azure sky.
The Twenty-sixth Patriarch, Venerable Amṛtodana, was in profound accord with the Patriarchal Hall, continuing its pure fragrance.
When the Crown Prince suppressed heterodoxy, the world was struck with awe; how could Dīrghanakha possibly have been a great [threat]?

The silkworm transforms; the mountain is empty, yet it seems to obstruct the lofty clouds. When the Eastern King attained transcendental awakening, what did he ultimately gain? That the holy successor returned once more—how could such a one be easily categorized among the multitudes?
Entrusted with the provisional name "Mind-Ground Treasury," there is nothing further, neither beginning nor end, that can be presented to you.
The twenty-seventh patriarch, Venerable Prajñātāra, skillfully raised the banner of the Dharma by responding to changes and seizing the opportune moment.
When asked about the pearl, he sought its lineage; what is so profound about his intent? In three springs, the fruit ripens beneath the Bodhi tree;

in a single night, the flower blooms and its fragrance fills the world. Yet, though he zealously transmits the lamp, he grieves over the transformation of beings; how could he worry that the water of the immortals might run dry?
As the years pass, I sigh anew that I have not yet seen the day of Maitreya; how many times have I wandered in verse, emulating the wildness of Jianzhi?

The Great Master Bodhidharma, the twenty-eighth patriarch, applied his wisdom according to conditions and refused to settle for ease; traveling through Liang and Wei, how many such journeys did he undertake? His cloud-piercing staff hung upon the thatched hall.

Silence. For the sake of the Dharma, one forgets the cold of a snowy night. Opening leaves and opening flowers, all are without substance; attaining the skin and attaining the marrow, the diversions are manifold.
In vain he left behind a single sandal at Mount Songyang; for descendants of later generations, it is difficult to find a foothold.
The Twenty-ninth Patriarch, Chan Master Huik’e, sat alone before the peak with eyes too weary to open.
The Buddhas and Patriarchs were not far away; he happened upon them in harmony. When his skull was exchanged, the mountain suddenly rose high;

when his wind-illness was expiated through repentance, the withered branches first revealed their vitality. That he secretly provoked slander is truly to be pitied; yet in his later years, he passed even through the quarters of butchers and wine-sellers.
Do not conjecture. Turn your head toward the road beneath the city of Ye: the spring breeze stretches endlessly through the verdant reeds.
For thirty years, the Zen Master Sengcan, the Patriarch, once saw that my Way was suffering from decline;
for ten years he concealed his pearl and lay amidst the green peaks, silently dwelling in the state of non-arising upon this flowery earth.

Entrustment: To seek understanding through the Dharma-gate is to realize it is not so. By the sea at Luofu, he leans long upon the railing; amidst the deep clouds of the mountain valleys, he returns, shaking his staff.
His name is not spoken—cease further questioning. In hand, he carries his straw hat and his old hempen robe.
The legacy of the thirty-first patriarch, Master Daoxin, whose diligent toil surpassed that of former sages, remains.
A śrāmaṇera heard the Dharma while still in his childhood; within the walled city he understood the thief, for divine soldiers had arrived.
Seeking the Buddha-nature on ancient paths, it was perfected; the white vapor already fulfilled the mandate of the lineage, and the purple clouds still bear witness to its breaking through.
At the head of the bed, the stupa opens to reveal the true form, majestic and imposing; it remains for the Chan school to transmit through the ages.
As for the thirty-second patriarch, Master Hongren:
who would say his golden body was lacking? He spoke of the ultimate nature with such loftiness that he transcended all neighbors. His holy fruition is highly esteemed as supreme among monks.

The seat, robes, and bowl were given by himself to those from Lingnan. At the third watch, they were already bestowed; when were they ever not bestowed? For seven hundred years we have been close companions—how easy it was to be so!
It is a pity for those who rushed about in pursuit back then; even now they are still brushing away the dust from their mirror-stands.
The Dharma-lineage of Caoxi, spanning ancient and modern times, has been cold since the time of the Thirty-third Patriarch, Master Huineng.
Now that the Master has arrived, he stirs up waves of awakening once more. Carrying his sack, he was pursued in vain by men at Mount Yuyong;

bearing his stone, the multitude at Huangmei found him difficult to recognize. His mind-field is suddenly awakened to its fragrant blossoms; as he wishes to return to his native village, the leaves [fall].
Withered and decayed. The true principle of distinguishing the wind and the banner remains; try looking at the top of the *kṣa* pole.
Chan Master Tianyi Yihuai of Yuezhou (three poems). On Seizing the Opportunity.
One, two, three, four, five, six, seven. Standing alone on one foot before the ten-thousand-fathom peak, he snatches the bright pearl from the jaws of the black dragon.
With a single word, he exposes the deception of Vimalakīrti.
Form is emptiness, emptiness is form; emptiness and form are both empty. The road at Tongguan Pass is blocked and impassable.
When the kalpa-fire blazes forth and even the finest hairs are consumed, the green mountains remain as before amidst the white clouds.
East, west, south, and north—eighty thousand and eight hundred [miles]. Śūnyatā (Emptiness) arises, leaving no room for calculation;
a lotus blooms within the fire. By the Reverend Jingzhao Zhenfu of Jingyin Monastery in Dongjing (Fifteen Poems).
Baizhang’s Second Visit.
A single shout clearly guards the dead ashes; from the azure sky, wind and thunder suddenly arise. Those standing by clap their hands and laugh aloud;
only the one who knows the sound comes forth with his tongue out.
Baizhang rolled up his mat and ascended the lion throne, already having perfected his realization; the Great Wise Śrāmaṇera rolled up his mat and departed.
The lion’s yawn was still somewhat tolerable, but the elephant king’s backward glance is even more startling.
The non-Buddhists questioned the Buddha with such earnestness regarding existence and non-existence; had he responded according to the wind, he would have spared himself much effort.
Though the clouds of delusion may be cleared away to allow entry, one still cannot avoid lingering laboriously halfway along the path.
Lingyun attained enlightenment upon seeing peach blossoms;
in the warmth of spring, peach blossoms open, bearing dew. At one glance, Lingyun awakened to the numinous mind-ground (*lingtai*).
Xuansha’s definitive realization has been transmitted through the ages—who can resolve the disputes and silence the doubts of the multitude?
Zhaozhou Examines the Old Woman:
Zhaozhou has thoroughly exposed the "Old Woman Chan. The flow of his words is clear before our very eyes.
Lately, those who study under the masters of the Five Lakes have been wandering like smoke along bypaths at the crossroads.
Not seeing a single dharma as a great calamity, nor seeing a single dharma as a calamity;
after the rains, the clouds have gathered up over the wilds and fields; at midnight on the Mid-Autumn festival, the lunar disc hangs high.
At how many places do people ascend the towers to gaze upon it?
Not seeing a single dharma is the Tathāgata;
not seeing a single dharma is the Tathāgata. To the south lies the Heavenly Capital, and to the north are the Five Terraces. Upon the river the snow has melted and spring has already grown warm;
mountain flowers bloom at dawn amidst the morning dew.
Baizhang’s “Wild Fox”:
questions asked and answers given, a complete cycle of causes and conditions. It has circulated throughout the world for several hundred years;
from ancient times to the present, every monk has passed it on to the next.

The four types of guests—host, guest, guest-of-guests—pass their days in solitude; what a sorrowful sight! Abandoning one's father to wander aimlessly in foreign lands, one has endured nothing but bitter hardship and toil throughout one’s life.
The Guest within the Host: Carrying a staff, he enters the marketplace without companion; though he may present himself face-to-face, alas, he cannot see his own true nature.
The Host within the Guest: Temporarily donning soiled robes, he mingles with the secular dust; responding to every situation without weariness, his compassion and wisdom are both perfected.
The Most Honored One is most majestic;
the Lord of Lords sits alone, towering high within the golden palace. The Five Lakes and Four Seas enjoy peace and prosperity;
everywhere civil culture is cultivated and martial arts are laid to rest.
In response to the monks' request for instruction, he showed them the Three Secrets.
The First Secret: If a patch-robed monk has not yet had a glimpse of it, and you further intend to ask "How is it?", your head must see blood from the blow of the staff.
The second secret: travelers of the north and south are cut off; not only did Elder Kāśyapa remain speechless, even Mañjuśrī was rendered tongue-tied.
The third secret: the Patriarch’s command is established according to capacity; on the mountain ridge in the twelfth month, plum blossoms cover the branches, exhaling fragrance amidst the snow.
Chan Master Fayan Yuanjian of Fushan in Shuzhou (One Poem):

A Song on the Clash of Chan Generals Viewing the clash of Chan generals is like watching a master archer encounter a golden-toothed warrior; their sharp wit and swift response are difficult for others to fathom.
Discernment! Whether advancing or retreating, capturing or releasing, their wisdom is merely a boast. Skillfully concealing the blade’s edge, they employ artful interplay.
Seizing the vital ford, who would dare point? A fragrant elephant roars, causing mountains and rivers to crumble; a lion yawns, and both ordinary and holy beings tremble.

Sometimes a probing pole, sometimes a torch, illuminating heaven and earth to test the true practitioner. At the moment of deliberation, guest and host are distinguished; in the blink of an eye, all is changed.
The armored horse has the momentum of a dragon and the vigor of a tiger; turning left and circling right, it seizes banners and drums.

Seizing the opportune moment, it shatters the iron gate; with resolute ferocity, it bursts open the golden lock. Its literary brilliance is manifest, its wind and bone revealed. Even if one were to fully wield this, it would not yet be the ultimate ground.
Casting off stars and wearing the seal, it falls upon the desolate wilderness. Marking the point where the bit bites, it traverses the Western Lands. To view it as a mere scholar—never!
No error. Whether it be a sharp-edged blade capable of providing protection, or a "blowing-hair" sword shimmering like the seven stars;

whether it be a golden mirror with radiant halos reflecting the eight directions, or shadows among the grass concealing an army; whether the wind and clouds enveloping the earth obscure one's bearings, or a single blade pierces through the myriad functions before one;
whether the dual clarity enters the assembly of a thousand peaks, or one proceeds with measured steps, bearing the insignia once more—a lone horse and a solitary spear.
Presented as an interpretation: Although they come across the bridge clad in armor, they have already been struck by the sudden, decisive blow of the Tang-dynasty decree.
Wielding the Mohe sword, the command is fully executed; illumination and function are simultaneous—who dares to stand their ground?

The wrathful Nātha loses his majesty; Khaṇḍa and Kharva stare with eyes wide open. Establishing the limbs, they assist the sovereign; they settle heaven and earth and bring all things to peace. The painted drums roll on.
The two armies withdraw after the clash; the horseman general shouts, "A fine hand!
Chan Master Xian-duan of Dizang, Fuzhou (Ten Poems), by Xuanchang.
Dizang has but one lute; who is the one who understands its sound? A hundred-foot cliff-pine, a thousand-fathom waterfall—what kind of lute is this?
It is the howl of tigers and the roar of dragons.

Dizang’s single arrow was originally not something forged through refinement; yet it pierces throughout the ten directions, leaving the hosts of demons trembling with fear. What kind of arrow is this?
It is the wind that causes the willows to blossom.

"Ksitigarbha’s single phrase leaves the Chan practitioners at a loss; it neither falls into the category of saint nor ordinary person, so how could it involve being mired in delusion or awakening? What kind of phrase is this?
It is the crossing of the ferry of Qingping."

The single secret of Kṣitigarbha is to provide whatever is appropriate according to the occasion. Should you ask how this is done, your head will shatter and your forehead split open. What kind of secret is this?
It is that spring is cold and autumn is hot.
The single path of Kṣitigarbha: whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, it is difficult to seek with intention, yet easy to reach without the mind. What path is this?
It is the vast, surging sound of pines in the wind.
Dizang gives one sweep with his whisk. It strikes the patriarchs, it strikes the Buddhas. Summer passes and winter comes; the sky clears and the sun rises. What kind of sweep is this?
It is like Xiao He establishing the laws.
Dizang’s single staff strikes the void and smashes through form; it eradicates the three stages of worthiness and banishes the six thieves. What kind of staff is this?
Its bends do not conceal its straightness.
The single pivot of Kṣitigarbha: a fine drizzle falls. Raising an eyebrow and blinking an eye; wading through water and dragging through mud. What kind of pivot is this?
Paying homage according to rank and honoring the superior.
Mount Dizang stands as a single peak, so steep it cannot be climbed. Flowers float upon the clear waters; stones are locked in patterns of moss. What mountain is this?
Its form is straight, and its reflection is upright.
The single water of Dizang is clear, cool, sweet, and pure; it flows vast and expansive throughout the great chiliocosm, where fish and dragons dwell at their ease. What kind of water is this?
It is the water in which Xu You washed his ears.
Chan Master Fayun Fashu of Dongjing (Six Poems) Seeking the meaning of the Patriarchs, I have crossed ridges and climbed mountains to come here;
at Shaolin, I did not expect my mouth to be so difficult to open. Even if it were empty space itself, it must swallow [this truth].
The staff! Who would dare to stir the clouds and thunder when facing its point?
From where does this chilling pure wind come? Who says that withered trees must wait for the blossoms to open? The rock-pine possesses its own power to soar above the clouds;
it does not rely on the thunder of the second month of spring.

The illusory body has a thousand heads and a hundred heads, yet it is but one head. Heaven-born flesh and bone are saturated with fat and grease. Sleeping among the clouds and reclining upon the waters, do not seek it elsewhere;
it is found neither in the poor man’s house nor in the wealthy man’s mansion.

The illusion is fundamentally and originally true; there is no need to flee it. Following conditions, it nourishes itself with water and grass like a fat beast. The six classes of ordinary beings and the four types of noble ones share the same essence;
why must one compete for wealth and status?
The Mind-Seal:
From of old, the patriarchs have never known the mind. The myriad phenomena of the forest and the heavens are submerged within it. The nostrils of Kunlun are three feet long;
O Persian from the South Sea, do not pour recklessly.
Forming a solid mass and a single cluster, spanning from antiquity to the present; throughout the five lakes and four seas, all float and sink. The iron ox has locked the waters of the Yellow River;
you who come to hear the judgment must not pour out your wine in disorder.
Chan Master Zanyuan Juehai of Mount Jiang at Jinling Prefecture (Three Poems) The First Essential of the Three Essentials:
Who dares speak when facing it head-on? A thousand sages arise all at once— How could one ever exhaust this wondrous mystery?
The second essential: A bright mirror set upon its stand reflects all; both Hu and Han alike are submerged within it. A green serpent slips from its scabbard to battle—this is the third essential.
One must know how to block this single aperture. When asked how to advance further, he claps his hands and laughs aloud.
Chan Master Dàtōng Shànběn of Fǎyún Monastery in Tōngjīng (Five Poems) Explaining the Principle: The Way of the Path is unobtainable;
Cultivating the mind, the mind is fundamentally empty. In fundamental emptiness there is no place of attainment; Do not say that this is merely escaping the cage.
Within these words there is no divergent path; how can one seek the wondrous intent? Red dust rises from the bottom of the sea; white waves deepen atop the mountain peaks.
In a place where neither Buddha nor Mara reach, who has known it through all time? The mist rolls back as a thousand peaks emerge; the clouds withdraw as a sliver of moon shifts.
The whirling wheel of lightning flashes; amidst the wind, not a speck of dust remains. If you seek the intent beneath the words, a single arrow passes beyond Western Qin.
It is not that there is no speech; rather, too much speech leads to further suspicion. Though he sat motionless for nine years, his voice shook like thunder across the Five Heavens.
Chan Master Dadao of Nan Yue Guquan (Eight Poems) The Song of Dadao:

The nature of this mad monk is fundamentally one of wandering at will. Wherever he goes, he settles according to conditions. His traveling gear consists of nothing more than this: he rows his boat down...
Who can manage his bent bamboo staff and hollow wooden ladle? Walking alone, sitting alone, he drinks alone. People of this age do not understand the mad monk’s intent;
they assume the mad monk is merely fabricating a pretense. His straight-lined cassock and paper patchwork robe—whose tattered seams who can possibly manage?
When Zen guests meet him, they all laugh; when Vinaya masters encounter him, they are greatly displeased. Facing the wind...

Sitting, sleeping facing the sun—this is far superior to the people of this age covering themselves with brocade quilts. Drifting and dazed, one merely prolongs the passing time; listless and dispirited, one remains forever as if drunk.
One is too lazy to wash the face and too lazy to shave the head; in walking or staying, there is not the slightest sense of propriety.
Not only across a thousand peaks and ten thousand mountains, one goes and returns at will, moving freely in every direction. Whether in brothels or wine shops, one claps one’s hands.
Singing loudly, he has no further worries. Everyone scolds and reviles him for his wild madness. Do not be surprised that his madness is exactly like this;
he wanders far and wide, entering sacred temples. Five hundred children are all at a loss; they only know how to contemplate emptiness while lying amidst white clouds.
How can they compare to this mad monk who expands his divine thoughts? When people of the time ask whether he exists or not, he simply lowers his head and picks up a mountain jujube.
The verse says:
Disheveled and forlorn, dwelling in the mountains or in the city walls; vast and uncultivated, regarding this as right and that as ancient;
clapping hands in great wonder—Yan Hui and Pengzu!
A monk of wandering and wild song, his nature free from all constraints. Wandering aimlessly and acting with unrestrained freedom, he lodges wherever he may.
Sometimes he breaks into a wild song, and suddenly rises to perform a dance. A Zen student said, "How extraordinary! Yet in the end, he remains as he was before. Sixty.
Six. A-he-he! For your sake, I shall relate it: The old fellow Fenggan rode a tiger out; on the road he met Shide, who laughed heartily.
Yet Hanshan, in turn, shouted "Duo-duo-duo! at him.
The Patriarch’s Nose (Six Verses) The Patriarch’s nose:
whether there is gain or loss, Mount Biyue is steep and lofty; the gait of the dragon and the prowess of the tiger—this is the nose of the patch-robed monk.
The sitting cloth is one foot two inches; do not ask about its length. The wind is high and the clouds arise.
The patriarch’s essential point flows like a rushing river without obstruction; golden lotuses spring from the earth as he holds the *cintāmaṇi* in his hand.
As for the essential point of the Great Way, when questioned, he is drowsy; with a gourd slung upon his back, he sings wildly and plays.
The mountain boy’s nostrils: the tea boils over in the cauldron. A guest asks, "How is it? [The master replies,] "It is not easy to have traveled so far.
The dispersed sage’s nostrils: playing as the occasion demands; surging east and sinking west, in the southern regions and the northern lands.
The Linked Blossoms of the Patriarchal Hall of Zen Master Zhengjue Benyi of Dongjing Zhikai (Twelve Verses) From Mount Ji to Caoxi,
those who upheld the main principles of our Way numbered thirty-three across the east and west. This single phrase of the separate transmission stands out so sharply that few people understand it.
Dwelling in tranquility, contemplate my Way;
those who grasp its essential principles will find the price of rice in Luling most extraordinary. Every year the fields yield great harvests; do not begrudge the slow pace of the marketplace.
Shitou Xiqian.
Regarding "The Outline of My Way": Mount Heng crouches upon the stone; do not let time pass in vain. Its bounty is so great it is difficult to repay.
Regarding "The Son of Heaven Awakens to the Outline of My Way": The Son of Heaven protects his descendants; with a single piece of steamed cake, our lineage shall shine for a thousand years.
Longtan was one who upheld the essential principles of my Way; the meeting of teacher and disciple was rare indeed. At Longtan’s night of extinguishing the lamp, Deqiao’s skull became dry.
Deshan [Jian].
Regarding those who uphold the essential principles of our Way: one constantly contemplates the ancient worthy Shanshan, who with a single fathom-long iron staff sat and cut off the Wuling Pass.
Regarding those who uphold the essential principles of our Way as preserved by Xuefeng: it is difficult to forget this Xuefeng; on Wangzhou and Woshiling, there is nowhere we do not meet.

Yunmen Wenyan, the one who upheld the guiding principles of our Way, said: "Impartiality is the ultimate discourse. Even the Buddhas and Patriarchs did not recognize this fellow who fills his bowl with steamed buns.
— Shuangquan Yu.
Those who uphold the essential principles of my Way are the worthy descendants of Shao Yang. From Shuangquan, one stream branched off; from Yunmen, it flowed forth ceaselessly.

As for those who upheld the essential principles of my Way far beyond Deshan—the iron-gate path was steep and perilous. After the people of Shaolin had passed, the paths north and south naturally diverged into many branches.
Kaixian Xian was one who upheld the essential principles of our Way. As for the ancient Buddha Kaixian, who truly succeeded to the ancestral wind? A single moon shines across the vast sky.
[This is] the general eulogy.
My Way rightly holds up the guiding thread; when its command is issued, who dares to oppose it? The Dragon Spring sword spans the sea of wisdom; its three-foot blade is like frost.
Chan Master Zhiben of Daolin Monastery in Tanzhou (One Poem):
A Song of Joyful Freedom.
This mountain monk finds leisure within the mountains; beyond his patched robe, bowl, and staff, he seeks nothing more.
When at ease, he takes long strides through the sutras; when weary, he leans against a stone amidst the clouds. Singing songs of joy—singing songs of joy! The pines rustle and the springs murmur.
Wildflowers and fragrant grasses, their names unknown; a single stroke of red from blossoms falling upon the crags. I yield to my indolence and forget all formalities.
At that time, one goes to the murmuring stream to play with the bright moon. How can the message within this be transmitted? Turning the head, one smiles and speaks together with the green mountains.
Chan Master Chiming Cishuang Shiyuan of Tanzhou (Six Poems):
The Three Instructions.
The First Secret: The great earth, mountains, and rivers overflow. As soon as Vimalakīrti nods his head, Mañjuśrī becomes loquacious.
The Second Secret: When unfolding and expanding, time and season are involved; how could speech and silence interfere with one another? It is like the autumn moon at midnight.
The Third Secret Instruction: The mountain is distant and the road difficult to traverse; rowing a boat upon dry land; picking out the sun and moon from one’s eyes.

Of these three phrases, the first phrase leaves both heaven and other directions utterly at a loss. The *Cakravartin* (Universal Wheel) turns topsy-turvy, presenting many arguments; yet its majesty remains unsurpassed.
Arriving at the Nyagrodha tree—this is the second phrase.
Linji and Deshan spread their influence along the road; before even crossing into Silla, the staff was already brandished.
Those who have attained realization point and direct wildly along the way.
The third line: Vimalakīrti manifested illness and Mañjuśrī went to visit him; their dialogue was a single silence that shook heaven and earth.
Even until now, it serves as a source of laughter.
Chan Master Guangjiao Jingyun of Baiyun Mountain in Qizhou (two poems).
The profound purport of Caodong lies beyond the lamp of the patriarchs; truly, the Way manifests spontaneously without effort. When the stone woman plucks the flower, the ten thousand realms tremble;
when the wooden boy draws water, the myriad waves surge. In the golden field, trees grow leaves like clouds; in the jade cave, there is no lamp, yet the sun shines.
Illuminating, skillfully transforming all capacities according to their needs, one uniquely attains the wondrous. A whisk made of tortoise hair is held in the palm;
idly, a mustard seed contains the three thousandfold world. The spiritual powers of the ancient sages act spontaneously:

they always send the cowherd boy to the side of the seat and occasionally instruct the stone woman to go before the cliff. The jade wheel grinds through the coral palace; the golden staff strikes open the lapis lazuli tower.
Agate Boat. Who has grasped the essential meaning of the Cao-Dong tradition? Sleeping facing the sun beneath the green mountains.
Chan Master Huiyun Sheng of Beichen (Eight Poems):
A single aperture in Jiahe; he holds fast to the three essentials. Linji and Deshan—ha ha, they laugh aloud! What kind of aperture is this?
Clouds arise from the mountain peaks;
the auspicious grain forms a single lineage. The myriad phenomena are all-encompassing and interconnected; Śākyamuni and Maitreya alike stand beneath its shadow. What school is this?
The evening bell tolls.
One word from Jiahe is transmitted together by the thousand sages; it harbors no intentional meaning. One must strictly avoid seeking it before the sound. What words could there possibly be?
The sky is clear and the path is dry.
Along the road of the auspicious grain, countless travelers tread with transcendence. What kind of path is this—from the Western Heaven to this land?

The hemp cloth of Qianzhou and the single lineage of the Auspicious Grain—do not ask about their width or narrowness; hell and heaven are not separated by so much as a hair’s breadth. What kind of lineage is this?
Blue, yellow, red, and white;
the *jiāhé* melody with its five tones complete—its musical mode is difficult to describe, yet those who understand it shall join in its continuation. What tune is this?
Twenty-eight, sixteen.
The Single Gate of Auspicious Grain: where ordinary and sagely beings alike hasten toward it. Though it possesses no locks or bolts, it encompasses heaven and earth. What gate is this?
Water flows from Kunlun;

auspicious grain is sealed by a single impression. Throughout the great trichiliocosm, it universally vibrates. In every movement and action, there is no meanness or parsimony. What kind of seal is this?
