Who dares to correspond?
Chan Master Doubi Congyue of Long’an Mountain in Hongzhou (Six Poems):
Returning to the Root.
Laughing, he takes Hanshan’s hand; together they cross the wild bridge. By the water’s edge they sit upon the same rock; beneath the forest trees each plucks a branch.
As the sun reaches its zenith, the clouds return to the valley mouth and vanish. Vast and empty beyond the realm of men—where is there not freedom and ease?

Having attained the essential meaning, I dwell among a thousand peaks; my idle mind severs all ties to the world. With a short staff across my knees I sit; upon a block of stone I rest my head and sleep.
I warm the fire to brew fresh tea; I draw cold spring water by the stream. As flowers bloom again in the secluded forest, I do not reckon at all with the passing years.
A profound resonance lies in stillness beyond the drifting dust; the streams and mountains correspond in their depth. The water flows with its inherent momentum;

the clouds gather without intention. A verdant bird perches by the brook; a green monkey chants at the cave mouth. Leaning on my staff, I look back: beneath the crimson leaves, the forest is shrouded in frost.

Throughout the twelve hours of day and night, how has the union of stillness and illumination ever failed to be as one? The clouds have gathered, leaving the azure sky vast; the moon sets, leaving the emerald pool empty.
The sound of the mountain torrent is inexhaustible; the verdant of the spring mountains abounds. Who can cast off worldly burdens and find joy in dwelling here in leisure?

Responding to the capacity of the occasion, how could one ever calculate? Who is the one who acts as the adversary? The divine immortals look on with their allotted share; black and white contend without cause.
Press firmly at the center; extend broadly from the four corners. If you seek it upon the board, you have not yet emerged from the ordinary.

The method for transforming earth into gold by grasping it with the hand is not transmitted through clever speech. Fire has always existed within water; beyond the wondrous, there is nothing further profound.
Roaming the Three Isles upon the sea, I meet the Eight Immortals amidst the pines. How many times have I longed aloud on nights of bright moonlight before the chaotic peaks?
Chan Master Shaoci of Wanshan on Mount Lu (Six Poems) Verse on Penetrating the Profound:

The meaning of the Patriarchs is boundless; do not ask for the West. How could one possibly establish a fixed acquaintance within such vast openness? Come further into the flash of a stone-tossing spark.
Seeking it out, one burns away that mass of brows right before the gate.
The ultimate principle is impartial; there is no need for conjecture. How could it have been transmitted from India? There is a path within the dust—you must discern it.
Upon the crown of the head, the adamantine iron eyes open.
The numinous sprout has no shadow; do not say it is high. Seeking its leaves and seeking its branches only increases one's toil.
If you step into this midst with a secure root and foundation, the great chiliocosm is but a single hair’s breadth.

In the battle of Dharma, neither side has ever been harmed; responding to conditions and acting in accordance with them, one enters the field of strength. As soon as the golden blade is raised, the demonic armies submit;
all the myriad origins are unified within a single village.
The Great Way is profound and mysterious, beyond all description; I shall briefly offer a single evaluation by means of a metaphor:
Look at those red peaches upon the branch—each and every fruit is originally but a seamless whole.
Transcending the mysterious pass, it cannot be blocked; returning to the deep reaches, one rows a fishing boat.
With no bait of many kinds hanging from the tip of the pole, catching the blind turtle is a matter of karmic affinity.
Chan Master Renshuo of Xinghua in Luzhou (Ten Poems) The White-Faced Tiger Hidden in the Deep Crag The white-faced tiger has always emerged from the ranks of beasts;
For now, he hides his majestic power within the Kunlun Mountains. Deep in the night, he lets out a roar facing the cliff before him.
The Moon. Boundless scenery clears the spirit;
the silver candles of the Five Heavens radiate their light, blazing intensely.
The Five Heavens illuminate one another—how fresh! The bright moon shines through, yet it is not yet [the ultimate].
Exquisite! Only when the brilliant radiance is overturned does one begin to penetrate the profound mystery.
The golden needle departs and returns;

its subtle function is such that the golden needle never shows its head. Coming and going without question, if it were merely a flowing current, then embroidered robes would not require the aid of the void and the mysterious.
With hands, one strives to complete every line and path.
Wondrous discourse does not depend on the tongue;

though the mouth praises it, the tongue itself is fundamentally non-existent. Within non-existence, the wondrous is performed as a brilliant plan; ruler and minister sing in harmony, penetrating the profound mystery.
The essential point is this: all under heaven return to the same source, cutting off divergent paths.

When the palace of Qin reflects the gallbladder, the radiant brilliance shines through the gallbladder and penetrates the heart with cold. Once beauty and ugliness are distinguished, heterodoxies are sufficient; when the blue-eyed one approaches the platform, he must be struck down.
It is shattered. To avoid it, the light and the object are both preserved in their entirety.
The three tiers of the iron saw blow forth;
the myriad phenomena of the universe are the original ancestral mind. At every turn, there is nothing that does not proclaim the perfect sound. *Cha-ch’a*: beneath the iron saw, the three tiers.
Chant! The strings, flutes, and reed organs harmonize with this song.
A dead snake leaps from the weeds;
it was hidden deep in the grass for an unknown time. One morning, suddenly active again, it is heard and known. It emits no spray of mist and yet continues to withdraw.
Fascicle. Nāciketa, the turtle-nosed one of the Southern Mountains.
A brocade curtain hangs before the Hall of the Bright Moon, yet there is no night-quilt; though it covers all, who knows it? Pushing aside the seamless, radiant light...
The inner lining is fully exposed, not created by the power of transformation.

Unraveling the needle from the dry bone, he chants while wearing soiled robes as he enters the assembly. Administering remedies according to the ailment, this is the wind of aiding the Way. The melody of the single chant on the dry bone—its tonal resonance...
He utters a sound; every sound is perfectly pervasive, reaching nowhere it does not.
Within the sleeve, the blue serpent roars;
within the sleeve, the blue serpent was originally hidden. Suddenly it bellows forth, revealing the True Constant. Before the gate, it startles and scatters the three thousand.
Guest: How could Zhuangzi rely on his own strengths?
A Ballad on the Knowledge and Insight of Chan Master Chenggu of Jianfu Temple in Raozhou (One Poem).
Stop! Stop! Stop! Great man, what a great error it is! To have groundlessly chewed upon the saliva of a wild fox; though your belly be full of those who understand, there is nowhere to place them.
Even if you manifest as a dream returning home, to speculate on that which transcends all things is in vain.

The provisional essentials of the double mystery display their mastery with such freedom that the sharp edges of their responses, whether contrary or compliant, flash like lightning. It is just like a mad ghost throwing the mind into chaos, or again, like...
The good man has taken poison; listen carefully! Quickly vomit it up! When the feverish illness awakens, one will then be shivering and cold.
Whether it be Japan or India, what does it matter if Mount Sumeru stands with its peak overturned? To pointlessly rely on one's own narrow views is self-deception;
to falsely poke out the eyes of the Chan lineage is a waste. Such loyal words are harsh to the ear for the ignorant; let those who have realized the Way judge them as they will.
"Mo, mo, mo! To open one's mouth toward you is already a mistake; to ask 'mo, mo, mo' again is even more so.
A lapis lazuli vase filled with filth and evil—the nectar of immortality turns into poison. Mo, mo, mo!
In a thicket of thorns, wild foxes run out into the desolate wilderness only to be bound again. Upon pure ground, corpses lie across the road; demons and heterodox paths stand headlong and defiant."
Mo mo mo! The nostrils of the Buddhas of the three periods are long; the eyelids of the six generations of patriarchs are thin.
To add a sharper point upon excrement—let the chatterers mock at will. Even ten thousand eight thousand *yojanas* cannot compare to my "mo mo mo."
Chan Master Furi Weiyue of Jingyin Monastery, Tokyo (Four Poems) The ancient sword leans against the heavens;
its numinous blade naturally shaves hair. It does not require further tempering at Mount Ye. Life and death race one another; the mechanism is like—
Thunder! From this moment, the eight directions lay down their spears and halberds.

The ancient zither has no tuning pegs, no bridge, and no strings; yet with a single performance of the *gong* and *shang* notes, it resonates throughout the great chiliocosm. The sound of water remains ever-present from dawn until dusk.
Listen! The mountain colors of past and present naturally span the heavens.

The ancient mirror was originally perfected; its casting must have been difficult. Its numinous radiance has chilled all who approach it for a thousand ages. Though there is no distinction between the Hu coming and the Han appearing—
Hidden. Who would dare stand before it and look directly?

A single expanse of cold light in the ancient pool reflects a mass of clarity; beneath ten thousand layers of mountain peaks, it governs the autumn sky. When the mind attains this, it is pure and transparent.

Later, he once sealed the silver hare [of the moon] as it completed its cycles several times. Chan Master Daoying of Jianfu Temple in Raoyou (Ten Verses on the Ten Essentials). **Ten Verses on the Ten Essentials** 1. **The Essential Point of the Ultimate Source** The ultimate source is originally without direction; How could there be east or west? If you wish to know the essential point, Look at the tip of the staff. 2. **The Essential Point of the Single Path** The single path is not a place for travel; It is where the myriad phenomena are exhausted. If you wish to know the essential point, Do not seek it within the ten directions. 3. **The Essential Point of the Two Entrances** The two entrances are like a mirror facing a wall; They do not reflect each other. If you wish to know the essential point, Do not look for it in the midst of confusion. 4. **The Essential Point of the Three Mysteries** The three mysteries are like the empty sky; They have no form or shape. If you wish to know the essential point, Do not seek it in words or speech. 5.

**The Essential Point of the Four Dharmas** The four dharmas are like a dream within a dream; They are all empty and false. If you wish to know the essential point, Do not grasp at them as real. 6. **The Essential Point of the Five Skandhas** The five skandhas are like flowers in the air; They have no substance. If you wish to know the essential point, Do not cling to their appearances. 7. **The Essential Point of the Six Entrances** The six entrances are like an empty house; They contain nothing. If you wish to know the essential point, Do not let the mind wander among objects. 8. **The Essential Point of the Seven Elements** The seven elements are like a mirage; They arise from delusion. If you wish to know the essential point, Do not follow after thoughts. 9. **The Essential Point of the Eight Consciousnesses** The eight consciousnesses are like waves on water; They are all manifestations of the one mind. If you wish to know the essential point, Return directly to the source. 10. **The Essential Point of the Nine Orifices** The nine orifices are like holes in a vessel; They leak away the vital essence. If you wish to know the essential point, Seal them with the great function. 11. **The Essential Point of the Ten Realms** The ten realms are like a single dream; There is no distinction between high and low. If you wish to know the essential point, Realize that they are all the Buddha-nature.

When discussing delusion and speaking of awakening, what is the ultimate conclusion? Is there no one in delusion, or are those who have awakened many? When delusion departs, it is certainly not a new world;
when awakening comes, it is still the same mountains and rivers of old. The rebel hordes at the gates of the senses all surrender;
the demonic armies of the hidden realms lay down their weapons. From this point on, dwell in peace within my kingdom; even Yao and Shun were but as others.
The Buddha-nature is perfectly interfused and discussed everywhere; yet among them, few truly understand it. According to capacities, paths diverge into thousands and tens of thousands;
reaching the very source, there is neither two nor three. Leaves fall as cicadas chirp at distant trees; clouds disperse and the solitary moon is reflected in the clear pool.
To seek branches and follow tributaries is truly pitiable; for this reason, these words are offered as a guiding compass.
Suddenly, beneath these words, one unexpectedly encounters Him. This bears a strong resemblance to the time when true gold emerges from the ore;

yet it must enter the furnace for further refinement and forging. Only upon the upper anvil can it withstand the heavy tongs and hammer. Whether one attains the skin or the marrow depends entirely on oneself; as for the transmission of the Dharma and the robe, who indeed is it that transmits them?
My narrow views and superficial learning are not worth mentioning; they only serve to increase the sense of self and other, perpetuating ignorance.
Gradually distancing yourself from your hometown, you become increasingly out of step; I urge you to long for home and return early. Roaming over level ground, there is neither high nor low;
activating the mysterious mechanism, there is both rolling up and unfolding. Wondrous indeed is Sanping with an arrow fixed to his chest; marvelous is Wanjuan with books stored within his belly.
Yet if one cannot clearly understand the root and the stem, in the end, one is no different from a fish in stagnant water.
The clarity of the Eye of the Way is truly difficult to attain; the sinking of the Dharma-body is all the more pitiable. When the robes are cast off, the whole body is revealed;
when the pillow and mat are left behind, both eyes open wide. Where they open, there is no realm of Māra; when they are revealed, how could there be the physical form of a Buddha?
If Mañjuśrī stirs for even a single thought of deviation, he too will come down to Mount Cakravāḍa.

To serve a teacher who is not upright is likewise a vain labor. Regarding what to leave behind and what to follow, I now exhort you all: simply seek a path that is pure and endowed with sublime virtue;

do not concern yourselves with the weight of fame or the age of seniority. You must truly humble yourself to seek the essential core of the mind; do not merely indulge in empty pretenses or arrogant spirit.
When the body and its karmic conditions are both fragile and unstable, upon what dharma can you rely to make them firm?
Seeing this established case, do not harbor doubt or suspicion; the Awakened Ones have clearly pointed it out for you. You may then learn that there is nothing to be done with clever artifice;
you should not be like Xiu, merely brushing away the dust. Cease from laboriously scrutinizing words of intimacy or estrangement;
in bestowing or withholding, you must still employ your own resources. Fundamentally, where do you wish to go? The perilous stone bridge lies at Tiantai.
Seeking within, one finds only remoteness; rushing outward in pursuit, one realizes only greater distance. The green willows and red blossoms fully reveal the truth;

the cawing crows and chirping sparrows have already provided a comprehensive account. Why must you insistently debate mind and objects? There is no need to clamorously distinguish between the correct and the false.
Know that birth-and-death and nirvana are but dreams and illusions; do not take these dreams and illusions and stubbornly attempt to divide them.
Formless and nameless, it spans all time; how could it allow the cold and heat to recklessly engulf it?

In the end, it cannot be called "Buddha"; why not let one’s outstretched hand point to it as "mind"? To see it and hear it is not easy to find; to leave sound and form behind makes it even more difficult to seek.
Piteous indeed are those who recognize only that which is bright and clear, yet claim to have received the robe and succeeded the Shaolin lineage.
Bound by tattered and filthy robes, this small transformation-body; there is not a single dharma to present to you. Within the robes lies a treasure year after year;
yet with no sinews in one’s eyes, one remains poor life after life. A straw dog is born as golden pheasant; a wooden cock devours the jade qilin.
To speak entirely of the profound and wondrous is like describing moats and trenches—how many can pass through them with ease?
Chan Master Shengqin of Zisheng Monastery in Xiuzhou (Five Poems) The Meaning of the Westward Journey—You Ask for the Meaning of the Westward Journey:
In the depths of spring, the rain falls in abundance. On Mount Xiong, a single shoe is hidden; barefoot, one crosses the shifting sands.
You ask about the meaning of the Westward Journey: the spring breeze remains as cold as ever. If you wish to travel beyond the thousand worlds, you must look closely with every step.
You ask about the meaning of the Westward Journey: the clouds are deep and the wrong paths are many. A warm wind blows through the dawn valley; the bright moon shines upon the misty vines.
You ask about the meaning of the Westward Journey; your clever understanding is blocked by New Ra. Even if you were to act just so, it would be like a crane in a phoenix’s nest.
You ask about the meaning of the Westward Journey; it is a journey of ten thousand miles across the vast distance. Look up at the Northern Dipper; there lies a multitude of stars in the heavens.
Chan Master Tanyi Daguan of Mount Jinshan in Runzhou (Five Poems) The Dharma-Eye school is one branch of the five schools of the Zen tradition;
Xuefeng was its patriarch. One must directly realize one’s own nature; one must not neglect cultivation and practice.

Question: When distinguishing guest and host within the inner realm, one speaks of a path forked in mid-course. If we discuss the fundamental matter, it is like striking a tile or divining with a tortoise shell.
Yunmen succeeded Xuefeng; his spiritual mechanism was identical to that of Muzhou. The principle lies beyond a thousand differences; the words return to a single phrase.
The rain on withered leaves in the ninth month; the wind scattering blossoms in the third. One often hears the Persians say: "The toad bites the tiger.
The biased and the correct interweave and intersect; one must remain far removed from the perfection of ten. One must penetrate the Dragon Gate; the Bird Path is not fit for travel.
A barren woman weaves amidst the frost; a clay ox plows within the fire. If one can be liberated from both ends, a single branch of withered wood will flourish.
When Moshan and Yangshan’s mechanisms are darkened, it is difficult to speak alone. Flying birds spread their two wings; a bright pearl turns upon a single plate.
Though square and round may coexist, their rising and sitting do not interfere with one another. Hand-dancing and foot-stamping are but vain efforts to display the tip of the tongue.
The fine descendants of Linji mostly discourse on staffs and shouts; unable to clarify the wondrous function, they merely study empty words.
When about to move, he first takes up his staff; as he departs, he knocks over the basin. Thus he transcends such views and understandings—a dumpling inside a wild duck.
Chan Master Chenghao of Yushan in Jingmen Commandery (One Poem):
The Song of the Cloth Bag.

Born into a state of wandering destitution, this Bagui (Luopu) freely follows his nature while residing within the city walls. His straw hat resembles a lotus flower after autumn; his trousers look like tattered, multi-layered rags.

His sandals have never been seen as a pair, and his coarse robe leaves nothing but dangling threads. At times he appears as if intoxicated or delirious; at other times he bares his chest and shoulders.
When hungry, he takes up food with his hands as they happen to reach it; when weary, he stretches out his legs in the middle of the street.
When the sky clears, one hurriedly puts on sandals; in an instant, clouds arise in the azure heavens. When spring rains wash the feet, one runs about;
in a mere moment, the sun shines upon the mountain pavilion. One’s entire life is but this single cloth bag, containing whatever is placed within, regardless of quality or strength.
Suddenly shaking it out before others, how could those of inferior capacity ever manage to find a place to settle? An iron pan simply says "iron pan," and a wooden ladle plainly says "wooden ladle."
Bowing his head, he unconsciously let out a "ha ha. In a moment of confusion, he suddenly let go of everything. At times he patted [the other's] back seeking understanding;
at others he turned his head and opened his eyes in shock. He stretched out his hand begging for a single coin—more than a mere case of a terminal illness seeking medicine.
Both parties suffer a profound loss; it remains uncertain who is the greater offender. Unaware that they have entered the water and the mud, everyone simply calls them mad and derisive.
At times, their joys and angers run wild; they disregard whether their words are good or bad, reviling the Ten Sages and Three Worthies, and even berating Master Zhi and Lou Yue.
Who says that one must sever delusions to pursue the Real? Who says that one must abandon suffering to seek happiness?

They further claim "neither arising nor ceasing," forcibly creating ravines and gullies upon level ground. The wise turn inward to deliberate for themselves; the foolish rely on others for divination and conjecture.

How can one bear the old man Zhuang Zhou, who recklessly attempts to grasp at empty space? Furthermore, there are Lü Wang and Huang Gong, who vainly discourse upon the *Six Tactics* and the *Three Strategies*.
When pressed by others to reveal their fundamental source, they cannot help but bow their heads and say "yes, yes. Below the Hall of White Clouds is the fisherman;
atop the Pavilion of Gazing Winds is the immortal crane.
Chan Master Guochang Baojue of Baolin Monastery in Wuzhou (One Poem):

A Song of the Plank-Carrying Hermitage This thatched hut is solid on the outside and empty within; the wondrous functions of the sands of Ganges all reside therein. Its back leans against the green mountains.
Clear waters; facing them, one beholds emerald bamboos and tall pines. Let the winds, cold, frost, and snow come as they may;

through many cycles of spring, summer, autumn, and winter, they point toward heaven and cover the earth, serving as the school of the Dharma-realm. When practitioners come to visit and admire, they encounter this in silent stillness. Look at the title.
Impenetrable as water.
*Jianzhong Jingguo Xudeng Lu*, Volume 29;
*Jianzhong Jingguo Xudeng Lu*, Volume 30. [Song Pan]
Compiled by Chan Master Fokuo (Dharma-Nation), Abbot of Tōkyō Hōun Zen-ji, [Subject] Yuibaku;
Verses and Praises from the Section on Illumination, by Chan Master Myōkaku Jūken of Setsudōzan in Mingzhou (Ten Poems).

I praise the Buddha, the scion of the Ikṣvāku lineage, whose merit exceeds the atoms of all lands. At the site of enlightenment, he manifested the causes for benefiting sentient beings. His thousand-spoked feet rest upon purple-gold lotuses;

his body of myriad virtues radiates white jade-like light. Standing alone in the Great Square, he relies on concentration and wisdom, viewing all classes of beings with equanimity and relinquishing attachment.

To enemies and kin alike, he is the Lord among those with the marks and signs of excellence; his fame pervades the earth as one who has transcended the world. His conch-like hair curls to the right, azure upon the islands of the immortals;

the crescent moon of his brow casts a fresh seal upon the gates of the sea. His gait is like the soaring crane and the dancing phoenix—of no ordinary sort—and his movements are like the turning elephant and the coiling dragon, beyond all comparison.
Amidst his clusters of jeweled necklaces, auspicious radiance surges forth; within the shadows of his flower garlands, he steals the splendor of spring. Such is his compassionate countenance.
The longing for his wisdom is boundless; the words of his Brahma-virtue cannot be fully described. The character upon his chest reveals immeasurable meanings;
the jewel on his crown constantly illuminates a hundred *yojanas*. Who could say that he entered parinirvāṇa at the twin śāla trees? He sits transcending heaven and earth, ever beholding the Truth.
After praising the Dharma, the mass of merit born from subsequent wisdom arises; through great compassion, it remains to spread its moisture to birds and fish.

Although the threading of flowers may be categorized into a thousand varieties, the moon that points to them returns to the single suchness of principle. Through immeasurable eons, it shall be widely disseminated according to the appointed time; in a single kṣaṇa of mind, it merges with the unconditioned.
Forgetting the written word, he casts forth crimson flames within the four-way crossroads; amidst the waves of the five desires, he causes white lotuses to bloom.
Expelling all demons, he ascends the realm of longevity; leading and carrying his children, he boards the carriage of peace. The celestial constellations of its meaning shine brightly;

the billows of the ocean of its words surge vast and wide. To turn one's back on such grace is difficult to remedy; having encountered this final age, how could one hesitate? Having heard this, [I rejoice].

Half a verse must be mutually studied; regretting our departure from the Golden Body, we shall not dwell together. My soaring eloquence laments that it once failed to respond to your stirring questions;

yet I rejoice in fathoming the profound mysteries and am glad to have avoided long sighs. Life after life, I shall revere you, for your brilliance reflects in the mirror of my mind; its vast illumination of worldly toil is truly more than sufficient.
How can the meaning of the monk’s square robe and shaven head be proclaimed? How could the continuation of a thousand lamps’ flame be a minor cause?

Though the rain of flowers before the seat still lingers in form, the tigers are tamed at the edge of the hermitage yet their true expression remains unexplained. Dwelling among crags or sleeping in graves, it is difficult to rely on outward appearances; with the countenance of a crane and a mind like the clouds, one turns back.

Tranquil and serene: the precious staff resounds through the night upon the cold peaks under the moon; the bronze pitcher rinses itself in the autumn mist above the azure pool. His name is inscribed among those refined in the *lianye* grove, purifying clamor and depravity;

his traces are mindful of the dark alleys of the world, awakening those in slumber. Beneath the forest trees, he is truly a guest beyond the mundane; amidst the human realm, he is fit to be a lotus born from fire.
His spirit is lofty, yet not for the sake of transcending the three periods of time; his Way resides within, yet is not identical to entering the four dhyānas. In this floating world...
Who knows my efforts as they flow like a rushing stream? Amidst deep peaks, I am content to listen to the flying springs. The fragrance of the *bhiṣmaka* grass lingers from the time of the Saṃghīti;
the tortoise-shell bowls were passed down by the ancient Buddhas. Cherish the True Son of the Awakened Sovereign, who strides tall through the realm of Kun to array the golden fields.
The rabbit-horn staff transmitted from Shaoshi: a staff of rabbit horn held by a thousand sages as their crowning mark. Like a tiger crouching and a dragon coiling, its power never ceases;
cloud shadows and mountain forms face each other in cold stillness. Sometimes leaning idly against the empty hall, it stands vast and silent, pervading the earth with its concentrated presence.
Autumn frost: sometimes it lets out a great lion’s roar. How vast and boundless were Deqiao and Linji!
Today I bring them forth without regret, clearly showing them to all you masters. Understanding how to wield the world, they roam at will;
how can their lofty standard of conduct ever be exhausted?
Names and realities have no fixed correspondence;

like jade turning and pearls revolving, the words of the Patriarchs and Buddhas remain. To be "proficient" in them is still to defile the field of the mind. Old Lu only knows how to husk rice for a living;
how could he have transmitted the legacy of Huangmei for all eternity?
Questioning the meaning of dependent origination, I list its principles;
yet I laugh at what I have not heard before. Who dares to display a "cloth drum" before the main gate? The Diamond Iron Seal is sought by all quarters;
it is reported that the three thousand seas and mountains are shrouded in darkness.
The Way values appearing as if ignorant;
after the rain, clouds gather as dawn half-breaks. Several peaks are like paintings, emerald and towering. Śūnyatā was not understood while sitting within the crags;
it provoked celestial flowers to fall and shake the earth.
In great mourning, one does not slaughter an ox;
atop Mount Niutou, heavy clouds lock the peak. Sitting alone in silence, this body is entrusted to these heights. A hundred birds do not come as spring passes once more;
I know not who is the person who reaches this hermitage.

The Perfected One is not confined to a single form—who could grasp him when he acts? His raising [of the hand] is never deceptive, yet such instances are rare. He shatters the steep and lofty, dissolving the profound and subtle.
The heavy gates were once grandly opened, yet those who have attained them do not all return together. The jade hare is now full, now waning; the golden crow seems to fly, yet does not fly. Lu...
Old age knows not where it shall go; white clouds and flowing streams remain ever close.
For the sake of the Way, one’s light diminishes daily;
two-thirds of one's years have already passed. That single point within the spirit-mirror has not been polished; one pursues life day by day in weary toil.
Go! If you do not turn back when called, what can be done?
Chan Master Changzong Zhaojue of Donglin, Mount Lu (Eight Poems) The Gate of Mañjuśrī’s Sublime Wisdom
Where is there that Mañjuśrī is not present? How could he reside only upon the peak of Mount Qingliang? Throughout antiquity and the present, he has never been hidden or manifest;
why must one debate the intimacy or distance between the holy and the ordinary? It is not merely to say that the Seven Buddhas are his patriarchal masters; he serves as a model for all living beings.
If one can directly perceive this wondrous attainment, then even carrying firewood and drawing water manifests Vairocana.

The Gate of Samantabhadra’s Wondrous Virtue: Samantabhadra, the Sublime Sage, is truly called "Worthy. Within his silvery radiance, he illuminates the great trichiliocosm; as every dharma is manifest and perfected, what fault or evil could there be?
In every atom, square or round, all is fully present; in a single thought-moment, Sudhana’s entire body is revealed. Universal Eye (Samantamukha) respectfully challenges him.
The essence is pervasive; its habitual practice has no original location. Mount Emei is merely a provisional manifestation for humans and devas.

The gate of Avalokiteśvara’s wondrous power is the place of Avalokiteśvara’s wondrous power within the cage of affliction. In the Dharma-realm where movement and stillness blend harmoniously, before the myriad sounds have even resonated, he has already performed his teaching.
How vast! A single sound is just split open, yet its principle is inexhaustible. Dignāga’s "listening" turns into an obstruction; Bhadrapāla’s "no-hearing" reaches far and near.
How wonderful that Mañjuśrī can skillfully discern this; from now on, let perfect penetration be neither east nor west.
The General Verse:
Sublime Wisdom, Sublime Practice, and the Perfect Sound— Together they reveal the heart-mind of the ancient Buddha Vairocana. Having attained this single intent, there is no divergence;
From these three gates, one perceives their profound depth. On the shore of the Cool Lake, cease seeking elsewhere; In the Flower Treasury and at Mount Emei, do not...
External seeking: A snap of the fingers is perfectly accomplished, yet it stands alone; how can deliberation withstand it when separated by a thousand peaks?
Principle is true while phenomena are false;
principle is without movement or change, whereas phenomena come and go. One thought contains two kinds [of delusion], leading to eternal saṃsāra. Once saṃsāra has ceased, [liberation is attained].
When principle and phenomena are held with equanimity, how could the nature of reality be otherwise? When paths and tracks are artificially arranged, one opposes others while claiming oneself;

yet in actual awakening, there is no mind. Where there is a mind, there is a basis for action. To revile the ancients and preserve the present, or to reject others and affirm oneself—such views obscure that the Dharma is fundamentally perfect and luminous.
What distinction is there between this and that? To further refine and carve it would only distance one from it ever more.

Internal mind and external objects—internal mind and external objects—are like mistaking one's head for its reflection, plucking flowers from the sky for fruit, or filling one's hunger with painted cakes. The three realms are vast and desolate.
The four modes of birth roll on incessantly; subject and object are suddenly forgotten. The root of the myriad dharmas is the mind’s view of arising and ceasing.

The ancestral Way flowed eastward, branching out and dividing into lineages. The essential points follow a thousand paths, and the capacities of beings follow ten thousand tracks. Yet these ten thousand tracks are fundamentally empty.
A thousand paths have been established, yet they do not unify the fundamental source.
Amidst the confusion of arising and ceasing, there is the Master Buddhatuo (De-xun) of Huilin Monastery in the Eastern Capital (seven poems):
The Meaning of the Non-Transmigration of Things.

Every thing is fundamentally without transition; year after year passes by. People depart toward the north of the mountains; swallows arrive and return to the south. Spring trees grow and then wither;
the silver moon wanes and then waxes full. Failing to understand Master Zhao’s meaning, I stand facing the north, utterly bewildered.

The Contemplation of Non-True Emptiness: Only that which is not true is called true. Every year in the second month comes spring; peach blossoms bloom across the green fields, and willow catkins escort travelers on their way.
Thing after thing is fundamentally not a thing; dust mote after dust mote is not dust. With clarity, there is nothing to be gained; thus one stands far apart from the land of Western Qin.
The Prajñā is the boat of non-knowing; if it is called "non-knowing," we meet and speak of where we have been.

Last year’s early summer moon, today’s late springtime—the spirit is robust when facing the water, yet the strength wanes when climbing the mountain. As we earnestly exchange news, a brow grows upon the brow.
Nirvāṇa is nameless; Nirvāṇa transcends all designations. The Tathāgata’s compassionate vows are profound: since when did he ever arise at the Bodhi tree?

How could he ever perish at the Twin Śāla grove? His wisdom and grace know no high or low; the *dharma* flower spans from antiquity to the present. Those who sit in meditation amidst the crags merely brood in vain all day long.

The wondrous realm of true emptiness is fundamentally not empty. Every day the sun rises in the east; flowing water differs according to its direction, yet the green mountains are the same everywhere.
Rain nourishes the lush beauty of the wild grasses; mist thins over the crimson of the field flowers. Before one’s eyes lies the realm of Vairocana; every gate and every path is open.
The principle and phenomena are unimpeded;

both principle and phenomena are individually unimpeded. To the south and further north, the hoofbeats and wheels do not tread upon the purple thoroughfares. At the green towers, songs and flutes stir;
travelers are surely in great haste, yet sightseers remain drunk and do not cease. The cowherd boy laughs as he returns home, blowing his flute while riding backward upon his ox.
Pervasive and all-encompassing—“pervasive” means to contain and embrace. Every single thing is the Dharma-realm; who would say that the Elder Meghashri did not descend from Mount Sumeru?
He sat in stillness upon the rocks of Songyang, idly listening to the temple bells of Yue. Where Sudhana turned his head back, beyond the dust of the world, there was no trace of his path.
Chan Master Jie of Zishou Monastery, Quanzhou (Ten Poems) *Avatamsaka Sūtra* Verse:

The true realm of the *Avatamsaka* encompasses the three thousand worlds; In every direction of the fragrant community, white lotuses are planted. As the snow melts from the pine paths, the melody of the spring water flows.
Far away, the wind is still atop Stone Tower as the sound of the chime resonates; clouds gather over the ancient hall where the incense smoke is faint.

As the sun turns, the shadows of the trees lean across the secluded courtyard. I am reminded again of the many wonders of Mount Wutai, where extraordinary flowers carpet the ground, soft as cotton wool.

The true realm of the Avataṃsaka encompasses the entire universe; like clouds dispersing across the vast sky, not a single drop of rain remains. Though the myriad vessels and azure depths receive the water equally, how could the single bright moon ever be partial?
Green mountains and verdant bamboos surround the monastic dwellings; jade gardens and crystalline flowers belong to the imperial capital.
Yet those who wander through kalpa after kalpa remain deluded about themselves; they drift and sink within the six realms of existence in the mere blink of an eye.

The true realm of the Avataṃsaka—why labor to seek it? Among the myriad phenomena in their profusion, who does not find it natural? A colorful phoenix returns to its painted pavilion in the cold of night;
a yellow oriole warbles through the fragrant groves in the warmth of spring. One must know that the ancient Buddhas were created solely by the mind;
it is simply that one’s own original nature has become submerged. Leaning against the railing all day, contemplate this with care; even casual discourse upon it is profound and mysterious.

The true realm of the Avataṃsaka is a vast and universal ford; ten thousand households and a thousand gates are everywhere intimate with it. Within the single seat of the Transformation City lies the pavilion of Maitreya;

from the four directions, Sudhana’s form is gazed upon with reverence. When the clouds clear and the sun appears, who is without their share? When the tiger roars and the wind arises, there is naturally a cause.
The turning of the Great Dharma Wheel is unfathomable to men; in humble self-abasement, he sits within a mote of dust.
The true realm of the Avataṃsaka reveals itself to all capacities; rain swells the rivers and lakes as waves surge boundlessly. Without advancing or practicing, one transcends the ten stages;
without hearing or attaining, one passes beyond the three great kalpas. On the Mid-Autumn Festival, the jade hare is full and round; at midnight, the moon’s crescent gradually wanes.
The Persian merchant entering the sea knows no satiety in his greed; he intends to trade porcelain for the *maṇi* jewel.
The true realm of the Avataṃsaka is beyond decay and flourishing; everywhere it stands majestic, dazzling the eyes. Crimson flames burn like autumn lotus stalks being snapped;
at the bottom of the dark green waves, night lamps shine bright. Geese fly through the vast void, two by two in a straight line;
snow blankets the long sky, all equally level. How laughable are those in the world who lose their way; they fall into pits and ditches, wandering aimlessly.
The true realm of Avataṃsaka unfolds like a sea of clouds; for what reason does the Boatman still cling to his fishing platform? Moving upstream and downstream, the path is crooked and winding;

traveling east and west along the banks, the way is circuitous. Though one gradually departs from conditioned phenomena by relying on the teachings, how could the sudden realization of non-arising require a go-between?
Failing to grasp the true purport of Vairocana, one wanders in vain, coming and going to visit spiritual teachers.
The true realm of Avataṃsaka manifests everywhere; once this is recognized, the road from the West is not long. When it is appropriate to advance, one should advance;
do not engage in deliberation where there is no room for thought. Silence does not necessarily mean one has surpassed Kanakamuni;
why need one praise Prabhāsa with a smile? To inform the virtuous masters of the Five Lakes: cease rushing about, spreading erroneous words and phrases.
The true realm of the Avataṃsaka is entirely uniform; to speak of it as effortless is yet to have effort.

Although the eightfold noble path is easily manifested, the myriad pāramitās are difficult to fathom. A fine rain lightly sweeps the perilous eaves; a chilling wind gives rise to coolness within the secluded chamber.
How deep is Sudhana’s desire to enter the fierce flames—how wondrous that he still finds joy therein!
The true realm of Avataṃsaka pervades the four seasons; at the end of winter, the ice-river freezes and does not flow.

The stone tiger has fangs but is not to be feared; the iron ox lacks a nose—how could it be restrained? In the golden garden, willows darken as spring draws to a close; in the jade well, paulownias thin out as the scene first turns autumnal.
One cannot look enough upon the wondrous peaks surrounding the seat; lingering and hesitating, one remains by the tower on the water’s edge.
Chan Master Tanyi Daguan of Mount Jinshan in Runzhou (Four Poems) The Buddha’s teaching began at the Deer Park and ended at Kuśinagara;
for forty-nine years he established the rules of conduct. Kāśyapa struck the bell to summon the assembly.

The assembly gathered. Ānanda ascended the seat to demonstrate the transmission and upholding [of the Dharma]: "The golden words are already like medicinal decoctions left over after boiling; the teachings of the Tripitaka are but empty pieces set down on a chessboard.
If one were to discuss a single phrase that is truly authentic, it would be like beating the drum at the third watch to perform a dance for the Persians."
Strung like flowers upon palm leaves from the Western Heaven, the Sanskrit texts were transmitted to this land and translated. Among the twelve divisions of the canon, it is not easily expounded;
within the five thousand scrolls, it is truly difficult to express. To speak of the "Three" is to fail to avoid the deviant path; how could the "First" ever have been in accord?
Those of superior faculties, having received and upheld this with faith as if they had fully realized it, shall never again fall into the village of entanglements throughout their successive lives.

As for the Vinaya, the World-Honored One entrusted the Vinaya Piṭaka to Upāli; one should strive toward the cessation of transgressions through śīla and be careful to avoid reproach. One must ensure that the faculties of body, speech, and mind are well-restrained.

Guard yourself; greed, hatred, and delusion must also be prevented in their subtlest forms. Allow yourself only morning and evening to hold your alms-bowl; do not permit wandering about even for a moment without your robe.
Failing to grasp the Master’s intent regarding skillful means is like a bird attempting to avoid the sky by flying.
The *Kātyāyanāvavāda-śāstra* uses its treatise to characterize emptiness; the intent of the Sūtras is that when the measures of reasoning are exhausted, one attains universal penetration.

It is hoped that the thousand dragons will be led back to the great ocean, rather than leaving the hundred birds stranded in the void. To rely on others for understanding is not supreme; it is primordially and spontaneously perfected. Unfinished.
Attaining the Middle Way. Beyond the Awakening of Faith, Yoga, and Vijñaptimātratā, who in the Caoxi tradition possesses the merit of Aśvaghoṣa?
By the Patriarch Xinxin Baojue Chan Master of Huanglong Mountain (three poems).
*Dazangjing*.
A single hair pierces through many apertures; the many apertures are gathered within a single hair. Clouds depart from the Imperial Capital; waters flow back to the Yangtze and Han rivers.

On this fragrant spring day, the ninety volumes of the *Chuan Deng Lu* (Records of the Transmission of the Lamp), bees compete to gather the blossoms. When the fragrance has returned entirely to the honeycomb, to whose house do the remaining leaves fall?

**Inscription on Faith** Even if you exhaust yourself to the very bottom, you will still be caught in the wind and waves. Since ancient times, poverty has been laughable; even a single body is regretted as being too much.
By Chan Master Yan of Mount Sizushan in Qizhou (Four Poems)
The Prajñā of the four seasons and the flowers of the three months bloom and smile in the warm sky. Floating clouds drift and meander, naturally entangling one another.
Without cause, they let fall rain for ten days, drawing green moss right up to the front of the seat.
The summer sun shines brilliantly, scorching the vast void; who would dare lift their eyes toward it?
The cool breeze is especially well-suited to the hearts of men, blowing lightly and gently from the Jade Pitcher.
What is it that makes one so beloved as autumn arrives? The ocean moon ascends steadily into the azure sky. Its boundless, pure radiance dazzles the eyes and mind;
with whom can one share a conversation of its fullness?
The north wind, mingled with snow, stirs the streams and forests; all things lie hidden in retreat, as if resentful that it is not yet deep enough. Only the mountain plum possesses much spirit;
before the end of the twelfth month, it has already revealed its heart of enduring cold.
Chan Master Yuan of Suzhou Kunshan (Four Poems) The Sword of Prajñā Its blade and hilt are never revealed;
how can it be verified? The Emperor of Great Peace sits within the realm, and the frontier regions are forever at peace.
The flames of the wolf-smoke have subsided;
at Mount Prajñā, travelers vie with one another to climb all day long. One must transcend to the ultimate summit, the place where the mystery is penetrated;
by no means should one settle one’s traces halfway through the valley.

The essence of Prajñā is vast and expansive, reaching to the very bottom of the ten directions; yet it manifests its entire body wherever contact occurs, so as not to require that person to perform prostrations from afar.
The function of Prajñā is to leisurely pluck and play the zither without strings, intending to strike a single note to reach those who understand. It is pure and self-sufficient.
*Huayan Helun* (The Combined Treatise on the Avatamsaka Sutra) by Chan Master Foyin Zhihai Qing of Dongjing, with five poems accompanied by the breeze from the pines.
The world of distinct golden hues is vast; who within it can say their mind has finally found rest? In the gardens, as autumn deepens, leaves compete to fall;
beneath the snow and rain at night, the heavens bear a chill. One need not deliberate over the distance between Buddha-lands; where could the flowers upon one’s path ever wither?
If you wish to know the infinite, layered realms, simply look toward the lands within a single pore.
At the eastern edge of the City of Enlightenment lies the primary cause; traveling southward, I sought out fifty men.

Though I have traversed the profound depths of the ocean, the sky of meaning is so vast it admits no dust. The cold pines with their snow retain their shadows forever; the tall bamboos holding the wind, their elegance becomes ever more fresh.
If one can cast off attachments within this very place, even the guardian deity of the city would surely be left at leisure.
The true realm of Avataṃsaka is originally all-pervasive; it is like the vast ocean that receives all streams. The six realms and four modes of birth are gathered within a single speck of dust;
the lands and atoms of the ten directions and three periods of time are contained therein. Every single point is the summit of the Wondrous Peak; every step is nothing other than Maitreya’s tower.
How laughable that Sudhana expended so much effort, traveling far to the south in search of something more!
The ocean of lands flows on, its source beyond inquiry; where in the ten directions is there even a speck of dust?
Having already endured the three winters' snows of the northern frontier, I now recall the spring of the second month in Jiangnan. What purpose is served by coming to this riverbank?
Why labor your spirit in throwing yourself upon the mountain of blades? Now I grow old beneath a thousand peaks; who is the deity of the harvest from those former years?
The true realm of the Avataṃsaka is free from even a speck of dust; having grown old, how could I hope to emulate Sudhana?
Beyond the birds, the mists and clouds remain eternally sovereign; for whom were these pavilions by the sea opened? Casually sitting upon a rock, I watch the flowing stream;
with nothing to do, I carry my staff around the green moss. I send this to my old friend in the cold crags: when we meet, do not turn away like an elephant king.
Chan Master Ganlu Shu of Yizhou (Eight Poems) The roots of the awakening tree do not take hold among the clouds of the mundane world;
its exquisite fruit relies entirely upon the winds of the true realm. Autumn rains and autumn gales scatter ten thousand [leaves].
All things grow lush and solitary within the palace of the Dharma King.

The awakening-flower, nurtured by grace, truly wafts with the fragrant breeze. Spring brings life to the tree of awakening, and the flowers of awakening bloom; who can fathom this fragrance of the ground of nature?
Consciousness: Rich and dense fragrances waft throughout the nine realms.
A single strike of the Dharma drum resounds loudly throughout the nine realms. Clouds rush and rain pours as all hasten to come; you must know this is no ordinary occurrence.
The resonance awakens the drunken eyes of gods and men;

the Dharma-banner stands tall within the true realm, its craftsmanship unfathomable. Pointing others who are lost toward liberation from the cage, how many heretical factions remain intent on destruction?
It destroys [defilements] and contests the indestructible merit of the Golden Man.

The true breeze of the kṣānti-grass nourishes the field of the mind with its grace; harmonious energy flows in abundance, and the kṣānti-grass flourishes. Though pressed by snow and battered by frost, it never [perishes].
Transformation: This lush green—ask not in what year it was planted.
The mind-jewel is without form, without thought, and without object; it is perfectly luminous and illuminates all, yet is not a mere emptiness. Even Li Lou’s keen vision finds no cause for reproach.
It is attained. As the faithful say, "The ears and eyes are clear and sharp. In the stillness of the pond, there are no forms;
it was not created by dredging or excavation. When the winds of sensory objects do not arise, it is naturally serene and clear. Vastly containing this brilliant purity is the sky of awakening.
The moon illuminates the great night of collective delusion;

the compassionate vessel lies all day long by the bank of the waters of craving. As the sails unfurl, one suddenly rejoices at the rising of a favorable breeze, yet the surging currents of the boundless, lost ford remain.
Crossing over, how could one refuse the vast and boundless journey?
By Yunju Shan Liaoyuan Foyin Chan Master (Four Poems):
Taming the Ox.
On the first day of learning how to herd cattle, man and ox exhaust their strength in contention; they prefer to wander off into the wild weeds rather than travel along the level path.

It is difficult to pull them back when the nose-rope is twisted, and the more one lashes the whip, the more the eyes turn away. Do not let them trample the crops; it is better to plow while the time is still right.
Suddenly turning his head, the dark expanse of his chest and waist gradually parts. Led by the wild flute as he leaves the pen, the evening song urges him home.
Seeing a fight, his passion remains fierce; encountering a herd, his gaze still lifts high. This is surely because the whip and tether remain; the state of his mind has grown increasingly like ashes.
How joyful that my whole body is white; I sleep peacefully upon the open ground. Body and mind are like earth and wood;

hearing and seeing are as if blind and deaf. A single cloud arises from the valley; it forms a mass and falls as snow into the sky. Pure and bright, there is no difference in color; I am now just like the common cattle.
Having been white, it has returned to black; I return this bull of yours to its own freedom. Let it roam at ease through the wild mountains, and for a thousand ages it shall have no more worries.
Majestic like the sun at the center of heaven, carefree like a drifting boat unmoored—transcending both the mundane and the sacred, who would dare to come forward and capture it?
Chanshi of Yuanming Temple in Anzhou (Four Poems) Universally illuminating both emptiness and existence, universally illuminating that which transcends both—wondrous essence is harmonious.
Within a single mind, there are hundreds of thousands of *sāhasra-lokadhātus*; for sentient beings who possess grasping, the truth returns.

Stagnant. Without thought and without seeking, matters remain unpenetrated; from the distant peaks, the green pines resound with clarity. Across the vast sky, the bright sun seals the void within emptiness.
Clearly revealed all alone—how can it be described? When spring arrives, the peach blossoms remain as red as ever.
The essence of transcendence and subtlety is pure;
the essence of transcendence and subtlety is the wondrous mind-source. This essence is凝然 (stagnant/immutable), its depths unfathomable; it is beyond form and name, outside the three realms.

It is identical with dust and identical with objects within the four modes of birth. Majestic and true, it is fundamentally not-existent; vast and profound, this dark void is originally— (Note: The provided text ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.)
Not empty. What does this single point of the spiritual source indicate? Last night, the night cypress gave rise to a pure breeze.
The fundamental limit is void and profound;
the fundamental limit is void and profound, wondrous beyond compare. Its application is boundless, its essence fully true. Perfectly luminous like the sun, it pervades all lands.

The realms are as pure as space, pervading the fields of form. Cranes cry out among the rocky pines to welcome the warm sun; Orioles sing at the mouth of the valley to bid farewell to the lingering spring.
When travelers arrive here, they should turn back their heads; There is no need to seek the source further or ask for the ford.

The fundamental tenets and essential meanings are rooted in both the principles and the branches; the profound significance is vast and far-reaching. A cold wind blows, severing the evening mist and clouds.

It is solely because the five natures are ultimately indistinguishable that the three vehicles appear to have differences. When lost in delusion, all are alike the moon within the clouds; only upon awakening does one truly believe with one's own eyes.
Central Flower. Although the paths of speech distinguish between delusion and awakening, the Dharma-realm is luminously one family.
Chan Master Ruixin of Jingshan in Runzhou (Four Poems).
Arising from Reality into Delusion.
The Dharmakāya leaves no trace throughout the three periods of time; these three periods, in turn, share its true nature.
A single thought suddenly arises within the true nature, like a fragment of cloud appearing to mark the vast void.

The extinction of delusion and the return to the True, and the arising of delusion from the True, have three conditions. In the gateway of the objective realm, the gateways are fundamentally quiescent; when the clouds vanish, one seeks them and finds neither inner nor outer.
How could one speak of wind and rain darkening the mountains and rivers?
Truth and falsehood are non-dual;

the great trichiliocosm is within a single bubble. When one contemplates the essence of the bubble, it is identical to the water. If the water were not the true void, there would be no myriad phenomena;
one must know that the myriad phenomena are themselves the true void.

When neither truth nor falsehood exists, the fault lies in universally hoping for a medicine; yet when the illness has vanished, do not marvel that the medicine was divine. Virtue and heaven, darkness and demons, Buddhas and non-Buddhists—all are the same.
How could truth and falsehood exist for one who possesses true wisdom?
Eulogy for Chan Master Ciyun of Jianmen Pass (One Poem) The treasure within the robe—
the treasure within the robe—
this treasure has followed me through kalpas, reaching every place I have gone. Today, its radiant light shines forth from within the robe.
Blazing and radiant, clearly manifesting the ancient Way, it is the treasury of true emptiness. Its light is brilliantly bright; this treasure abiding within is peerless in its excellence.
The Three Sages and Ten Holy Ones all share this same path; they clap their hands and proclaim it with one voice. The impoverished son recognizes the pearl within his drunken robe;
the dragon girl attains Buddhahood without aging. One should enjoy this and attain mastery; throughout the great chiliocosm of worlds, it is ever-present.
Obscured. At the crossroads, the old woman’s house: the radiance bursts forth from the tattered sack.
Chan Master Fǎhǎi Mínghuì of Fúzhōu (ten poems).
Delusion.
This matter remains, day after day, as if in a state of delusion; one casts doubt upon the eyebrows and face within the mirror.
Having wandered through the long thoroughfares until the frenzy finally subsides, the door is closed against the spring breeze in a time of silence.
Frivolous toil gives rise to turmoil, drowning the true nature; all day long one busies oneself, pursuing false causes.
At this time of wandering through the sea of existence, one further suspects that red dust rises from the Eastern Sea.
The mind dwells upon various views, yet the principle remains obscure; empty flowers fill the eyes, their branches unrevealed. The empty fruit is not yet realized and the mind does not cease;
one doubt is resolved only as another arises.
The faculty of consciousness discriminates among the various sensory objects; in darkness, it pursues the passing moments of time—do not be like this. What a marvelous state:
there is no place for entry at the crown of the head; the green mountains and flowing waters communicate in vain.

Feelings come and go, utterly unknown; how many times have I turned my head, enduring parting? After the cries of monkeys at the long bridge and the wild inn, with every passing autumn wind and every fall of rain.

When thoughts and suspicions stir in secret day and night, you have likely never known where you have been for a hundred years. Though the spring flowers have not yet been plucked, their fragrance still lingers;
pairs of butterflies circle the old branches.
The wisdom of wisdom shines bright through the ages, its spiritual penetration renowned; day after day, one forgets even the merit of decisive judgment. Heaven, earth, water, and clouds are all eyes;
from the pines and bamboos of the four gardens, a pure breeze arises.
Wisdom shines its light upon all, without distinction of high or low; herein there is not a single dharma that can cause delusion. Many thanks to the Lord of Spring for leaking this news:
throughout the garden, the spring colors are full and the partridges sing.

The faculty, object, and consciousness—these three—are all clearly perceived. When emptiness is thoroughly understood, even beyond emptiness there is nothing that is not so. Ten thousand li of the blue river, with mountains layered upon one another;
a single speck of cloud flies freely across the expanse.
Awakening after awakening, the ordinary mind is exhausted and all doubts are severed. How many people can truly know this mind? At that time, one simply thought the flower had been plucked away;
today, as before, its red blossoms fill the branches.
Chan Master En of Da Hong Shan in Suizhou (Four Poems) The sound of a withered tree like a dragon’s cry;
autumn fills the great earth. To offer even a slight response to the very first phrase— The old hermit of Shaolin laughs at this.
Speech: Listen quietly as the pine wind nods its head in the dark.
Form:

To the utmost of one’s vision, all is vast and silent, utterly beyond the reach of emotion. The dust-motes and lands of the ten directions are together clear and bright. Beneath the mountain of Stone City, there is no root.
Grass. Once spring comes, it turns green once more.
My ancestors sang the song of priceless incense;
this harmonization is not of today alone. Ten thousand varieties are gathered together within the *campaka* grove; nine refinements must be undergone.

This is the *pāramitā*. Its name and its reality transcend both truth and falsehood. In knowing and seeing, what gain or loss can there be? To speak of Ox-Head (*Gokhura*) is to describe the treasury of the elephant;

it is like the appearance of the *udumbara* flower or the *maitrībala*. Through skillful response, devas and humans attain perfect penetration; through right reception, spirits and ghosts achieve the Unsurpassed. How marvelous!
Precepts and meditative concentration are like incense and medicinal ointments; they bring benefit and joy to all living beings within the vastness of the *dharmadhātu*. For this purpose...
The clouds form a terrace that can be beheld; who can perceive the corresponding faculties and vessels? This song wondrously penetrates the Land of Fragrant Accumulation (*Gandhavyūha*).
To truly open the incense, one must sever delusions. When the gate of the treasury of virtue opens and the torch of wisdom blazes, the pure wind disperses—how could it have any limit?

A Ballad of Returning Home: Let one be free and unconstrained. Let one be free and unconstrained. Birth, old age, sickness, and death are already errors. The Five Constants and the Three Jewels refine the spirit;
the One Nature and the Six Faculties play with frivolity. When meeting conditions, life arises; desire is like a bond. All is nameless, unattached, and beyond measure.
One knows only that smoke-bands bind the void; one is unaware that radiance issues from the pavilions.
Resting where rest is found, acting where no action is made—thus following conditions, the mind is already at ease. On the single road back home, I inform others:
driving alone the white ox, free from ropes and traces, a boundless pure breeze arises in vast clarity; there is no need for heaven and earth to serve as a coffin.
Continued Lamp Record of the Jianzhong Jingguo Era, Volume Thirty (End).
Letters, Memorials, and the Succession of Transmissions are appended at the end of this volume.
Recorded by the monk Xishi, who received the purple robe for his studies.
A Letter to the Emperor,
dated the Fifteenth Day of the Seventh Month. Submitted respectfully by the Dharma-transmitting Chan Master Foguo, Abbot of Fayun Temple, Your Servant Weibai.
I submit this memorial at the risk of my life to Your Majesty, the Emperor. I have heard that Heaven and Earth are lofty and sublime, vast and profound;

it is by these qualities that they cover and sustain the myriad things. The sun and moon are radiant and bright, shining forth their light; it is by these qualities that they illuminate the myriad regions.

Confucius and Mencius took benevolence as their foundation and righteousness as their ancestor; thus they taught and nurtured the myriad customs. The Buddhas and Patriarchs exercised wisdom while harboring compassion; thus they awakened all that exists.
Among these four, there have been few throughout antiquity and the present who could equal their achievements.
We respectfully venerate Your Majesty, the Emperor: your virtue extends as far as heaven and earth, your brilliance surpasses that of the sun and moon, and your Way transcends...
Confucius and Mencius—whose natures were equal to those of the Buddhas and Patriarchs—personally inherited the great enterprise, and in a single day the whole world turned toward benevolence.

From the Confucians, Buddhists, Daoists, and the laity, down to plants, trees, birds, and fish, all were drenched by their vast grace and profound bounty. From antiquity until the present day, this has remained so.

There has never been anyone like Your Majesty who could equalize such merit. (Your servant) Zilin is but a blade of grass; yet within two years, I have thrice encountered Your Majesty’s edicts to propagate the spirit of our school.
This is truly a fortunate convergence of a thousand-year era. It is for this reason that (your servant) presses his hand to his breast and reflects...

How shall we repay [Your Majesty’s] kindness? (Your) servant Dingwai has observed in private that when Emperor Zhenzong ascended the throne and changed the era name to Jingde, the monk Daoyuan of Wuzhong compiled thirty fascicles of the essential sayings of the patriarchs of the Chan school and presented them to the Emperor.
By imperial decree, the Hanlin Academician Yang Yi composed the preface; thus it was titled the *Jingde Chuandeng Lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp from the Jingde Era).

I, Zhang Dunli, Marquis of Madou, together with [others], have generated sincere devotion and strictly prepared my own stipends.

I have carefully selected craftsmen in Hangzhou to carve the printing blocks and produce thirty volumes of the *Jianzhong Jingguo Xudeng Lu* (Continued Lamp Record of the Jianzhong Jingguo Era) and three volumes of its catalog.
I have placed the Imperial Preface at the beginning of the work and hereby submit it to Your Majesty for review.
A Memorial from Your Servant Dunli to the Emperor.
The Imperial Edict and the record of the successive stages of receiving the imperial favor are appended below. May these be circulated throughout the empire.

May all the merit and victory thus gathered serve to assist the Imperial Sovereignty and to pray for the Emperor’s sacred longevity, lasting forever through ten thousand years, infinite and inexhaustible, throughout the entire Dharma-realm.
Sentiments. May all equally partake of the primary cause of Prajñā and together attain the Vajra-Seed Wisdom.
Written on the tenth month of the first year of the Jianguo era, on the occasion of the Tianning Festival, by the subject Zhang Dunli, respectfully inscribed.
